text: This is NEWS & NOTES.  I'm Ed Gordon.

On today's Roundtable, a homeland security scare in the nation's capital      and a tax on fast food in Detroit, also putting the snipers, the DC      snipers, on trial once again.  Joining us from our bureau here in New      York, Bob Meadows, writer for People magazine.  Also with us, Bill      Rhoden, sports columnist of The New York Times.  And from Boston, Callie      Crossley joins us.  She's a social cultural commentator.  She can also be      seen weekly on the television show "Beat the Press."
All right.  Thanks for joining us, folks.

The whole nation saw it, a scare in Washington, DC, the White House,      Congress and other buildings surrounding that area evacuated, reminiscent      of, of course, the infamous day, 9/11.  We saw planes in the skies.      Fighter pilots going up, forcing a plane down.  First and foremost, Bill      Rhoden, when you heard this, what was your initial thought?

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: Oh, I was      actually watching it and it was surreal.  And it did bring back those      flashbacks of 9/11 because, you know, I'm in New York, I saw it.  But,      you know, the thing that I guess was a little disturbing was that again      it continues to feed into this whole `the sky is falling' syndrome.      `We're evacuating the building! Women and children first!'  And I think      that as a nation, we're so on edge and I think that this--it was just so      far away from breaking this cycle of sort of terrorism, that anything      could set us off.
Bob.

I guess what more was on my      mind was what was going through this pilot's mind who kept coming even as      he was given all these warnings and I guess he probably wasn't heeding      them.  I was happy to see that the F-16s were right on it.  They fired      warning shots.  This guy, he came within three miles of the White House,      but obviously he would have been shot down.  He would not have come any      further than that, but, of course, the image that really stuck in my mind      was when I heard later on that, well, you know, the president was out      biking which seemed somewhat appropriate for some reason.  I don't know      why.
I think that was...
That's because he's a fit president, right?  Go ahead, Callie.

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: Not fit to be president.

The thing that was scary for me is that I don't understand      how you can fly into the no-fly zone anymore.  I mean, I really don't      understand that.  This brings up so many questions for me about security      because if you can't protect this most important piece of landscape in a      very serious way, I don't understand...
What would you have them do, though, Callie?  Would you have      them shoot them down just as soon as they crossed that barrier?

No, no, no.  What I'm saying is--there's two things that I      want to say.  First of all, I would imagine that every pilot knows when      you file a flight plan--I don't care how small your plane is--you can't      fly in this arena.  So right away what's going on here that he was      allowed even to get into it because that should have been on the flight      plan.  And the minute that he started going astray, something should have      happened before we got to the point of having to evacuate folks.  I'm      glad to see they did use some restraint because, you know, as it turns      out it's some guy who didn't know what he was doing.  On the other hand,      it makes me a little nervous that we don't have something a      little--operating quicker to figure out this is hostile, this is not      hostile.  This is the most important piece of landscape we've got.

Well, Bill, pick up on that point, but I also think, too, a      great degree what I'm most alarmed about is what I hear from Callie, the      idea that when something like this happens, there is no fail-safe means      of protection in totality.

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: Yeah.  Well, I mean, I think if you listen to the air      traffic controllers that maybe they were trying to protect their, you      know, behinds. They were saying they were fairly sure that this was an      accident, this was not sort of the, you know, real deal.  And I guess you      could argue--I think in my heart of hearts, I believe that if they really      felt that this was a real threat, I'm not sure that it would have gotten      to that point.  I think that at some level people were convinced that      this was a guy going to North Carolina that had made an error and they      weren't going to blow him out of the sky for it.

But if that's the case then, you're evacuating buildings,      and by the way, the thing that really distresses me about this is that      Mayor Anthony Williams said his team, he and his team, were not alerted.      So there's half the people are being evacuated; the other half aren't.      The people in the Pentagon weren't.  I mean, this seems to be not as      tight as it ought to be for this very important piece of landscape.

Well--and to some degree, I guess this is one of those measures      that can be used as a tool to move forward because there are also reports      that in some portions of the White House, the alarms were not heard and      people did not evacuate because they did not know about it.  So again      it's a question of how safe can you be.

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: You know--and I think that's the great point.  I must      confess that, you know, on my level of alarm buttons, 10 being the      highest, this is kind of two.  And I guess after everything we've been      through, after, you know, being in New York for 9/11, after watching      nightly bombings in Iraq, you know, that's my focus.  You know...

That's actually one of the things, what you say, Bill, is      that there's so much else going on in the world right now--you have North      Korea, you have Afghanistan, you have what's going on in Iraq and the      still protesting in the West Bank and everything--that this incident did      not seem all that difficult and they were right on it.  They were...

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: Yeah.
...ready to shoot these people down if it got any--if it      reached that point.

Well, I think what this does show is just the precarious      position that the government, frankly, is placed in in terms of homeland      security and, frankly, the times we now live in and will continue to live      in unfortunately for some time.
All right.  Let's move our attention to the Motor City and that's      Detroit. And let me say now, 'cause Bill Rhoden--OK.  Pistons lost last      night.

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: Oh, thank you, Ed.  Thank you.  No, I...
Let's just get it out of the way...

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: That's right.  You've got it.
...talk about something important.  We will be back.  Let's talk      about something important...

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: That's important.

...and that is that Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick--and we all know that      Detroit is going through some woeful economic times--is putting this to      voters to approve a 2 percent fast-food tax on top of the already 6      percent state sales tax that's applied to restaurant meals in order to      gain more dollars to the coffers of Detroit.  Critics say the tax would      be unfair because it disproportionately burdens the poor and hampers      economic development in the city, they say.  I'm not sure how it would do      that, but the idea that you're taxing fast food.

I agree.  I mean, I'm all for it.  First of all, you know,      these kinds of taxes could be argued about whether or not this is really      effective economic policy, but that aside, it's fast food.  Lots of folks      with no money are going there.  We can argue about whether the food is      good or not. That's not the question.  I don't have as much problem if      you're taxing luxury items.  I mean, if you're going to slap some tax on      alcohol, if you're going to put something on higher-end restaurants--I      don't know how you do that--but I think on fast food, you really are      targeting the poor whether you intended to or not.

You know, I think Kwame faces, Detroit faces a $300 million      deficit.  This is in a city that has a vanishing population, that has      increasingly lower economic base, and honestly, what else is he going to      do? This tax is expected to bring in about $17 million which is also      probably a commentary on how much fast food is being eaten in the city      but that's another discussion.  He has to come up with some means to make      money.  As you said, Ed, Detroit already has all these different taxes,      income tax, property tax, taxes on the casinos.  The only way they can      make money is by raising taxes, and it seems to me that Kwame should be      doing just about anything he can short of putting it on his credit card      to bring in money for the city.  And I have to imagine this is going      to--the Whopper costs $2.50.  With this tax, it's going to be $2.55.  I      know people count their pennies.  I really, really know that, but I      really don't think this is going to be that arduous a tax.

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: And the fear of politicians--and Kwame's the ultimate      politician--you sort of follow the truth where it leads and you're      looking to get, you know, blood from whatever turnip you can squeeze it      from.  And, frankly, you know, when I first heard about this tax--I'm not      a fast-food guy--I thought, `Well, maybe this would, you know, given all      the problems that poor folk, black folk have with high cholesterol and      all that, maybe this could kind of steer them away from something to      their health.  That's not why he did it, you know?

Detroit was voted the fattest city in the country by Men's      Health last year, so I agree with you.  But I was reading that this one      girl said that, `No, me and my friends were actually probably going to go      to Bloomfield Hills now to get our McDonald's,' so I'm like...
Bloomfield Hills being the suburb of Detroit.
So it's not going to help them after all.

Let me ask this then before we move on and, Callie, you touched      on it.  It would seem to me politically--and you say he's a smart      politician, Bill Rhoden--if you are, it would seem to me that you would      do a dual introduction of tax when it goes to food.  One might look at      trying to tax meals across the board in the city of Detroit--so you do      the high-end restaurants and the executives from General Motors and Ford      and Chrysler and the like eat there--would also be hit by this tax in the      same way that disproportionately the poor will be hit by this tax at      Wendy's and McDonald's and Burger King.

I think that's the way I think it's unfair otherwise.  And      then one of you mentioned, `Well, he's already taxing the casinos.'  OK.      Well, put five more cents on the casinos.  Now we're really talking about      a luxury.  You have time to go gamble and you want to put your money      there, fine.  You know, I don't have a problem with that being taxed      more, but I think on this end as much as I don't think fast food is the      way to go particularly for our communities.  I just think it's an unfair      burden.

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: At the risk of being cynical, I'm wondering if the reason he      didn't do, Ed, the luxury food and that kind of thing is maybe he's      looking at his support base, you know, who can hurt him politically?

Well, truth be told, though, that support base in Detroit is      going to probably be for Kwame Kilpatrick to people, in fact, who are      going disproportionately to these fast-food restaurants if indeed he's as      smart of a politician as you say.  These are the people he's going to      have to generate to keep him in office.  We should note that this is an      election year for the mayor of Detroit.

All right.  Let's move our attention to Virginia, Maryland, Washington,      DC, area.  Once again--and this is raising the infamous names of John      Allen Muhammad and Lee Boyd Malvo, known as the DC snipers, already      sentenced to death the elder, Muhammad, in 2003 and the younger, Malvo,      is sentenced to life in prison without parole.  Now the other state,      Maryland, wants its try at these folks.  Our question here, Bob Meadows,      is:  Aren't we wasting money if, in fact, these gentlemen have been      convicted of these heinous crimes? They're already put away, one for      life, one to a death sentence.  Why bother doing it again?  Some have      suggested that this is a stopgap, a safety measure?

I have to say no, I don't think it's a waste of money.  The      relatives want this to happen.  They want these two gentlemen to answer      for the crimes and to answer for killing their brothers and sisters and      mothers and daughters.  This was a type of thing where I think people      perhaps need some closure.  Certainly they've already been sentenced to      life, and death for Muhammad, but maybe they're wondering maybe Malvo      will also get death perhaps in Maryland.  And I actually sort of relate      it to exhuming Emmett Till's body. The killers are dead, they've already      confessed, but people want closure.

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: And I guess the question is and, I guess, Ed, that's what      you were getting to:  What else can you do?  I mean, you know, somebody's      already going to be killed, you're going to kill them again, and, Ed, I      think you're absolutely right in that, yeah, I think this is for the      relatives.  One of the relatives is saying that, you know, `Well, at      least now they're going to answer for my son.'  And I guess if you put      yourself in that position is you've lost somebody, none of this is going      to bring anybody back.
Right.  Right.

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: It's going to open up another wound, but, you know, if this      is our way of getting closure, then, you know, so be it.
Callie.

When I first heard it, I thought, `This is really overkill      literally,' and then I thought to myself, `We've seen stranger things      happen where some law changes, somebody gets the ear of someone in power      at the time, and the convictions or the rulings about how long they      should be or whether they should be on death row get changed.'  And I      think this covers all bases, and particularly for those relatives who are      concerned, they don't want to look up one day and see that these guys got      out on a technicality.  And this way, they have two states in which they      would have to have some overturning of the convictions or some reducing      of the sentences.  So in this way, I think they have made certain that      all bases are covered.

Let's quickly go further south.  An interesting note from the      governor of South Carolina, Mark Sanford, who suggests that it will be a      long time before a black candidate is elected to a statewide office in      South Carolina.  The governor is a white Republican.  We should note that      he is suggesting that the only way for a black person to assume a      statewide office in the foreseeable future is to allow governors to      appoint some positions that are currently elected.  Some of those      positions are attorney general, secretary of State, education      superintendent and the like.  Now the cynical person may say that this      might be a means of this governor and other Republican governors being      able to, in fact, appoint people to these offices. Others will say that      this is simply someone telling the truth and saying to our nation once      again, `We aren't where we say we are by means of race.'

I think you can tell the truth and still be cynical.      Count me among the cynical.  It sounds as though he is moving toward      assessing more power, and, you know, good for him if he can come up with      a way of doing it, but I think the folks need to understand that's      exactly what's going on.

Absolutely.  I mean, right now, you have to agree with      that. It does sort of sound like a power grab, but it also--as Callie      just said it sounds--he's actually sort of telling the truth.  I mean,      you have--What?--Barack Obama.  You've had Doug Wilder.  You've had Gary      Locke out in Washington who's Asian, governor there.  You don't really      have too many people of color achieving statewide office.  So you almost      have to agree with him.

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: But I never want to see--not never, but I wouldn't want to      go to an appointment system.  You know, if we have to do more with voter      registration, whatever we have to do, I think that what this governor has      done is issued a challenge.  I mean, I see it as a challenge, and let's      accept the challenge.  Let's not just say, `Well, OK.  Let's go to an      appointment system.'
You know...

Interestingly enough, though, and pick up on your point, Bob,      but interestingly enough, there are those who were interviewed after the      fact in South Carolina.  Many African-American politicians at the time      who suggest that they agree.

Absolutely.  That's definitely--they did agree as I think      we all do, too.  One of the things I noticed is that blacks tend to be      Democrats. As you can see from the makeup of Congress and the Senate and      the president, white Democrats are having difficulty being elected to      statewide offices.  So it's going to be even more difficult I think when      you have a black person trying to run in that same party.

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: But that--but, yeah, let's just be clear, though, that not      everybody agreed with this.
No.  No.  I know that.
Right.

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: I mean, you had--and I think that's very important.  You had      Fletcher Smith, the representative, who said that it's unfortunate that      after all we've been through, after all the people, you know, who have      died and all that, that you've got a governor saying, `Well, blacks will      never be elected to statewide office.'

Right.  But what he also did not say in that is that he      disagreed. He said it's unfortunate and that the governor said all that      but he didn't necessarily disagree that that was the case.  Callie, you      want to wrap up with about a minute to go.

Yes, I just wanted to point out that while we mention      Barack Obama and his victory that for most of the time in the early days      folks thought this was not something he could achieve, and so that even      in a tough situation, it doesn't mean it can't turn around.  It just      means, you know, folks have to work a little harder to do some of the      kinds of things that we've already articulated here with the voter      registration, with making people understand how important this is and      also with messaging so that it reaches across party lines if necessary      and certainly across all kinds of constituencies.

Well, an interesting case study will be the state of Maryland      with Kweisi Mfume, and he, in fact, may have an African-American running      on the Republican side for that Senate seat statewide.  So we'll see what      happens there.
Bob Meadows, Bill Rhoden, Callie Crossley, thanks very much for joining      us. Greatly appreciate it.

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: You're welcome.  Thank you.
All right.
Thank you.
Go Pistons.
All right.

speaker_label: Mr. BILL RHODEN (Sports Columnist, The New York Times)
text: All right.
Coming up, Wanda Sykes on the virtues and pitfalls of being loud      and blunt.
You're listening to NEWS & NOTES from NPR News.
This is NEWS & NOTES.  I'm Ed Gordon.

On today's Roundtable, filibuster love:  Is it all over?; a review of      what we just talked about in segment A; Donald Rumsfeld being sued; and a      teacher's essay goes awry.  Joining us from our New York bureau is Bob      Meadows, writer with People magazine.  Dawn Turner Trice, columnist for      the Chicago Tribune, is at our bureau in Chicago.  And George Curry,      editor in chief of the National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service, comes to us this day from Maryland.

All right, folks, before we get into some of the other issues, we wanted      to go back to what we just heard in segment A, and that's this question      of foster children being used for experimental drugs to try to eradicate      the scourge of HIV and AIDS during the late '80s and early '90s, the AP      report bringing out the fact that, in some states, it was required for      these kids to have advocates, overseers, if you will, and that wasn't      done.  And it also raised the question as to whether or not these kids      were being taken advantage of, because, obviously, they do not have the      same type of muscle, if you will, a lesser voice than most in society,      unfortunately.  Bob, as you listened to the segment, what were your      thoughts?

My thoughts were that--I was thinking      back to that time, and I remember that AIDS had caused a great hysteria,      for valid reason, and that was, of course, the context that we have to      look at this. But I think the worst thing about it was that these      children had no advocates speaking for them.  That's really the thing.  I      understand that tests are necessary.  I just did a story, in fact, on      doctors going to Ethiopia and needing to test AZT drugs on children,      teaching the doctors there how to use AZT drugs, because you can't use      the same dosage for a child as you can use for an adult.  Definitely      understand that.  But these children needed to have advocates to give      that permission, to speak for them.

Dawn, what of Dr. Kline's response with the idea that--and let's      take a state like Texas, as he suggested, that did not have, at least on      a federal level and in that case on a state level, the law that suggested      that they had to have advocates, that these kids, many of them      disproportionately poor, disproportionately minority, were now given an      opportunity, a better chance, if you will, if these drugs worked, to live      out a longer and a better-quality life because they were engaged in this      study?

I think that that's definitely      a benefit of the study, but I think it does not take away from the fact      that the trials may not perfectly parallel the Tuskegee experiment that      you guys talked about earlier, but the overall fallout could be the same.      This type of thing doesn't engender trust among African-Americans or      minorities in the health-care system, and I think that, while it may have      helped a number of young people, I think overall the fallout can be a      negative one.
George?

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: I think we have to be careful.  First of all, we need to      clarify about the Tuskegee study.  The Tuskegee study did not inject      people with syphilis.  What it did was allow people to go untreated.
To die.  Yes.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: So we have to be careful about that.  Secondly, we're talking      about kids who were already infected with HIV, and this was not a case      where they used placebo; that is, you know, water, fake stuff that's not      going to be--I mean, they were dealing directly with what became known as      AZT, which is very, very important.  So I think it's crucial that      HIV-affected kids be involved in trials.  The problem is, and the only      problem as far as I'm concerned, the lack of having a medical advocate      there.  And what we have is a patchwork of state policies, so they differ      from state to state.  We need a federal policy to make sure that each of      these kids have medical advocates. But as far as involving them in these      trials, I think that's excellent, but their interests have to be      protected.

I'm glad to know, as the second doctor said--because I was      concerned about this--that most of the children, I believe he said, are      alive today because they had access to these trials.  As was pointed out,      these are children who are already infected with HIV or AIDS, so they did      need treatment.

All right.  Let's move on to a subject that seems ongoing, like      the Energizer Bunny; this from Senator George Allen, a Republican of      Virginia.  He says, `The honeymoon is over,' and he simply means what we      saw earlier in the week, the idea of these centrists in the Senate coming      together to stop the proposed filibuster as relates to the judges--we can      now see the blocking, in many people's minds, of the vote for Mr. Bolton      to be UN ambassador.  Now we're going to wait until the holiday is over      and we're going to see if cooler heads prevail.  And here is a man who,      clearly, the White House is behind, and they say, `This is our man.'      Democrats are saying, `No, we don't want him.' George Curry, what      happened to the honeymoon?

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: Well, wasn't never a honeymoon because there was never      agreement. First of all, let's be careful.  Now these issue are not the      same issues as judges, and that's what people want to mesh and pretend      that they're the same. The real issue, and the only reason the Democrats      are filibustering now, is because they have requested certain documents      from the White House and the White House has refused to turn them over to      Congress, saying, `You have what you need.'  And that's the tension we      have here.  And the Democrats are doing this only because they don't want      to be just rolled over by Republicans, which they're being done anyway,      but they're saying, `Look, either you give us the documents we request,      or we going to filibuster this.'

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: Now the real issue here is you have a major tug-of-war between the      executive and the legislative branches of government where the White      House is gaining more power, and they're using this to do this, and      Congress must assert itself--at least, that's what the Democrats are      saying--even though the Republicans have the votes.

Dawn, a number of people are going to counter what George says      and simply say that's splitting hairs.  This is the language that Harry      Reid, Joe Biden and others are using but, indeed, they are trying to      filibuster this vote, that they don't really care about this information,      that they know enough about Mr. Bolton to make a decision and they want      to see this up-and-down vote.

Well, that's exactly what they're doing, but I think that      it's the right thing to do in this case.  Bolton is not the best      candidate to head the United Nations.  He's a man who, by many accounts,      is a bit of a tyrant when handling his subordinates, and he's accused of      aggressively interpreting intelligence to argue that nations are more      dangerous than they are.  The stall vote just comes at a time when      Republicans and Democrats are trying to make nicey-nice on this whole      issue, but that's exactly what's going on.
Bob Meadows...
It is a stall, and it's a legitimate stall.

Bob Meadows, there are people who are going to disagree with      Dawn there and who are going to say that Mr. Bolton is exactly the man      that is needed to push the doldrums out of the United Nations and get      them to face reality.  That being said, is this not just the way of the      world, the political world, and Washington as we know it?

I love it, Ed.  I love it.  The Democrats, coming right      back--you know, you think you got peace, but no.  The Democrats, they      took a lot of heat--so did the Republicans--for that deal they brokered      last week. This is an opportunity, perhaps, for the Democrats to kind of      show a little backbone.  But the thing that I love even more is that      Senator Thune, the Republican from South Dakota, says he's going to      probably vote against confirmation of Bolton, too, partly because he      doesn't think Bolton's the best man, but also because the administration      is including an Air Force base in his territory as the ones they're going      to close down.  So he's playing politics, too.  Everybody is.  That's the      name of the game.
That's the name of the game.  George...

And it's such a partisan time right now.  If you--you have a      senator from Ohio, Voinovich, who is also the Republican who's going to      go against--who has said that he's going to vote against Bolton.  And I      think that you really have to take note when there's somebody on either      side who's going to step outside of the--go against the party line.

But that being said, George Curry, the reality is, unless they      just continue--and I guess here's the argument for the filibuster--John      Bolton will probably be nominated.  He probably has--well, not probably;      they do have the votes to put him over the top.  A lot of people say this      is the quagmire, the conundrum, that people get tired of in Washington      and why we don't see positive movement, more positive movement, from      politicians.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: There's no question that--and you look at the latest polls;      the public is absolutely disgusted with this whole action even over the      filibuster.  But I agree that Bolton will get confirmed after the break,      but there's still the issue--and I don't want to underestimate it.  There      is an issue of whether a White House can decide what it turns over to      Congress.  And that's what's at issue here.
And you truly believe that to be the bigger issue?

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: Yeah, because, see, this is not something you want--I don't      think Democrats really want--I mean, this is not something you want to      fight over. Bolton's going to get confirmed.  The real fight is over the      judges, and the reason there are big fights now is because they're      getting ready for the Supreme Court showdown.  It's `throw down in the      showdown.'  That's the real issue, and that's what all the maneuvering's      about.

And, George, what of the idea--and I brought this up with      Professor Ogletree just the other day on the Roundtable--part of that is      not as many people are looking at Chief Justice Rehnquist and his      inevitable move out, and if Scalia moves up, as many people are      suggesting, replacing a conservative there, it really is the swing      seats--i.e., one person that's being looked at as a possible out is      Sandra Day O'Connor.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: Right.  The issue is, they replace a conservative with a      conservative, the vote will still be the same.  It would be that second      nominee which would really make a difference.  And I know Ogletree had      mentioned Justice Scalia, but it's still between Scalia and Clarence      Thomas. Don't throw up.  It's still between both of them as to who will      be the next chief justice.
All right.  We can put some money down on that one, but that's a      later time.

Let's take a look at what's happening in a 150-year-old Washington      retirement home.  It's a veterans' home.  There are inhabitants there who      are suing the US Defense secretary over budget cuts that they say have      harmed the medical care standards in that home.  They say they are      putting their health in danger.  It is a home that--we are now seeing      on-site pharmacies.  Treatment rooms have been closed.  X-ray facilities      and others have been removed; the number of dentists on site reduced.      Their contention is this is happening because of all of the monies that      are being spent on the war; therefore, other areas are being cut.  The      government, while not dealing with this specifically, is suggesting that      there is confusion because there are other primary care services ahead      when they open a new clinic in July.  It is just interesting, Dawn, to      see veterans of previous wars, who typically stand in gale winds when you      talk about the military, suing the secretary of Defense and also the      home's chief operating officer, among others.

Absolutely.  And the suit may be largely symbolic, but the      reality is that there are 26 million veterans in this country.  About 30      percent of them are disabled, many requiring some form of long-term      medical care.  And we send these men and women off to protect this      country, and then when they return, we have very little to offer them in      terms of medical care.  And I think it's a shame.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: What's interesting about here is you're talking about people      who really have devoted a lot of time to this country.  One, they must      have served in a war zone; they must have been in service at least 20      years, active service; they're all over 60 years old; and they're unable      to make a living, whether it's service-related or not.  I mean, this is a      vulnerable population.
Yeah, those are the requirements to get into this home.
...(Unintelligible).  Yeah.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: Yes.  So this is a very extremely vulnerable population, and      this really should be an embarrassment to this country that we're not      taking care of these veterans.

I looked at it very similarly.  This is the way we treat      our poor people who did not serve in the military.  Their benefits are      cut.  They don't understand what's going on.  A lot of people blame the      war for all this, for the budget cuts, and as George has indicated, these      are people who really served their country and should be getting the      support, but they're not.

All right.  Let's quickly move to Louisiana.  Fun time down in      the hot state of Louisiana; a public schoolteacher there is fed up with      his students' behavior.  He found a way to berate them.  He wrote a      two-page essay to his fourth-grade students saying that he hated his job      and he blasted the children's behavior as animalistic and even identified      some of them by name. And then he turned around and suggested that the      students write a 200-word essay on how the teacher should treat them.      Now before we get into some specifics here, Bob, when you first heard      this, what's your thought?
I was reminded of--OK, I was a bad kid.  I was reminded of      making teachers so upset, me and my classmates, that they--they didn't      put it on paper, though.  See, that's the difference.
Right.
They would say stuff like this to--I honestly thought this      guy had a really bad day.  That's what I--you know, he talked about the      root canal that he had.
Yeah, he said he had a root canal...
Right.
...and didn't have sleep before, that night.
I thought, `Man!'  You know, I could understand.  I could      understand his point of view, based on what teachers told me a long time      ago.
Dawn?
And you also felt that if he found it therapeutic to write      something down, maybe he should have just written it and then chewed it      up...
Sure.

...as opposed to passing this out.  I mean, it just didn't      make sense.  And I got the feeling that he probably said what a lot of      teachers across the country feel, want to say, almost every day.      But--and providing that this isn't the guy--this isn't a guy who's just      kicking his cat every morning and really hates the job.  I mean, he may      need to quit, but it sounds like he had a really, really bad day.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: What he had was a really, really bad lesson plan, and he      needs to go in the corner and stand on one foot until he gets himself      together.  I like the idea of the interactivity, though.  I mean, I kind      of like that idea of the students being forced to write something, but      that, I don't think, is the right approach.

What of the thought, though, here that there is--and maybe we're      missing the bigger picture here.  There is a sense, an environment in      many schools, that this is what goes on, on an everyday basis--the      occurrence of unruly students, the occurrence of an inability to truly      set an environment that's conducive to learning.  You know, we laugh at      this and we feel bad for this teacher, but the reality is this is more      typical than we'd like to believe.
Well, you know, we discussed on here...
But I think that what happened...

...a few weeks ago about the kid--the teacher--I believe it      was in Queens or Brooklyn--who called the kids animals, the Haitian kids,      and made them eat on the floor.  This is something that goes on all the      time, and what you could really--what I really looked at with this      teacher was he was trying to have a spelling bee, which is a fun thing,      and he said the kids were just so bad...
Unless you can't spell.
Unless you can't spell--right.  And, you know, he was      trying to do a fun thing for the kids, and he was like, `They're just so      unruly, they mess up everything.'
Yeah.  Yeah.
And I think that...
Since we're telling the truth, I was one of those kids who took      the early seat.  `The:  T--oh, shoot.'
And the teachers...
Go ahead, Dawn.

...are being asked to parent as well as teach in a lot of      cases--not all cases, but in a lot of them.  And I think that that's      fortunate.  I mean, as a parent of a fourth-grader, who's soon to be a      fifth-grader, I can't tell you how many warnings that we've had, just so      many challenges.  But by the time I drop this child off, what I tell her      is, `I love you.  Have a great day.'  But what I want to say, what I'm      thinking is, `You know, you better get out of this car.  You know, go      on.'  So I think that it's just a trying time across the board.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: I think many of us are removed--and I'm the first to admit      that I'm one of them--in terms of what's really happening in these      classrooms.  My youngest sister's a teacher in Tuskegee, Alabama, and      we're talking about the kid, five-year-old, being handcuffed.  She said,      `Hey, I understand it.  Come get some of mine.'  And I was shocked.
Right.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: So I think we really don't know what's going on in the      classroom.

Yeah.  I think that we talk a lot when we talk about, you know,      that children are our future, our most precious resources, but I think      that's a lot of--well, you know what I think it's a lot of.
Baloney.  Baloney.  Baloney.  Baloney.
Baloney.
Let's say baloney.

Because there are tremendous problems going on in our schools,      not just in behavior but, as we've talked about before, lack of books,      lack of opportunity, lack of everything that one needs to have a formal      education. And it's difficult.  I think we really have to start looking      at that.
All right.  Enough of my preaching.  Bob Meadows, Dawn Turner Trice and      George Curry, thank you all for being with us today.  Enjoy your holiday.
You're very welcome.
George...

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: All right.  You, too, Ed.
You, too.
Not too much eating, man.  Be careful.

This is NEWS & NOTES.  I'm Ed Gordon.

On today's Roundtable, the latest on the NAACP, and a man sues for the      right to be drunk.  From our New York bureau, Bob Meadows, a writer with      People magazine, and E.R. Schipp, a columnist at the New York Daily News;      also with us, Glenn Loury, professor of economics at Boston University.      He joins us from member station WBUR in Boston.

All right, folks, let's get right into the NAACP.  They are meeting this      week in Milwaukee to talk about a number of things, but most      interestingly, Julian Bond is once again railing against the president.      He suggests that the president likes to talk the talk, but doesn't like      to walk the walk.  That's what he told members at the annual convention      this week.  He also chided the president, saying, `Mr. President, we're      extending the invitation a year in advance.  We want to see you with us,'      and he's talking about next year, when the NAACP will meet in Washington,      DC.  Those of you will remember that Julian Bond attacked the president a      few months back and the IRS was looking into the NAACP's status as a      non-profit, so some will suggest that, perhaps, Julian Bond did not learn      a lesson many believe the White House was trying to teach him.  Bob      Meadows, what's your thought here?

So many, Ed.  You know, I covered the      NAACP for years, and I'm really glad to see them back in the news.  I'm      thinking that the NAACP--this--they might be in for their most public      contentiousness since Ben Chavis, because while you have Julian Bond      making these claims, he seems to give the same speech, as you said, like      every few months, every year or so.  Bruce Gordon, the new executive      director, he wants to reach out.  He's actually saying he wants to reach      out to the Bush administration, get friendlier ties with them.  And I'm      wondering, as people have wondered for years--Bruce Gordon does not come      from the typical NAACP background for their leadership, and there's a      wonder:  Will the members of the NAACP actually follow what Bruce Gordon      wants to do?  The way Julian Bond is speaking, I question it.

Ms. E.R. SCHIPP (New York Daily News):  You know, I have known Julian      Bond for years.  When I was a big Afro-haired University of      Georgia--thought of myself as a radical girl, I asked him to become my      campaign manager when I ran for president of the United States of      America.  That's a long time ago.  But I have to say that I have long      thought the NAACP was kind of stuck in the mud. I don't know Bruce      Gordon, but it may be a desperation move to pick someone like him, who's      so different from all the previous leaders, but it also could be an      inspired move.  And whether the rank and file follow suit, I don't know,      but it may bring in new people.  And I think if the NAACP is going to be      around and be relevant, it needs to bring in newer people.  I ha--I'm not      a lifelong member of the NAACP; I've never thought I wanted to join the      NAACP, because they always seemed a little bit too irrelevant to what I      thought needed to be acted upon.

Let me ask this, Glenn, and you can pick up here on your      thoughts as well.  But with the president once again declining the      invitation of the NAACP to speak--and before, we should note that the      White House and the president suggested why would you go speak to what he      characterized as a hostile group? He believed that the NAACP, at least      the powers that be in the NAACP, were hostile toward him.  And, of      course, after that, he did have a meeting with Kweisi Mfume before he      stepped away.  But we should also note that the NAACP invited Mexican      President Vicente Fox to come down and speak to the group after his      controversial comments that we've covered on this program.  He, too,      declined two invitations to attend the convention.  Does this speak to      the power, or lack thereof, of this group in terms of being a muscle      force that people have to deal with?

Absolutely.  I mean, you      know, how many troops has got the NAACP?  I mean, I don't--I wish the      NAACP well.  I think it would be very important for the NAACP and for      many black institutions to think seriously about redefining their mission      in the, you know, current situation.  But the fact is that they're not      exactly an important movement or institution within what is now a      minority political--you know, political orientation.  Now the president      and his party are building power across the board.  Why would you go and      talk to the NAACP?

But you know how they're doing it, though?  They're doing it      through going to some of the institutions that are more closely connected      to local communities.  They're going through churches, for example.
They're going around the black leadership.
They're going around the...
Absolutely.
...self-appointed, in many cases, black leadership, or the      press-appointed...
But we wouldn't have George Bush if...
...black leadership.

I mean, anyone that George Bush talks to is going to be de      facto black leadership.  Are we going to let George W. Bush decide who      are the black people we're talking to and we're hearing from in this      country?
No, but we can show up at the meeting.
Well, but isn't it easy...
But critics for years...

...for us to criticize?  And it seems to me that there are a lot      of African-Americans who criticize groups like the NAACP, the National      Urban League and the like, yet when the--when individuals get in trouble      or groups get in trouble, they do look to these organizations and, quite      frankly, many of those who criticize either have not joined these      organizations or are doing very little on their own to change the state      of black America.
Well, you know, Ed...
That certainly wouldn't be true of me.

...it's sort of like with the police.  You know, the police      get criticized a lot as well, but yeah, when somebody robs your house,      that's who you call.  One of the things--you know, for years, the NAACP      has been--the critics say it's adrift, you know; it doesn't have a focus      or anything.  The NAACP made its bones on legal cases, on legal      battles--housing discrimination, job discrimination, etc.  A way for the      NAACP to really get back in the mix is by going back to those roots.  We      have a lot of legal cases coming up right now.  The Supreme Court      just--we just lost O'Connor; Rehnquist might be going out.  There are a      lot of things that the NAACP could be tackling right now, and I think      that's where it needs to regain its focus.

Let me just add one thing.  I mean, I think that we have to      get beyond race.  I--with great due respect, I think the problem for the      NAACP and like organization is to translate the historical claim of      blacks, which has come out of civil rights, into a universal, progressive      claim to be a part of the rebuilding of the Democratic Party and the      rebuilding of a, you know, center-left kind of politics in the United      States.  We got to be talking about--what about the Mexicans?  Now do      they take part...
Glen, is it realistic to assume...
Let me just finish this point, Ed.
Is it realistic to assume--but let me interject here.  Is it      realistic to assume that you can get away from race when the country      doesn't?
Well, why can the country get away from it if we're not      getting away from it, is kind of, I think, what you're saying, Professor      Loury.

It's a transition.  I'm saying coalitions have to be built.      I'm saying people have to be looking down the line.  We need to be      moving from the historical civil rights orientation into something else,      and the something else, presumably, will span racial bounds, and that the      responsibility of the NAACP now is to manage this kind of transition.

You know what?  One of the things I often tell my students      is that the words `civil rights' are not synonymous with black people's      rights. Civil rights applies to all of us.  That's what the first 10      amendments to the Constitution were kind of trying to deal with.  All of      us, supposedly, have these rights, and if somehow the NAACP and other      organizations can communicate that, I think that will help us to get down      this road that you're talking about, Dr. Loury.
All right.  Let me bring up the...
I don't think the NAACP, though, can be a catch-all for      everyone.  And also...
Why not?
Because you're extending yourself too thin if you're going      to...
What...
...do everything for everybody.  Again, I real...
Well, what are the things they're doing?
The N--like I say...
Everybody needs good housing.  Everybody needs good health.      Everybody--so what's the problem?
Certainly.  Certainly.  I agree with that completely.  But      I just don't believe that you can encompass every single person.  You      have to have a focus, and that's what they lack.
The focus should be the issue, though, not the color of the      skin of the person.
All right.
Hoo-wee!
OK.  Look...
Hey, if noth...
As blacks we agree to disagree.  That's all right, though.
If nothing--yeah.  If nothing else, this may show how far      African-Americans have come in the fact that we're having this discussion      and this deviation of thought here.

Something interesting came out of one of the local papers in Milwaukee      based on, obviously, the NAACP being there and the convention.  One of      the papers talked to local leadership, civil rights leaders within the      city of Milwaukee. One of the interesting points that one old-school      local leader suggested that--is that we have seen a shift, quite frankly,      in what African-Americans and the community needs to look at by virtue of      what's "holding us back," quote, end quote.  His suggestion was, in the      old days, it was a legalized system of segregation, but today the      African-American population is being destroyed by its own youth.  He      called it an enemy from within.  I'm curious, Glenn Loury, what you think      when you hear of this.  Quite frankly, this is talked about, ofttimes      behind closed doors, that we are now our own worst enemy.

Well, you know, we've been at this for a long time.  I      actually wrote a piece in The Washington Post 20 years ago, literally,      with the title: Blacks Must Now Confront the Enemy Within.  And I'm not      saying that to pat myself on the back, just to say this is a--this has      been going on for a long time.  Bill Cosby is now going around doing what      he's doing.  I mean, yeah, it's true.  We do have some serious problems.      I don't much like this metaphor `the enemy within,' because, of course,      our children are not the enemy.  I mean, that's obviously wrong.      Moreover, whatever the nature of those problems, there still remain      public, civic and political issues, like what do police do when they have      the capacity to use violent force on people, like what are the programs      and the institutions that we have to take care of people who are      destitute or who don't have opportunity, like why schools don't function,      etc., etc., etc.?  And those are public questions.  They don't have to do      with enemies within.
So, you know, yeah, duly noted, there are some problems with      African-American youth, but let's keep our thinking straight about what      the political and public questions are here.
Well, let's get that...

E.R. Schipp, historically--let me ask you this.      Historically--and this is no different, perhaps, than what we saw in the      past, but I'm curious, your thought here.  We have often seen local      leaders, like this gentleman in Milwaukee, be more apt to say      controversial statements or statements that some will say will get to the      crux of the matter, vs. national leaders who may believe that that is too      incendiary to say in public and perhaps too politically incorrect.  Is      that part of the problem, that we're not seeing our, quote, "national      leadership," get up, stand up and really be willing to look in the      mirror?

I can say yes on that, but I also have to go back to what we      talked about before:  Who are the national leaders and who picks the      national leaders and all of that?  One thing about this particular issue      that comes to mind is that some of the particularly local leaders who are      familiar with what's going on in their communities are quick to jump on      white people doing something against black people.  But--and that's      important, as Dr. Loury just said--we have to focus on the public policy      aspects of some of that.  But at the same time, you don't hear them      speaking, whether publicly or quietly, to the people who are doing      something wrong.

I think about that Howard Beach--the most recent Howard Beach incident.      Three young black men were set upon by some white guys.  The story then      became that white guys were beating up black guys.  The message that was      lost was that the black guys, apparently, according to the reports, were      there to steal a car. So yes, you don't want the message to be that black      people can't go into any neighborhood they want to be in, but you can't,      at the same time, not hold the black folks accountable for what they were      doing wrong.

So in that sense, I applaud this man in Milwaukee talking about the enemy      within, whether or not we agree with the phrase.  He is focusing on      something that we know is true.  There are people, young, sometimes not      so young, who are doing wrong, and we don't hold them accountable.

All right.  Let me get to something very quickly, with about      three minutes left, and it's something we spoke of yesterday on this      Roundtable, but subsequently, we saw the White House really have to put      up and circle the wagons yesterday.  Spokesperson Scott McClellan was      stonewalled with questions about Karl Rove's alleged involvement in the      leaking of the CIA operative, and the story obviously later became part      and parcel of two reporters facing jail time for not revealing their      sources.  We've dealt with that quite a bit, but, Bob Meadows, I'm      curious what your thought is of the fact that the White House for some      time denied the fact, adamantly, quite frankly, that Karl Rove was the      leak when asked, and now their suggestion is that he's done nothing      wrong, and they're trying to obviously jump over these questions as      quickly as they're coming.

Bush said he would fire whoever the leak was.  Last time I      checked, Karl Rove still has a job.  Those two things are kind of a      contradiction, I believe, not that I'm surprised.  Bush very well may not      have known that Karl Rove was the leak, I'll give him that much.  But      once he found out, after he's been saying this for two years, that he      would fire the leaker, he should fire the leaker.
But he needs Karl Rove as his political strategist.
True.
So now he's challenged to see which is more important.      Maybe Karl Rove will lose his job at the White House, but still be his      political strategist in whatever endeavors the GOP needs him.

Glenn Loury, does the president have to do something if, in      fact, we hear definitively from Karl Rove that `Yes, I am the person who      made this suggestion'?  And we should note that there's some      hair-splitting as to whether or not he said the name exactly, etc., etc.,      but...
Whether `is' means `is' and `are' means `are.'
Exactly.
So that being said...
I don't know...

...will this president have to do something?  Will he have to      hold, as Bob Meadows suggests, to his word?  And we saw the president      adamantly come out and say, you know, `I hate leaks.  This was wrong.      When we find out who it is, they're gone.'
Well, Ed, I have to tell you, it's a Washington story, and      I'm up here in Boston, you know.  I mean, seriously...
That's the point, Dr. Loury.  It really is a Washington      story.

It's--you know, I mean, we've seen this before.  Obviously,      it's a fire that they're going to have to put out at the White House.      You know, I don't know all the facts, but, you know, from the...
Well, forget the facts.  Forget that it's a Washington story.      Forget that you're in Boston.  Here's the question.  He said...
The answer is no.  The answer to your question, in my      opinion, is no.
OK.  There you go.
He does not have to fire Karl Rove because he is George W.      Bush.  He's the man in town.  And if he doesn't fire him, people will      squeal for a week or two and that'll be the end of that.

But you know what?  I know you've covered this story before,      and--but it still seems to me it's so convoluted that most people don't      even get it.  I think what people need to know from this whole business      is that the First Amendment rights that all of us think we have are being      trampled upon, and that two people--actually, one person right now--is in      jail for not having written a story about somebody she talked to who      leaked information to somebody else...
Right.
...and now we got this whole convoluted thing going on.  But      the whole point is, all of us who know what the First Amendment is      supposed to guarantee...
Right.
...should be worried that this White House, in particular,      is circumventing the First Amendment.
All right.  And that would be Judith Miller of The New York      Times, a reporter.
Judith Miller of The New York Times.
Right.  All right.
And it wouldn't be for the first time...
Real quick.
...that they have done so.
OK.  Bob Meadows, E.R. Schipp, Glenn Loury, we thank you very      much for joining us for today's Roundtable.  Greatly appreciate it.
Thank you.
Thank you.
