Today on a special one-topic Roundtable, President Bill Clinton's legacy      and enduring relationship with the black community.  Joining us here at      WCLK in Atlanta, Bob Meadows, writer for People magazine.  Eric Deggans,      columnist for the St. Petersburg Times, joins us from St. Petersburg,      Florida.  And Mary Frances Berry at the University of Pennsylvania and      former chair of the US Commission on Civil Rights, joins us from      Washington, DC.  We should note that was an appointment by former      President Bill Clinton.

Mary Frances Berry, let me start with you, since you have a personal      relationship with this man.  Talk to me, if you will, about why--I asked      him this question--why you believe much of black America has such a close      and enduring and endearing relationship with this man?

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: You can't      help liking Bill Clinton, unless you just made up your mind before you      ever saw him that you were going to hate him.  You can't help liking him,      because he engages people.  It's the voice.  It's the moves.  It's the      way he looks at people, without looking around to see who else is there      before he focuses on them.  It's the warm approach he has to      African-Americans, the people he calls friends.  It's social skills.      It's the personal thing.  I used to say to people at the end of the      Clinton administration that I'd been to the White House so many times      that every time they invited me, I'd say, `Oh, do I have to go over there      again?' because you were always over there.  There was always something.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: I mean, there were always black people in and out of there and his ease      with them, so it's the personal thing that people see not just in the      black community, but other people, but that's what--that he understands      you, that he likes black people, he's comfortable with black people, and      he said, you know, after Toni Morrison said it, that he, you know, was      the first black president, jokingly.  He even tries to walk like black      guys sort of walk on the street. I don't know how to explain it on the      radio, but those of you who know what I mean...

Well, I think those people can get that picture in their minds,      exactly.  Bob Meadows, let me ask you this, though, and Reverend Sharpton      intimated this to a degree, did not say this--I want to stress that--but      there will be some who will say at the end of the day and at the end of      the administration, that is really all that black folk got from Bill      Clinton, to a great degree, as a whole, is a good feeling, a guy that      liked them, that appeared on "Arsenio Hall," but in the grand scheme of      things, didn't do a whole lot more than most.

I think that that is true.  I mean,      that is always what we always come up against, with the problem with the      Democratic Party, is that we always say, `Well, they just take us for      granted.'  But one of the things that Clinton had in his favor was when      he was president, the economy of this country just took off, and black      people were swept up in that. Now sure, we still lag behind white people      in every single category, but we improved so much, I believe, and plus,      what Clinton did was he brought a sense of inclusion.  I personally      remember that when he had his first inaugural and Maya Angelou made her      poem, it was honestly the first time I ever felt like I was actually a      part of this government.

Eric Deggans, let me ask you this; in talking about inclusion in      the Clinton administration, he used to boast the idea that his Cabinet      looked like America.  He talked about his close relationship with Ron      Brown and Alexis Herman...

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Vernon Jordan.
...and others.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Vernon Jordan.

Vernon Jordan, obviously.  But outside of that, this current      president, one who does not have the same kind of relationship, can boast      that he has given two African-Americans two more powerful positions than      any other president ever did.

Yes, certainly.  Bill      Clinton--the interesting thing about Bill Clinton is that his personality      and charisma and love for black people I think sometimes distracted      people from the fact that some of his policies and some of his actions      didn't fully back his sentiments. I mean, you look at NAFTA, you look at      welfare reform, you look at some of the things that he did when he was      particularly kind of appropriating Republican concerns and advancing his      own agenda with them, and they weren't necessarily measures that helped      black people, and he was able to get away with that because there was      this immense sort of personal love that people have for him, and he      obviously values black people, but the question is did he always reflect      that in his policies?  And there were some pretty big ticket items that      indicated that he didn't go as far as maybe he could have.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: There were some other things, too.
Mary Frances Berry, yeah...

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Yeah.

...I was going to say, though, pick up on the idea that Al      Sharpton points to the omnibus crime bill as a problem that came about      under the Clinton administration.  Many people forget the flap that he      and Jesse Jackson had.  They've become fast friends, but they had over      the Sister Souljah controversy, and Bill Clinton was a moving force      behind the DLC, which assisted in moving the Democratic Party from the      left to the middle, if you will.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Yeah.  Let me just fairly tick off the negatives about Bill      Clinton.  First of all, he named me to the Civil Rights Commission      because the Black Caucus was on his rear about Lani Guinier, who was      supposed to be a friend of his, dumping her for no reason at all and not      following through on the appointment; some budget cuts that he made in      the first term, and they weren't even going to let him speak at the      caucus dinner, and then they said they'd let him speak, but if he came,      they were going to boo him.  So they quickly announced that I was going      to be chair of the commission, even though I had criticized him for not      changing his Haitian refugee policy, which he promised in the campaign      that he was going to start letting those poor people stay here instead of      sending them back, and he didn't do it.  And I criticized him for a whole      bunch of other stuff, and they didn't want to.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: He always said that when he asked me whether he'd done anything right on      civil rights, I'd always tell him I'd give him about a C-minus, and      that's about all I'd give him.  Now Lani Guinier, not loyalty to his      friends.  Bush is loyal to his friends.  He even gives them, you know,      medals when they mess up.  He--on the policy side, welfare reform,      everybody says it's a great success, but there have been recent stories      about all the people left behind and what happened to them.      Rwanda--never forget Rwanda.  That will be on his conscience, I'm sure,      forever and ever, when he did nothing about the genocide in Rwanda.  So      that Clinton was lucky in terms of he made some good appointments.  He      had some good people he appointed--black people who he appointed to      positions.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: But on the policy side--the crime, the incarceration that Al Sharpton      mentioned of all the black people who were in jail, not just men but      women, too, and the drug issue and drug treatment and, you know, we can      go down the list of all the things that Bill Clinton didn't do.  I think      the fundamental flaw with Bill Clinton, he hadn't the courage to stand up      and fight for some things that were unpopular, which this Bush guy who,      you know, I don't have much good to say about, does do.  He sticks by his      friends, and he stands up to fight.  At the end of the day, Clinton would      make a political calculation about whatever it was, and he knew that      black people would love him because he loved them and then he moved on.
Exactly.

Eric, I have suggested--and pick up on that point--but I have      suggested that if you really have ever spent any real time with this man,      I think those who write that he's the consummate politically really,      truly underestimate that he is--he and Jesse Jackson almost mirror each      other in the sense that they are truly the personification of the      politician.

Oh, yeah.  And I think that's something that people      constantly downplay when they talk about presidents in general.  When      they talk about this president, George Bush, they constantly      underestimate the power of their charisma and the power of their      personality, and that's something that Bill Clinton was always a master      at; not only appropriating the Republicans' biggest points and turning      them against them, but also doing it with a charisma that would make the      people that he was kind of shafting smile, even as he was pressing these      policies that would hurt them.

Now the thing about George Bush, though, you know, his Cabinet may be      more diverse, but we don't know if they can think for themselves.  We      don't know how much of what they're doing is their own initiative and how      much they're just reflecting George Bush's desires, so there may be more      diversity in this current Cabinet, but we don't know how much autonomy      these people have, and we don't know how much of their culture affects      how they do their jobs.
Bob Meadows...

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Well, that's true...

...I was at the convention yesterday in relation to the speech      that he gave to the black journalists.  He did admit, as Mary Frances      Berry suggests, that he had tremendous regret in not moving against      Rwanda.  It's interesting--and Eric touched on it--the idea that we used      to call Reagan the Teflon president, but not much really stuck to those      who loved Bill Clinton in terms of the downside of this man.

Well, Monica Lewinsky maybe, you know, stuck to him, I      think. And you talk about his legacy, that's probably what he's most      going to be remembered for.  You know, in speaking about Rwanda, I      thought, as you just mentioned, you know, Bill Clinton, perfect      politician speaking yesterday, he says, yeah, it's his greatest regret.      He said that, you know, since then, he's done whatever he can to make it      up to them with all this.  Well, yeah, 11 years later, that's great to      say.

The thing that really struck me most about his speech yesterday was when      he brought up the issue of apologizing for slavery.  He said he      apologized for slavery in Africa, but he said, `I would have apologized      for slavery if somebody had asked me,' to us, black people here in      America.  And I thought, wait a minute, I know that came up during your      presidency and you didn't. Why?  Because it was politically unfeasible to      do that.  That's why...

And, you know, I would like to jump in, too.  One of the      things that is interesting about Bill Clinton, I mean, we also have an      AIDS crisis here in America amongst black people, and we've had it for      quite a while. What did he do during his presidency and what is he doing      now?  I mean, I'm glad to see him active in Africa, but what are people      doing to stem the HIV infections amongst African-American women, which      are amongst the highest they've ever been?  You know, this question about      what is he doing substantively in this country remains.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Well, it's much easier to deal...
Mary Frances Berry, one of the things, though...

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Yeah.

...we should touch on, Mary--and then, please, continue your      point--on the plus side of Bill Clinton is if you are around this man and      watch him, he is one of the smartest people I've ever met.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Well, he's smarter than almost anybody I've met, except      Hillary. His wife is smarter than he is, I think.  And it is a      pleasure...
Well, I haven't spent quite as much time...

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Well, it is a great...
...with Mrs. Clinton as I have with Mr. Clinton.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Well, I haven't either, but it's been enough to compare.      It's been a great pleasure to just sit around where Bill Clinton is, when      he was president, a lot of times, you know, in meetings and stuff, and      have him just informally tick off, as he did with you when he was talking      to you.  He mentioned, you know, what--Emory University had just done      this study and how many--whatever, whatever.  He is a walking      encyclopedia of ideas and information, and he will pursue them and he      will talk you to death.  I mean, I've been over there at dinners where he      talked everybody to death, and I got up and left before he did.  I said,      `I'm falling asleep.  I have to go home.' You're not supposed to go home      before the president.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: But he's full of ideas and proposals, and somebody mentioned earlier      about black unemployment and the economy.  For the first time since I had      been keeping track, which was forever, the black unemployment rate was      not twice as high as the white rate two years of the Clinton      administration.  I thought, this is fantastic, for the first time.  But      his ideas, while he's a policy wonk in that sense, a lot of them, he      didn't follow up on.  He made a mess, for example, of Haiti.  That's why      Aristide is in South Africa now.  We got him to--black people did--by the      way, we did encourage him to apologize, so I just want you to know that.      We got him to, as black people--Randall Robinson, me, some other      people--got him to go and intervene and put Aristide back in Haiti.  But      after he did that, he didn't follow up.  He took the troops out too      quickly.  The whole thing fell apart, and it's a mess.  So he wouldn't      stay the course.  He doesn't stay the course, and he doesn't make tough      decisions and stand up for people that he should stand up for.

Bob Meadows, let me take the other side of the coin, and that's      black America and what they should have looked to from Bill Clinton.  I      worked at MSNBC through the impeachment debacle, if you will, during the      Clinton administration, and almost every day, ironically if you go back,      you would have seen black politicians on the air at MSNBC almost daily,      which you would never see in any other period of time.  Almost in      lockstep, in unison, black America helped, quite frankly, save this man's      presidency...

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Oh, yeah.

...because they came out and stood steadfastly with this man.      He mentioned it just a few moments ago during the interview.  In return,      one has to say, if politics is tit-for-tat, I thought black political      leadership failed greatly in getting something back from this president      during that time.

You know, I think one of the issues--one of the worst      things that happened to Bill Clinton was the fact that Al Gore lost in      2000.  His legacy sort of stopped then.  I mean, that was 1998, of      course, when the whole impeachment thing went down.  Clinton didn't have      a lot of time left in office.  I think what he's doing now is wonderful.      I think maybe he was even handcuffed by the office a little bit.  You      have to be the consummate politician.  You can't do what you want.  Now,      he can, and you look at what he's doing over in Africa, and that is a      fabulous thing, especially after the way he messed up Rwanda and Somalia      and Haiti, too, you know, with the AIDS. He's a big dreamer.  One      million--What?--antiretroviral by next year, that's what he's hoping to      get.  He's a huge dreamer.  And as Dr. Berry said, well, hopefully, he      will be able to follow through with these dreams.  And so I think that's      really where he's going.
Mary, what do you think about that...

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: I must...

...the idea of black leadership and what they did or did not      receive from this man, outside of--as I told many of them one night,      you've got a nice picture in the Rose Garden with him, but that's just      about it.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Well, you have to first make this point.  Remember that he      lost the Congress for the Democratic Party.  His being re-elected twice      was a great personal triumph, political triumph for him; first one since      Roosevelt or something to be re-elected.  But he lost the Congress.      Remember the Gingrich revolution?  And so when he lost the Congress, some      of the ideas that he had in mind, he couldn't put into place anyway.  I      mean, he didn't have the House of Representatives and then, you know,      there were all these political problems.  And in a sense, his politics      led to the failing fortunes of the Democratic Party to where it is now,      the triangulation and all that stuff that he did.  And there were a lot      of things that were unpredictable.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: But black politicians weren't hard enough on Bill Clinton.  I was      probably--I'm not a politician, but at the commission, I was hard on him.      I criticized him for--somebody ought to read the report we wrote on his      administration; some was good, some was bad.  But black politicians were      seduced by him, too, and so they would lean on him, but they also knew      that black people liked them, liked Bill Clinton, and they represented      black people.  And they knew that black guys were giving high-fives in      the barbershop to each other when they heard about the Lewinsky thing.      So that's what I was told anyway by my brother.  So...
They probably did.

You also have to bear in mind that black politicians were      kind of caught between Bill Clinton and a very aggressive, very      conservative Republican Party.  I mean, what were they supposed to do?

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Right.

And Bill Clinton was two years from the end of his      presidency. He was about to be a lame duck anyway.  He was coming off of      an impeachment. It's amazing that he got anything done after the      impeachment...

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: He didn't have a Congress, right.

...was done.  He didn't have a Congress.  I don't know that      there's much that you could have expected from Bill Clinton after the      impeachment.  He was seriously hobbled by it, and liberal politicians, in      general, and black politicians, in particular, didn't have many options      in terms of who else they could turn to to get their ideas implemented.

All right.  Well, you guys are giving him a little more rope      than I'm going to give to him.  But let me go around the horn, very      quickly, with about a minute left, literally.  Give me a grade,      legacywise, Bob Meadows, what you think Bill Clinton and black      America--his relationship to black America--give me a grade, if you will.
You know, I'd have to give him about a B-minus, largely      because he was lucky enough to have a great economy while he was      president.
Eric, what about you?
Emotionally, I'd say an A-minus.  People love him.      Substancewise, C-minus.
Mary.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: I'd give him an A on the personal side and for his      commitment. I'd give him a B on the policy side and mainly because of one      we didn't mention, not just the appointments, but `mend it, don't end      it,' which saved affirmative action during that period...
Yeah.  Yeah.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: ...and led to still having it today.
All right.  Bob Meadows, Eric Deggans and Mary Frances Berry,      thank you very much for a look-back at Bill Clinton and his continuing      relationship with the black community.
You're listening to NEWS & NOTES from NPR News.
This is NEWS & NOTES.  I'm Ed Gordon.
On today's Roundtable, a showdown at the ranch, and do female pedophiles      get a break?

Joining us from our New York bureau, E.R. Shipp, a columnist at the New      York Daily News, and Bob Meadows, a writer for People magazine.  Also      with us, Nat Irvin, professor of future studies at Wake Forest      University.  He joins us from member station WFDD in Winston-Salem, North      Carolina.

Folks, we want to first take a look at a woman who's receiving a lot of      attention.  Her name is Cindy Sheehan.  Miss Sheehan is outside of the      ranch where the president is vacationing.  We have seen her over the      course of the last couple of days on all of the newscasts, and she is      protesting.  She says she wants a meeting with the president to talk      about the war effort, her son killed in Iraq.  And the president has      refused to this point to meet with her while he spoke yesterday in saying      that he understood the angst and concern that people had with this war.      He has not seen fit to meet with her and a growing number of protesters      who are now gathering outside of the ranch.
Bob Meadows, when you see this and hear this now, what's your thought?

You know, I know that the president      did actually meet with her shortly after her son was killed.  He met with      her and a group of parents, but, of course, now she would like to meet      with him one on one.  He did send two high aides--I've forgotten who they      were--to meet with her.  I believe it was Sunday.  But I think this marks      something for the president.  Unfortunately for him, he now has a face of      somebody who opposes the war, a gentle face, a mom who's lost her son,      and I don't think that can help his cause.

And we should note that the meeting took place in June of 2004,      but she said that she wants another meeting based on the fact that this      meeting was prior to the idea that most Americans believe we had faulty      prewar intelligence and that obviously the basis of why we went to war.

Ms. E.R. SHIPP (New York Daily News):  I think there's nothing for the      president to gain from a meeting at this time.  He has--I'm not defending      the decision to go to war, and I'm not defending the way the      administration has conducted the war, but there's nothing to gain by      giving in to this kind of protest.  He has spoken out about what the      goals are for bringing democracy to Iraq, and when the troops will be      brought home.  So I think knowing the way this president      operates--remember, he hasn't met with the NAACP since he's been in      office.  He takes a stand and he's stubborn.  So he's not going to meet      with her.

Well, I agree with you,      E.R., he's not.  There's nothing to be gained by it, but I think--I read      Cindy Sheehan's piece.  She called it `This is George Bush's      accountability moment.' And I think she pretty much summed it up by      saying--and the president actually is in a position that reflects where      the country is in Iraq.  We have no very good options.  He certainly      cannot meet with every widow who has suffered the ultimate loss in this      horrible war, but I think it reflects the reality that now most Americans      are starting to put a face on the war.  I think at this point, the      disapproval of the policies in Iraq has reached 61 percent.  It turns out      that there was never any more than 40 percent at any point who thought      that this might have been a good idea.  So now we find out that, you      know, the premise on which the war was originally fought was wrong.  If      you ask Americans now, I don't know who's going to have some real clear      consensus as to why we actually are there now.  The idea of trying to      bring democracy to Iraq--I don't think most people would have agreed nor      agree now that that's worth American lives.  And if I were in Crawford,      I'd be in sympathy with Cindy Sheehan.  I would...
Ms. E.R. SHIPP (New York Daily News):  Well, you'd probably sit outside      of his house and, you know, have a fine time protesting, but that would      not accomplish much...
No, it wouldn't....
...in terms of policy.
No, it wouldn't...
Let me ask this.
...but I...

Let me ask this, Bob Meadows.  E.R. Shipp suggests that there's      nothing for the president to gain, and that is the thought of, it may, in      fact, be a lose-lose situation for this president.  But is there      something to gain if, in fact, he grants a meeting, albeit brief, with      this woman, sits her down, explains his position, in the compassionate      way that many say that he can one-to-one and then have her march out and      say, `I have a new understanding'?
No.
Well, you know, I...
Dreamland.
That may be dreamland, but...
What understanding?

...there's never anything wrong with PR.  Right now this      woman has the floor.  She's getting all the sympathy.  You're right.      Bush does have a very folksy way about him.  Meeting with her might be a      great PR move.  He doesn't have to change his position by any standard,      and I don't--of course, he's not going to.  As he said yesterday at his      ranch, their pulling out would send a terrible message to the enemy.  But      sitting down and talking to her might actually stave off some of the      criticism that he's getting by just letting her be out there right now,      ignoring her.
E.R., if I hear from you...
But it's not going to be a one-one-one meeting.
...you're suggesting there's nothing that he can say.
Right.  There's not going to ever be a one-on-one meeting.      It's going to be the one-on-one with the press involved.  So he's already      had...
Oh, you're just cynical.

...press conferences.  He's already given speeches.  He's      already done those kinds of things to give his position on the war.  So      he's not going to change anybody's thinking by having a sit-down with      this lady.
And the other thing is, does he meet with every widow?
Or mother or a brother, or a sister...
Yeah, right.  He just...
Well, no, but if we--let's assume we're allowing her to be the      collective face of those grieving, he can...
Why her?
...in turn, turn it around and suggest that he meets with her      symbolically as the collective face of those who are grieving.
He's done it at the White House already.
This is a hostage choice.
Yeah.  All right.
He's done it at the White House already when he's met with      various family members.  He's done it at the hospital.
Right, but...
Yeah.  The president just can't do this.
All right.  Well, I'm sure...

I don't see how the president can do this unless we're      going to pull out of the war and the number of troops who have been      losing their lives suddenly stops.  This is a slog we're in, and it's      unfortunately...
I'm sure the White House...
...very difficult.
I'm sure the White House appreciates that thought from Nat Irvin      and E.R. Shipp.

So let's move our attention to what is becoming frighteningly too      familiar in terms of the headlines and video that we see, and that is a      young woman arrested--a teacher--for having sex with a child essentially.      A former elementary school teacher pled no contest to having sex with a      13-year-old boy, a student of hers, and will get nine months in jail.      We've seen the pictures of this young woman; 28-year-old Pamela Rogers      Turner--is her name. We should also note that there are a number of these      cases, including yet another one yesterday that did not receive the same      kind of attention that Ms. Rogers Turner received.  This Alisa      Kawasaki(ph), 25, pled no contest to a felony count of unlawful sex with      a minor on Thursday as well.  She was accused of having sex with a male      student who is now 17, but she faces three years in prison and will      likely receive probation.

The question here, folks, is, as we take a look at females--female      predators as some will call them--society still does not see the female      pedophile in the same way we do the male pedophile.  Is this problematic,      and if so, what should be done about it?  I mean, let's be honest.  There      are men who still, with a wink and a nod, say, `Man,' particularly if the      woman is attractive, `what a lucky kid.'
I tell you what...
Who are you asking that one to?
Whoever's brave enough to take it, E.R.

Boy, I'm glad my kids are all grown up.  I'll tell you      that. The last one is 18.  This is such a--I really have struggled with      this, not just from, Ed, the point you make about the sentencing aspect      of it, which is, you know, a reflection of the larger context of what      happens when you suddenly see mothers do bad things, but I have not yet      come to grips with the fact that we have women or even men who are--that      teachers and children in the elementary schools are having sex.  I mean,      I'm still having to come to grips with that.  And then now to put it      in--and I think this is probably a reflection of why the justice      system--we don't yet quite know what to do with women who are pedophiles.      This is still very new to most of us, and you know, now, of course,      every day you hear something like the Mary Letourneau case coming out.  I      think it's just going to take a while for us to start to realize that      this may be a growing problem and we're going to have to come up with      some public policy.  I think I am reflective of the larger society on      this.  I don't know what to do with it.

Well, I don't know that it's that complicated.  Teachers have      a very important position in the lives of young children, in the lives of      the communities.  And whether they are male or female, they should be      held accountable.  Whether the law permits the kinds of sentences that      we're seeing in these two cases you've mentioned with probation added      on--I think this woman in Tennessee has eight years of probation facing      or something like that.
Yes, she does.

Well, then if that's what the law permits, that's fine.  As I      recall the prosecutor saying is that because this woman had no prior      criminal record, it was unlikely they would get anything more than three      years and possibly less than that in terms of prison time.  So that's a      specific kind of sentencing thing.  I think that the broader issue should      be whoever is preying upon children should be punished to the extent the      law allows.
Bob, it just seems to me, though, and I'm going to go back to my      first point, which I don't know that we spoke to...
Yeah.

And we should note, E.R., that she will have a supervised      probation for eight years.  She's been suspended, unable to teach, and      she'll have to register as a child sex offender as well as the judge      implementing the idea that she will not be able to profit from this case      and she will not be allowed to...
By selling her book or movie rights.
Right.  Exactly--conduct interviews during this time period.

That being said, Bob, again, I go back to the idea that society seemingly      does not see this with the same sense of urgency.  Had this been a      28-year-old male and a 13-year-old girl, I contend, and if we'd seen the      rash of male teachers doing the same thing that we've seen over the      course of the last two years as we have with female teachers, I think      society would be more up in arms than we see right now.

Yeah, you're right, Ed.  You're exactly right.  Men are      viewed as predators because that's typically what we are.  So it would be      more of a predation thing, and as you indicated, I mean, there have been      movies made about, wow, you know, a young boy losing his virginity to the      older woman. That's just society and just the way it is.  I mean, you      would definitely believe that if it was an older male having sex with a      younger girl, that he coerced her into doing it, whereas with a boy, it's      just, like, well, you know, boys will be boys; you've got to lose it      sometime.
Yeah, and I think...
But we shouldn't tolerate it.
No, I don't think anyone...
Yeah, specially when you're talking about teachers.
...E.R., is suggesting that.

Yeah.  No, especially when you're talking about teachers.      But I think Ed's point is just the larger context of how we look at      between males and females, and I think you're right about that, Ed.  But      I'm saying that as we sort of come to grips with the role that women play      in every other aspect, the sort of, you know, the equality of roles, you      know, equal opportunity for sexual predators, too, we'll have to adjust      our attitudes.  And I'm not quite there yet.
Why?
Let me...

Oh, I don't know.  I think it comes to the point that Ed      was trying to gently touch around, the way that we see men and the way      that we see women.  It takes some adjustment.  I'm having to adjust to      seeing--it's something I never saw when I was a kid.  How's that?

Well, as a woman, I must say, I don't see that there's a      difference in the way we should be holding teachers accountable.  But I      wanted to say something.  As I grew up in the rural South in a very poor      family, it was teachers who took me under wing and my parents would      actually let me go home with them for the weekends to Atlanta.  And      that's the kind of thing that would no longer occur because everybody's      afraid of sexual misconduct or the appearance of impropriety.  So I think      kids are losing something that they might have gained in the past by      having a more close relationship with the teachers at that stage in their      lives.

Turn our attention to another issue that I would suspect many      people would be surprised at the silence that we're seeing, and not that      the uproar would be able to change anything, but that is the price of      oil.  The price of oil is now at $66 a barrel, and that is very, very      high, for those that don't necessarily know anything about the pricing of      oil.  But we are seeing the continuous climb, and the thought that we may      see something that hits most of us, and that is when you pull up to your      gas pump, your local gas station, do not be surprised in the course of      the next six months whether or not you see a 3 before that decimal.

I have to say, I'm glad that I take the subway.  I'm not      affected, but I feel for everybody who drives, absolutely.  You know,      being from Detroit, the Motor City, of course, you know, the hometown is      suffering quite a bit, I'm certain, and all those people with SUVs      can't--you know, now you can't drive, you can't take the car out.  You      can't go on driving vacations, things like that.  A month ago or so,      people were up in arms because it had reached $53 a barrel.  Now it's at      $66.  You have to wonder, when is this going to stop?
Well, with the United States...
Well, it's not going to stop anytime soon.

Well, when the United States gets its good friends in Saudi      Arabia to do something about the oil.  I must say that I don't drive,      deliberately so, but I do take public transportation and understand that      that public transportation, whether you're talking a van from here to      there, a bus from here to there or a plane from here to there, is      affected by this.  But one thing to keep in mind--this is not going to be      popular with drivers--the more expensive the gas, the less likely they      will be to drive, and the better our environment will be.
Now you...

Well, Ed--listen, I just would add this, that--and this      won't make anybody feel any better either, E.R.  But, actually, when it      comes to the price of gas adjust for inflation, it's actually cheaper now      than it was in 1980.  Now I find that hard to believe, but those are the      statistics.  The second thing is...
Yeah.

...to make us feel even better, the price of home heating      fuel or even natural gas in a couple of months--right now, the      projections are that it's going to either be 25 percent higher or a third      higher.  And so we're going to have to deal with this energy problem for      a long time.
Yeah.
But one thing to keep in mind...
Obviously, it remains...
...we're still paying little money...
It remains...
...compared to Europeans.

And the Army--they've already shortened the term of      service. Now they're going to ask Congress to increase the enlistment      bonuses.  So these are really--and this is still not working.  This is      something that the gentleman said--they really need to resolve their      recruiting problem.  Well, their recruiting problem is that they have      these various wars going on and these different soldiers are dying and      coming home in coffins.  That is a problem that they're really not going      to be able to tackle.
Here's something else that...

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, Northstarnetwork.com)
text: Now also...
Go ahead, Walter.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, Northstarnetwork.com)
text: Another disturbing trend is their marketing for recruitment.      It is heavily geared towards urban communities.  They are heavily      investing in black media, whether it's magazines or television.  There is      a real pitch towards our community to try to get our young people to      enlist, and they're trying to make it look sexy and glamorous.  They're      trying to put it in a style of videos because they think that's what our      young people will be attracted to.  So we really need to open our eyes in      terms of what is actually going on with the military coming into our high      schools, coming into our middle schools, trying to recruit our kids.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)
text: And doubling the bonus from $20,000 to $40,000 is      certainly a part of that.  But, you know, I think it's also worth noting,      as far as this conversation, though, that the Army says that its      retention is above its goal, that they retained 108 percent of its goal      in terms of the Army's retention. So in some ways, there's a disconnect      there between the inability to recruit the number of people they need,      yet they are more than meeting their goal. Now perhaps their goal      wasn't--was set too low to begin with, but that's what they're saying.

Here's an interesting juxtaposition.  We had the president      giving this speech yesterday, and then we also heard from New York City      Mayor Michael Bloomberg who suggested that there were real and credible      threats against the subway system here in New York City.  And here's the      interesting point: Homeland Security made a point to come out and say      while this chatter was, in fact, real, they did not see it in the same      heightened measure as New York City did.  There are a lot of people here      in New York who were suggesting that they want to listen to Police Chief      Kelly instead of...

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, Northstarnetwork.com)
text: Yes.
...the Homeland Security divisions based on what we've seen over      the course of the last month, but you know...

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, Northstarnetwork.com)
text: I can guarantee you, folks who are on the subway this      morning are being very cautious and are looking, because I think there's      really confusion over how these warnings have been issued, particularly      from Washington, DC.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)
text: But you know what?  Also--if you want to play the      Machiavellian game, it also would make sense for the officials in      Washington to play up threats like this in order to feed into the desire      on the part of the American people, if that's what it is, to fight the      war against terrorism and the war in Iraq.  So I did find it pretty      interesting that the people in Washington were saying essentially these      threats are not credible; all the while, the officials in New York who,      in this case certainly are closer to the situation, are increasing their      security.
Well, and suggesting, we should note, that they did not say they      weren't credible, but they felt the heightened concern that New York City      was placing on it was perhaps a bit premature.

And that probably stems from the fact that they're not here      in New York City.  They're not the ones who are going to have to jump on      the subway.  Even a lot of people at my job, when it came around on the      e-mail yesterday and in the news conference, yeah, we looked outside, and      those bus lines were pretty long, pretty crowded.

When you think about this, Joe Davidson, the idea that if, in      fact, as many people assume, the military is stretched to the seams,      there's already taxing measures being put on many of the organizations      that have to fight terror based on domestic problems here, one more event      really is going to challenge this administration and the government, is      it not?

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)
text: Well, I think there in Mexico--in fact, I mean, I think      that the government and the administration is already very challenged,      certainly in terms of its--you can see that in terms of its plummeting      popularity.  Of course, President Bush cannot run again, so it will not      affect him personally, but we do have the midterm elections coming up,      and so we can see just how the Republican Party, and the Democratic Party      for that matter, meets that challenge and also its impact on the next      presidential election.  But there clearly are a number of things that      have been challenging this administration from the war in Iraq, its drop      in popularity, the situation involving various members of the      administration or the Republican Party generally being indicted or called      before a grand jury, so that whole kind of corruption cloud is starting      to get a little darker over their heads, the response to Katrina.  So      yes, I think there are a lot of challenges out there.

And, Walter Fields, there are some real on-the-ground      challenges, whether or not you'd be able to deploy people and resources,      if, in fact, heaven forbid, we face another particular--in particular      terrorist attack.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, Northstarnetwork.com)
text: Well, one thing, you know, Katrina should have taught us and      Rita also, and particularly if you look at a city the size of New York,      and what I've always cautioned people is to believe that if we have a      tragedy of the magnitude--either terrorist or natural, in a place like      New York City, that all hell would break loose.  You cannot evacuate New      York City.  You can't even cordon off parts of this city; it's so large.
Yeah.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, Northstarnetwork.com)
text: You're talking eight and a half million people.  Then if you      talk about northern New Jersey, you're going to add another eight million      people.  What do you do?  We have no plans for that.
Yeah.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, Northstarnetwork.com)
text: We have not contingencies for that.  And I think we're at a      point now where we have to realize that our government is really      unprepared to handle any of these situations.
All right.  Well, let's hope we don't have to face any of those.      Some people say it's not if or when, but I'm going to continue to bet on,      you know, the ifs.  So we'll keep that.
Walter Fields, Joe Davidson, Bob Meadows, thanks very much for joining us      today.  Greatly appreciate it.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, Northstarnetwork.com)

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)

Thank you.

This is NEWS & NOTES.  I'm Ed Gordon.

On today's Roundtable, we'll take a look at the use of torture as a tool      in the war against terror.  Also we'll look at a British opera that says      that its performers should no longer perform in blackface.  Joining us at      our New York bureau, Bob Meadows, a writer for People magazine.  Also in      the bureau there in New York, Marcelo Suarez-Orozco.  He's a professor      and co-director of immigration studies at New York University.  And from      our headquarters in Washington, DC, Dr. Mary Frances Berry, professor of      history at the University of Pennsylvania.

Hi.  Thank you all.  Let's get right into what is being seen as a closer      look at the idea of whether the United States has, in fact, engaged in      torture in relation to its, quote, "fight against terror." Mary Frances      Berry, we are starting to see hairs being split, if you will,      particularly by the secretary of Defense, Donald Rumsfeld, I think,      without saying to a great degree the Bush administration, outside of Abu      Ghraib, has admitted almost to engaging in some forms and acts of terror      in the need of--or in the word, I should say, of saving us against the      terrorists.  How much do you buy that this is going to explode in the      face of the Bush administration?

speaker_label: Dr. MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: I'm not sure,      because the House has not passed any legislation or even considered any      while all the debate that the public has been transfixed with is going on      in the Senate with McCain and others with the bills that have been passed      there.  But everyone in the country should know by now, given what's been      publicly disclosed, that the United States has used torture.  I mean,      that shouldn't even be up for debate.

speaker_label: Dr. MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: And also one can tell from the comments of Rumsfeld and Cheney and others      that the administration intends to use torture again if they feel that      they believe that they should.  I myself am so cynical about this that I      think that even if a bill were passed--and remember, there's nothing up      for passage in the House--that if they felt they needed to engage in      torture, they would probably do it.  They have said that they want the      CIA to be able to do it.  Everyone who knows the history of torture knows      that people lie when they're being tortured.  They give false information      that doesn't really help.  It's not that it's going to make things any      better or that you're going to get better information, but I think they      are bound and determined--they--most of the public now doesn't even talk      about Abu Ghraib.  You don't see anything about it in the news or      anywhere else.  They think that people will forget this debate, too, and      that they will use it if they believe they need to use it.

Marcelo, we heard from President Carter just a few moments ago      in talking about the idea that in his mind, it's almost unbelievable to      suggest that we are actually publicly talking about torture as a tool.      Yet one would say historically, behind the curtain in Oz, we know that it      has gone on.  Are you surprised that it has become so public?

Torture has been      used in various contexts.  We have the French experience in Algeria.  We      have the experience in Indo-China, Vietnam.  We have, of course,      widespread use of torture in Latin America.  And what the historical      record--what the comparative record suggests is that torture really      doesn't work.  Torture only works in terms of spreading terror in a      population, which is, in the current context, not the best way to proceed      as we ease out of Iraq and as we try to, let's say, win the hearts and      minds of the Iraqi population.  The fact that this is being widely      discussed now is in a way a symptom of a policy that is out of control,      where there are contradictions, where there are ambiguities, where really      there is a lack of clarity moving forward as to how we're dealing with      the mess in Iraq.

Bob, what of the idea that there is no real benevolence in war,      some would say, and the thought that this is all just part and parcel of      what goes on, and doggone it, get a grown-up view of what's happening?

You know, it's really--that's really      definitely a strong issue, because certainly the idea of torture is      reprehensible to most people, but it is--and the United States has had      policies against it.  But when you're out in the field, I imagine, and      you're in the war and you're seeing your buddies being blown up and      you're seeing them being tortured, it seems like that's really what we're      trying to protect against, and it's really not being done.  That type of      thing is perhaps a bit more understandable.  But it seems like what the      White House is discussing and plans to veto is calculated torture, where      you're actually planning to torture people, and that's what I think is      something--yeah, in the heat of war, it's one thing but boy, when you're      out there and planning to torture people that you're going to try and      interrogate, that's a whole different level and I think really needs to      be looked at.

speaker_label: Dr. MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: One of the things that amazes me about this discussion all      the time is how policy-makers--We're not talking about people on the      battlefield somewhere who may, in a moment of hot anger, do something...
Exactly.

speaker_label: Dr. MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: ...but how policy-makers who have available to them      information about the history of torture and what it does and how      ineffective it is and all the rest of it, would make policies, as Bob      said, to calculate, to engage in it and seriously think this is a great      idea when they should be leading the way and not understanding that if      you perpetuate torture, then that means that your own forces are at      greater risk of being tortured.  I just don't--you know, it just amazes      me that this illogicality proceeds with this discussion all the time.
Yeah.  All right.

We'll move to a list that has been making headlines over the course of      the last couple of days.  This is a list that is produced by Morgan      Quitno Press, a publishing company that over the years has looked at the      10 safest and 10 most dangerous--or, I should say, 20 safest and 20 most      dangerous cities in the country.  The list is controversial by virtue      of--and we'll get into that in a moment--how the basic categories of      crime are put together and then, of course, the list derived from that.      But of the top 10 cities, number one, Camden, New Jersey, then Detroit,      St. Louis; Flint, Michigan; Richmond, Virginia; Baltimore, Atlanta, New      Orleans; Gary, Indiana, and Birmingham rounds out the top 10.  One of the      interesting notes there, Mary Frances Berry, as we take a look at that,      these are majority minority cities and many of them, the majority of them      are very poor cities.  Does this speak to the idea that obviously      violence and poverty often go hand in hand in this country?  But it also      speaks, when you look at that list, to a group of cities that have fallen      on hard times and have been there for decades.  Any hope of these cities      climbing off of this list and out of this kind of despair?

speaker_label: Dr. MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Every single one of these cities, as you said, and even going      down to the whole 20 of the cities, they are places where unemployment,      devastation, some were old manufacturing cities and now there are no jobs      and no one has done anything.  Others are places where there have been      pockets of poverty, poor people with no development forever, as long as      anyone can remember, and any plans that local people make or governors      about what to do in the state always passes them by.  So you would expect      robbery and all the violent crimes.  And of course, those crimes should      be punished, but that's not really the issue.  The issue is, is there any      way to make it better?

speaker_label: Dr. MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: And if you contrasted those with the safest cities, every single one of      those is a bedroom city or an ex-burb or someplace where the people have      money, where you don't have to worry about it.  And if you were to look      there to see what kind of crimes were committed, you'd find embezzlement,      white-collar crime, domestic violence and other kinds of things.  So      obviously there's a connection between the situation of these cities that      they found themselves in--drugs, other things, places where the people      from the ex-burbs buy drugs--that makes them on this list.  So rather      than just lamenting and saying, `Oh, my gosh, they're still on the list,'      if anyone really wanted to do something about it, sure, they'd punish the      crime and accelerate that, but they would do something so that these      places would not continue to be bypassed so that every single time you do      this survey, you come up with the answer that you already know you'll get      when you do the survey.

We should note, though, that the methodology used by the      publishing company has come under attack regularly by criminologists and      sociologists who criticize the company for not placing the data in      context that gives equal weight to six basic crime categories.  That's      homicide, rape, robbery, aggravated assault, burglary and motor vehicle      theft.  That being said, Bob Meadows, these are violent and dangerous      cities, often, as Mary suggested, left in despair for years.  When you      look at the idea that so many people said that Katrina, quote, "uncovered      poverty," which we have found laughable often on this program, the idea      that this list does not uncover the violence that many of these folks      live in, for those of us who look at this, isn't it time for America to      take a deep, hard look in the mirror and really, as Mary suggests,      correct some of these problems?  Because it cannot be done solely      locally.

Yeah, and the cities have tried.  Camden, I read, has the      redevelopment program in the works.  You know, of course, you know, not      being from Detroit, you know, we know all that the cities have done      there.  As Dr. Berry said, these are cities that have had long legacies      of this.  Detroit has always been a very hard-scrabble city, even back      when it was predominantly white.  Boy, you know, Lyndon Johnson's war on      poverty, Martin Luther King, that became his big issue; these have been      ideas that have been tossed around. But what it seems like is every time      that the country gets going pretty well economically, the Republican      administrations always come in and start cutting taxes and cutting      programs, and so anything that poor people even had to hold on to is      taken away from them.  I'm just...

Marcelo, I said in Detroit this week, when you hear the      announcement from GM, 30,000 jobs lost, many of them are going to affect      particularly the ripple effect in the belt here, the Midwest belt here      where a lot of auto industries have had their plants and the like.  One      cannot assume that any of this bodes well for these cities.  What do you      believe can be done to help spark a resurrection, if you will, of these      cities?

Well, again, it really goes back to the issue of      work and of meaningful opportunities.  The work of Bill Wilson at Harvard      on the disappearance of work, very, very powerfully suggests that when      work disappears, when there are lack of meaningful job opportunities,      when you confound that with anomie, with a lack of the patterns of social      cohesion and the social structures that can prevent the kind of data that      we're looking at, we really need to be thinking in terms of a massive      re-investment in meaningful job opportunities at a time when the global      economy sees a growth in the outsourcing of our jobs.  Good jobs are      disappearing and this moving forward suggests a lot of serious problems      in these large metropolitan core centers where the African-American or      Latino or minority populations are really resegregating and      hyperconcentrating and confounding deep poverty with deep segregation...

speaker_label: Dr. MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: And it may happen, too, that if something isn't done, that      the next time they do this survey, some of these other places in the      country where these plants are closing down and things are being      outsourced--I noticed Oklahoma City was big in the news last night as a      place where GM is closing down plants--that if we don't do something      about making work for people, meaningful work for people everywhere, we      may see some additions to this list the next time it comes out.
Yeah.  I just...
Mary, how realistic is it to believe that something along the      lines of a Marshall Plan, if you will, might be really broached by      politicians?

speaker_label: Dr. MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: It's not going to happen in Washington.  Governors--it seems      to me that governors of these states need to take the lead and      legislatures in the states on trying to come up with something.  In some      states they have tried and they've lacked resources generally throughout      the state.  In others, there hasn't been really any focus.  And people      have tried--if you look at this list, Cleveland, they tried building a      stadium.  A lot places have--Baltimore built a stadium.  People build      stadiums and hope that that brings some jobs.  But given the massive      problems in these areas and how long they've been going on, it's      difficult.

speaker_label: But I point out something else
text: Not all places in all of these cities      are dangerous.  If you look at the list, Washington's on the list like at      13.  Not all of Washington, DC, is dangerous.  It's the places where the      poor people live and have no work.  Not all of New Orleans--even now      after Katrina, the French Quarter isn't dangerous.  The Garden District      is not.  Atlanta is not dangerous everywhere.  What we're talking about      is places where--and the more concentrated the poverty is and the more      poor people and unemployed people are there in the cities on this list      and the longer it's been going on without anybody doing anything about      it, except lamentations, then you see that the problem is more      concentrated and more difficult to deal with.  It's very interesting and      it's a challenge for policy-makers to say, `Deal with it.'

Yet, Bob Meadows, what's interesting here is the browning of      these cities that we've been seeing, or in cases like Washington or      Detroit, the flat-out blacking of these cities, if you will.  Perception      is everything, and there are going to be those who will not associate the      idea that the overwhelming string here that runs through all of these      cities is poverty. People are going to equate that also with the idea of      black and brown folks just can't control themselves.

Even though Flint is 40 percent white and St.  Louis is 43      percent white, you're absolutely right.  That is what it's going to be      associated with.  That is--I should say, that is what it is associated      with. Blacks--the median income for black--median household income for      blacks in this country is $30,000.  That is--it's not officially poor,      but you know if your household is earning $30,000 a year, you're pretty      much struggling. These are issues that--they don't have a color, but      color is assigned to them. And so yeah, people are definitely going to      look at this as a black and brown issue.

And, Marcelo, the catch-22 here is what Bob spoke to, with the      idea of this kind of list coming out, it makes prospective investors and      others leery about going into these cities and infusing money.

Sure.  And the other thing we didn't talk about is      the issue of education.  Again, in the context of developing meaningful      work, work that will not be outsourced to China, to India, to other parts      of the world, we really need to rethink the role of education in the      generation of meaningful work opportunities for our minority populations      moving forward.

speaker_label: Dr. MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: I need to make just one other point, Ed, and that is that the      answer to this problem, according to some urban experts, is      gentrification, and in the cities on this list where some gentrification      is ongoing and is taking place, the idea is that they'll move off the      list that way.  Of course, that doesn't answer the issue of what happens      to the poor people.
Yeah.

speaker_label: Dr. MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Because in gentrification, they lose, but the city can get      taken off the list by becoming gentrified.  It's a very interesting      conundrum.

And is not always an easy equation, as we saw with Detroit in      particular, that gentrification about 15, 20 years ago looked as though      it was turning the corner and whites were coming back in, and then that      stumbled and certainly has to a great degree hurt the city by virtue of      tax base and all.

All right, folks.  Thanks so much.  We were going to talk about blackface      being banned in the opera overseas, but we'll get to that maybe tomorrow.      Thank you, folks.  Mary, Bob, Marcelo, appreciate it.

speaker_label: Dr. MARY FRANCES BERRY (University of Pennsylvania)
text: Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you.

This is NEWS AND NOTES. I'm Ed Gordon.

On today's roundtable, people will receive notice of home demolitions in New Orleans. And another NBA player heads into the stands. Joining us today from New York, John McWhorter, Manhattan Institute's senior fellow in public policy. Also with us, Bob Meadows. He's a writer with People Magazine. And from our headquarters in Washington, D.C., Mary Frances Berry, professor of history at the University of Pennsylvania. I thank you all for joining us.

I want to get into what we broached with the secretary just a moment ago, and that's that a federal judge has approved a settlement this week in a lawsuit over the first demolitions of New Orleans homes ruined by Hurricane Katrina. City officials suggest that they will give advanced notice to homeowners before the demolition begins. But there are a lot of people who are crying foul, suggesting that this seven to 10 day notice before demolition will occur is unfair because the way the notice will happen is the city will publish an advertisement over three days in the local newspaper there, listing the addresses affected. They will also post warnings on their website, and they say they will try to contact owners by mail. But many of these owners, Mary Frances Berry, will not be able to be found, quite frankly.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Well, I think that's right, but I think that balance, this is probably the only solution we can reach. And I also know that some of the local community organizations are in the business of trying to notify people and tracking people. Everyone who has looked at that area, and I just spent three weeks down there on the Gulf and in New Orleans, knows that those buildings need to, or what's left of them, need to come down. The question is, how to do it, and what is the fairest way to do it, and what's going to happen to the people and their property.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: But I wanted to add to the interview you had. I just must say this. That HUD has done so little to help the people down there to either find housing if they were in public housing before, or to make sure that they are not discriminated against. And the Fair Housing Agency inside HUD is one of the worst run federal agencies. You can read a report on the website of the Commission on Civil Rights. You can go back over the years and read every single report evaluating the agency. It's always been under-resourced. It doesn't handle complaints when they're supposed to, on a timely basis. So it's nice for them to have an ad campaign, but the housing part of HUD hasn't done its job in trying to help people in a way that housing would be made available. And the enforcement part, I just think that the ad campaign is nice, but it is window dressing.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: But on balance, I think that the judge's order down in New Orleans is probably the best way we can go at this time and try to notify people, because the property needs to be cleaned up. Those areas, there are many places where there is wood and bricks and everything else out in the street, and obstructions, and that's got to be cleared away before we can do something else.

Bob Meadows, it must be difficult though, if you're an evacuee, and you see the structure that is not just a structure to you, but your home, and knowing that emotionally you believe and hope that you'll be able to save it. But as Mary suggests that possibly it is the emotion in your heart thinking more than your need.

Certainly, it is. And that was one of the things that people were arguing for and asking for them to delay, or at least try and give notice, is that so people would at least be able to try and get home, try and come back and at least go through, because one of the things we have to remember is that we're not necessarily talking about physical structures that are standing.
Mm hmm.

A lot of these places, as Dr. Berry implied, these places are rubble, rubbish, just refuse left over, but they do want people to at least be able to come home and perhaps go through it and see if they can find anything that means something to them. But, as we also said, this is the Lower Ninth Ward that they're starting at. A lot of these people were people who had to be evacuated and, therefore, are scattered around the country. Seven to 10 days? Not likely they're going to be able to get home in time.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Mm hmm.
You know, one of the most…
Sorry.

Let me ask you this, John, and then pick up on that point. Mary raised an interesting question and I thought it was interesting to hear, when I asked the secretary about the idea of HUD and their thoughts of what had been going on and his suggestion that that is more a regional than a local issue, but knowing that, they may in fact have to come in on the backend and provide housing.
There still seems to be the idea of, this whole situation, this whole region, this whole area, of being too much of a hot potato for anyone to want to hold.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Public Policy, Manhattan Institute)
text: : Yes, there is a problem. I mean, nationally, in terms of what the people we're talking about have had to go through, these are people who, you know, don't have apartments. And in terms of the trailers, there's this not in my backyard issue as to where the trailers are going to be. People are being kicked out of their hotels.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Public Policy, Manhattan Institute)
text: And it seems to me we definitely have a situation where the local organizations are going to have to do most of the work. And the exciting thing is that there are community advocates for these people, such as Tracy Washington and Bill Quigley. And it seems to me that in terms of looking ahead, I really agree with what Mayor Nagin said about the chocolate city and I eagerly anticipate it. And so with all sensitivities taken care of, I want to see these houses raised so that we can build a functioning chocolate city and show that there can be such a thing that is not a pit of destruction.
Washington, D.C., will tell you it's chocolate city two.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: And chocolate city, chocolate city, by the way, Nagin had used it in speeches before. And as listeners might know, I'm now a great defender of his. And before, what he didn't understand is after what happened down there and these issues now, he couldn't just say something like that and have it taken in the same way. He should be more careful about what he says. But I realize the stress that he's under.

All right. Let's turn our attention to something that's very interesting, quite frankly, and that is, surprise, surprise, that we are now seeing Democrats and Republicans vying for the first to be true in talking about the idea of truly reforming lobbying in Washington. We had on this week, two African American lobbyists who clearly want it known that by virtue of their prism, they believe lobbying is doing just fine and there are only just a few rotten apples in the bunch, but now Democrats are suggesting that you ban all gifts and travel paid for by lobbyists. They're aiming to seize this issue, obviously, as people take a close look at this. Republicans counter with a 24-page document targeting Democrats as being hypocritical and the hypocrisy, quite frankly, is flying on both ends here.

How realistic, John McWhorter, is it to be believed that we are going to see any kind of real reform when it comes to lobbying in Washington when you know the kinds of dollars that fly in the nation's capital?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Public Policy, Manhattan Institute)
text: Oh, well, please. I mean, we can chase an ideal, but this doesn't get to the heart of it which is the influence that special interests always have and I think always will have on legislation. That's the way the Republic has always operated, for better or for worse. And it does bear mentioning that I think that in the case that something is being lobbied for that is considered a good thing by what you might call the blue state crowd, somehow I think we're a little bit less indignant, sometimes a little bit of lobbying can be a good thing.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Public Policy, Manhattan Institute)
text: Obviously, the Abramoff scandal is the bad kind of lobbying. This is too flagrant and too sleazy. But we're not going to really change anything. Don't we see something like this happening every, about every 20 years? This is just the latest episode.

Well, Mary, I was going to bring that up and I'm curious what you think about this Democratic plan, as I suggested, would try to curb all of these perks, if you will, barring lobbyists from giving gifts to members of Congress. The Republican plan, like this one, said they want to end fact finding trips, that's where these trips are paid for by often lobbyists...

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Well, it's where you go play golf in Scotland.
...and deemed as fact finding. But you do all of these wonderful things in lieu of finding fact.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Right, absolutely.

They also want in-dead-of-night insertions of special interest legislation and we should note that that is the pork barrel spending that is added on to bills that most people wouldn't blink an eye at and it's usually done “late at night" and in hopes that people won't realize it. This has been going on for years and years and years. Mary, this has been talked about, reform has been talked about, nothing happens.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Absolutely, absolutely. And both sides have done it. The problem now is that what Delay and the crowd did was over-the-top. I mean, and they were so open about it, this K Street Project. I mean, saying publicly, you know, you guys, I know some people who run lobby firms here and they tell me, we were told you better hire so many Republicans if you don't hire them by whatever, don't, you know, come in here and they better be these people. And so it was sort of over-the-top and there's nothing wrong with lobbying.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: What's wrong is the money, the influence, the payoffs and all the rest of it, that have been going on. I think the legislation should be passed. I think the Democratic legislation is a little bit stronger, and it should be passed. And if you wonder why it's not as much of a political problem for the Democrats is because, you know, Willie Sutton robbed banks because that's where the money was. The Republicans got most of the money because they're the ones who have the power. They're the ones who control all three branches of the government.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: But the problem is whether or not the reforms when they're passed, and something will pass before the election, whether they will be enforced on the Hill and they're not because the House Ethics Committee doesn't even work now. It hasn't even met and it isn't even doing anything. And in fact, Abramoff would not be known about publicly as this guy who was crooked if some reporter hadn't done a big series in The Washington Post and then that forced the Justice Department to go out and take a look at him.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: So this is all happenstance that is happening. Yes, it should be passed. Also bottom line, if we don't do something about campaign finance and the money that's paid for campaigns, all that will happen is the money that's going now for the lobbyists, the lobbyists will give the money to the campaigns and then they'll get the same result.

Bob Meadows, let me ask you this: Is it smart for Democrats to use this as a campaign issue when, as Mary and John both noted, that this does happen on both sides of the isle. Can this come back to bite you?

Sort of like Ted Kennedy challenging Alito's membership and then finding out that he had his own. It is the pot calling the kettle black as they say, but you know, I thought it was interesting that Barack Obama, who's new to the Senate said that, you know, Republicans have suddenly found religion. But I think it's actually everyone finds religion on this and John said every 20 years.

I think it's every two years because that's how often the elections come up. This is something that the Democrats want to grab onto and hope that they can ride. They have a 12 year losing streak in Congress right now. They want to grab onto to this and hopefully ride it into more seats in both Houses.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: But let's not forget though, it is an important issue. Even though we're talking the inside baseball on it. It is a very important and serious issue that money can influence us directly and if you've got a whole big pile of money, you can influence what projects get approved and get earmarks and do all this kinds of stuff. Whatever party is doing it.
It's the money.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: And right now, the Republicans have the problem because they get most of the money and they have most of the ties with most of the guys who turned out to be crooked. So in that sense, it is a good political issue.
So, John, Should we believe that that will not change today and that we will see a lobbying effort against this, money being thrown toward this, and we're going to see a watered down reform package?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Public Policy, Manhattan Institute)
text: It seems to me at that this point, I think as we're all concurring here, there's certain gestures going on that are just based on which party is in power and which party would like to be in power sometime in the near future. But really, I think the ideal that we should seek is just that there is lobbying on both sides, that's it not intimately tied to the sleazier sorts of exchanges of money and trips that we're talking about, because we can admit that lobbying can actually concentrate forces for justice, if it's done right, and would inevitably arise in any governmental system.

Let me bring this up, particularly since we have two people who spend a lot of time on college campuses and with young people, I'll be interested in your thoughts here. If alumni groups weren't in the news enough already this week, a fledging group in California, UCLA, is now suggesting that they're going to offer payments to students up to $100 per class to provide information on instructors who are "abusive, one-sided, or off topic" in advocating political ideologies.
This is an organization, the Bruin Alumni Association, if you were going to give it a political slant, it would slant to the right. It says it wants to expose UCLA's radical professors.
Mary, let me start with you. You are a professor. When you hear this kind of thing, what's your thought?

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: My thought is that most students, at least most of mine, wouldn't know whether what I was saying was off topic or not, simply because they're in the class to try to learn something. And so, I'm wondering if this guy who's running thing, who's a graduate, I guess, out there, whether he would know that.
