They have freedom of speech and freedom of expression and they can do whatever they like and if they want to spend their time doing that, let them go ahead and do it. But I think that it is crazy and if you look at the people who are on their board, some of them, they wouldn't know whether what I was saying was off topic or not.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: I mean, if I say Benjamin Franklin said if you give up your liberty for the sake of security, you deserve neither liberty nor security. Does that mean I believe we shouldn't wire tap? You know, and am I trying to give a subtle message against policy? So if they want to spend their time doing it, let them go ahead and do it. I think it's silly and it's the sign of our times in that rationality seems somehow to have escaped people on occasion.

John McWhorter, there are those political neophytes that run around college campuses who aspire and hope to be the next you-name-it, who would, in fact, not only spurred on by the idea of being a poor college student and looking for that hundred dollars, but also trying to make their mark, if you will.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Public Policy, Manhattan Institute)
text: Oh, yeah. I mean the money part is, that's bound to create, people creating things, et cetera. I think that it's sleazy, it's virtually unethical. It's very small thinking. But the idea behind this, I think, is dead on. Tenured radicals was just a cute title for a book, but it is definitely true that on college campuses there is a strong tilt to the left in what students are taught in classes in humanities and the social sciences.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Public Policy, Manhattan Institute)
text: And, frankly, it's more than a tilt. And it's largely a matter of just what is not talked about. But another thing is that, one, to truly understand what goes on, does need to have some live exposure to what actually goes on. There are courses that I remember other people teaching where if you looked at the syllabus it looked okay.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Public Policy, Manhattan Institute)
text: But if you actually watched the professor doing what they do, not a zealot, but clearly one was being inculcated into what was considered a certain, you know, leftist way of looking at things, such that there are many very reasonable people who think that the reason, for example, that there are so view avowed conservatives in top political science departments is because science and reason simply couldn't support any view on the right, which simply isn't true. So there is an issue that this guy is dealing with the method of getting at it, I think, shall we say, draconian.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Well, I just, I don't, no, no...
Looking at his Web site, you know, he also is...
Bob, real quick.

Yes, he's also talking about, he's against the African American studies. He's against the bias. He's talking about the biased admissions policies. You know, we can talk about this with hiring the students. That's sort of an acute issue maybe. But he's got some very serious issues on his website that could lead to something even worse going on.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Well, what it is, all of this is part of on the political side and Bob, you're right on. It's part of the whole attack on the kinds of changes that are taking place in the academy that have made it more inclusive so that there are people there as students who wouldn't have been there before. There are classes there that wouldn't have been there before, many of which need to be there because it reflects the changes in knowledge and the changes in interest that ought to be there.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: And so this whole thing about left bias and all the rest of it is all part of an attack and one should look at the website and take the whole thing, take it whole, and decide where the motives are and whether one would support it, I would think.

All right guys. We had hoped to get into an incident that happened last night at another NBA arena where Antonio Davis of the New York Knicks went into the stands for fear that someone was harming his wife, but we're running out of time. We'll probably pick that up tomorrow.

speaker_label: Ms. MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Ed, it was time out though.

It was time out, but he still went in those stands. But we'll talk about it. Certainly a different circumstance than what we knew in my hometown of Detroit. So, Mary, John and Bob, thanks so much. Greatly appreciated.

This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Ed Gordon. On today's roundtable: more trouble surrounding the Cheney shooting and trouble in paradise for some sheriff deputies. Joining us today to discuss these topics and more: from our D.C. headquarters, Karen Narasaki, president and executive director of the Asian American Justice Center. John McWhorter joins us here in New York. He's senior fellow in public policy with the Manhattan Institute, and Bob Meadows is a writer for People magazine. We welcome you both.

Let's talk a little bit about what we just heard, and that is the response from Republicans essentially--this huge report--very scathing, Bob Meadows, from Republicans, and we should note that Democrats didn't want to involve themselves in this study because they believed that Republicans would not be forthright in their investigation, but they were very hard-hitting. One has to believe, to some degree, it's an election year--that played in to this.

That's exactly what I'm thinking. The Republicans, they don't want to come out looking soft on this. This is obviously, Katrina, a big issue that continues to resonate with the American people. Those images of people being stuck at the convention center are still strong in people's minds, so yeah, this attack was blistering, and I think it was surprising for a lot of people except in the context of an election year, and they blamed everybody for this fall. They blamed Bush. They blamed the governor. They blamed the mayor. They blamed FEMA. Everybody took a hit on this, and I think that's actually, probably, what people wanted to hear.

Interestingly enough, John, one of the groups that did not get blamed in this report, surprise, surprise--was Congress. You heard me ask William Jefferson whether or not oversight should have been better prior to the catastrophe. We've heard many people yell about the problem that was coming. It came. Congress did little to nothing prior to.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN McWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Yeah, it's clear that this is a nation that isn't good at preparing for things like this, and that does make you worry about what sort of preparations for terrorist threats.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN McWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: However, what's interesting to me is that any of this is considered a surprise. Like, talk about the FEMA part of it, it's as if 13 years ago was sometime during the Coolidge administration in 1992, Hurricane Andrew happened, and all of the same stuff with bloated national bureaucracies meant that people of Homestead, Florida--who are mostly white as butter, for the record--had the same problems, the same five-day wait, the same media scandal. I think only because the internet wasn't around, and so you can't link too many files of it, are any of surprised now that this sort of thing happened.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN McWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: We've got a chronic problem, and it would be nice to be look at even these previous occasions to see that what we're dealing with is structural and permanent unless we really wake up.

Karen, here's the interesting point. To me, it's almost as though we took a peek behind the curtain and saw that the wizard wasn't as big as we thought he was when looking at the government. There is also an audit that shows that millions and millions of dollars have been wasted by the government, squandered, in terms of preparing the evacuees to get back on their feet. That juxtaposed with this report does not speak well to, as John suggested, being able to deal with catastrophes of this size from the federal government.

speaker_label: Ms. KAREN NARASAKI (President and Executive Director, Asian American Justice Center)
text: Well, I think it shows what happens when the hiring of leadership is based totally on friendship and political donations and not on whether you have the professional qualification and experience to actually do your job, and that's clearly what happened here.

speaker_label: Ms. KAREN NARASAKI (President and Executive Director, Asian American Justice Center)
text: I do want to say, you know, for the Republicans, to give them the benefit of the doubt, I don't think that it's just that it's an election year. I also think that this is a region where there are Republican members of Congress--the governor of Mississippi is Republican--where their own constituencies and themselves felt the brunt of this, so I think there is some personal interest in this that goes beyond the election.

speaker_label: Ms. KAREN NARASAKI (President and Executive Director, Asian American Justice Center)
text: The other thing I want to note is I was just down in Houston with chairs of the Congressional Black, Asian and Latino Caucuses doing a town hall meeting, and what frightens me about these stories about fraud is there's still thousands of people who haven't yet registered for help or people who are being denied help from both FEMA and SPA who clearly do deserve help. They're having trouble getting through the bureaucracy, and I'm worried that these kinds of stories are going to make people think we're done, and clearly we're not. There are just so many victims who need help and aren't getting it.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN McWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: You know, one thing I want to add is that there is a statistic making its way around that 900,000 people who applied for aid gave false addresses or false social security numbers, and I'm really dismayed to see that that many were pulling that kind of trick. I'd like to see exactly what was going on because, frankly, I doubt it. It couldn't be that that many people were pulling that kind of (Unintelligible).
That was actually more than one-third of the applicants, which is an astonishing figure.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN McWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Yeah, they must be giving this wrong data for a reason or something. I hate to think that there was that much of that going on.

I do want to give FEMA a slight benefit of a doubt, just a slight benefit, because we do have to remember that at the time that this was going on, unless of course it's still going on right now, there was a huge rush--this was a frenetic rush - to get these people from New Orleans into--from the South rather--into places that are safe.

You know, you talked about the $399 rooms in Chicago. A little bit of research into that, that was actually a family of - I mean, it was two families and it included meals, so it wasn't really quite as bad as the numbers seemed, necessarily.

Well, but then it's almost like the Defense Department and that $9,000 hammer or whatever it was with the toilet seats, you know. There is a sense of whether that be the case or paying $375 a day for a beachfront condo to put folks in. There was a fiasco of the debit card that was given out. Much of this was response to the idea that a lot of heat was being taken, and rather than somebody taking a step back and a breath and saying, let's get a hold of this, they just started, as we heard from Christopher Shays, admitting that even the Congress just started appropriating money because the heat from the public was white hot at the time, Karen.

speaker_label: Ms. KAREN NARASAKI (President and Executive Director, Asian American Justice Center)
text: Well, I don't think Congress was running around appropriating money. They haven't appropriated enough money. They haven't come close to the amount of money that's going to be necessary. Houston had to open two additional high schools and has had no help from the federal government or anybody else to deal with the new numbers of people that they have in their community, the numbers of elderly, the people with disability, the thousands who need mental health counseling who aren't getting it, the small business owners who are suffering--the bureaucracy for that is ridiculous. I'm really surprised at the high number that's purported in terms of bad addresses because the reports we kept getting were it was impossible to get online and to register. There were thousands of people who ended up in church basements and homes who, you know, these reports don't reflect, really, the fullness of what's really going on, and...

Well, the interesting point here, and I promise this because I've lived in Washington for years and know there will be another shoe to drop. Someone will fall for this, whether it's Michael Chertoff, but someone will be the fall guy for much of this, and the White House is making sure that it's not going to be the President.

Let's turn our attention to the White House and Dick Cheney. So many people talking about the hunting accident, and unfortunately, the gentleman that Mr. Cheney was hunting with now has suffered a heart attack. It just seems to exacerbate the ire of many that this White House wasn't as forthcoming as many suggest that they should be.
We also saw it in the press corps yesterday. NBC's David Gregory taking to task the White House. Let's take a quick listen here.
Well, hold on a second, I've got one last question...
Well, other people in this room have questions, and we've got to (Unintelligible)...

I understand that, but I'm not getting answers here, Scott, and you - I'm trying to be forthright with you, but don't tell me that you're giving us complete answers when you're not actually answering the question because everybody knows what is an answer and what is not an answer.
David, now you want to make this about you, and it's not about you. It's about what happened...

All right. That's David Gregory from NBC, Scott McClellan, White House Spokesperson, John, and those of us, again, who know Washington know that you rarely get answers, so to see David stand up and other reporters really at a point of feeling like I'm going to kick back a lot more than they normally do. Is this much to do about nothing, in your opinion? Some people feel as though it was a hunting accident. They were friends or acquaintances, and we're making far more out of this than we should. Others suggest, look, it's the vice president, you need to be forthright and forthcoming.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN McWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Ed, I frankly think that it is actually puerile, the kind of attention being paid to what is a private issue. I think the reason we're giving it so much attention is because Dick Cheney is a man who a lot of people love to hate, and of course, he makes it worse by being so private, but he was out hunting and he accidentally shot someone.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN McWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: In the meantime, the homicide rate is up in various cities, particularly among young black man. Milwaukee, young teens are going in gangs and killing adults and this is becoming a copycat effect in Milwaukee. We have people who have not been given housing because of Katrina. There's serious issues, and we're dealing with Dick Cheney in an Elmer Fudd costume. It's just--we're just picking on somebody like we're in a classroom in fifth grade.

While all that's true, Bob, much of this would have been diffused had the White House just come out with a statement to say, this happened at this time, this happened, and not allowed the ranch owner to take the onus and the impetus to get it out to the press.
That would have stopped some of it, Ed, but it wouldn't have stopped Leno. It wouldn't have stopped Letterman.
No, of course not.

This is the type of issue that, even if Cheney had come out--I believe one of the gentlemen said, no matter what he does, he's going to look ridiculous. He's just going to do his own thing, so he's got--Cheney did need to come out. He needs to take some responsibility for this, which I guess he has. He's admitted that he shot the guy?
Publicly?

But it's still, this is still going to be the type of issue that we will be talking about because, it's not a funny thing, but it can be made into something that's funny especially because the guy old.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN McWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: I hold Cheney accountable for telling us about Iraq, not about him shooting somebody in the body while he was off on a weekend...

But, Karen, it just seems to be, particularly during this second, that here is a White House that continues to stumble, at least from a PR stance, forget whether or not you agree with its policies or not, particularly that juxtaposed to their first couple of years where they seemed so much in control in everything they did.

speaker_label: Ms. KAREN NARASAKI (President and Executive Director, Asian American Justice Center)
text: It has become the gang who couldn't shoot straight and I think part of the challenge here is it does happen in the context where there is concern that there's been cover up after cover up after cover up of things that sometimes you don't even need to cover up. There is so much control and secrecy in this Administration and this is just an outward manifestation of it and I think that's why it resonates so much; it's not just the fact that it's Cheney, but it's in the context of an Administration who's been less than totally forthright.

All right let me take you to a private matter, John McWhorter, when you talk about his private for this Vice President. There's a county in Florida where the Sheriff's Department is now saying, members of that Sheriff's Department, if in fact you commit adultery you will in fact lose your job. So much so was the adultery rate amongst the employees and the Sheriffs there, it had gotten so out-of-control that they had to step in. Is it fair, even though you can question it morally whether a police officer certainly should be held to a higher standard, et cetera, et cetera, is this fair, in what you're doing in your private life to possibly cost you your job in this case?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN McWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Well, in this case it's a rather specific ruling. I mean, if it's going to be about paramours.
...private.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN McWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Very private, but the problem is that it affects the public performance of the job and so if people having affairs will affect the quality of police work, then I can see there being some rule against it, which you assume will be broken off; and making it about adultery suggests that this is somebody with particular beliefs and he's enjoying the opportunity to impose them.
Yes, and when it's a matter of private affairs having an effect on the public, Dick Cheney's hunting habits don't affect me, my pocket book or anything (unintelligible).

All right, well, let's take it a step further, Karen, and use John's analogy of whether or not it affects the public. If I'm one of those Sheriffs who's having dalliances on the side, as long as I show you that, hey I'm not doing it on company time and my beeper, pager, and gun is beside me on that nightstand every time I'm with this person, I can get out to an emergency call; shouldn't I be allowed to do this?

speaker_label: Ms. KAREN NARASAKI (President and Executive Director, Asian American Justice Center)
text: Well I think that as an employer I really don't want to know the sex lives of my employees. So, I'm really surprised that the Sheriff is choosing to delve into this. I do think that it is a little odd that his next step might be, well we're not going to allow you to start dating or if you have a bad relationship we're going to start penalizing you for that. I mean the reality is people are people, they have lives. Some of the things that happen in their lives do affect their jobs, but I don't think you can really legislate for that.
Police officers who are boinking each other may pay more attention to each other in dangerous situations than to others or even to the public, that's the problem.
Well, but here's the interesting point, Bob, it goes beyond just whether or not I'm having an adulterous affair with a co-worker, it's whether or not I'm having an adulterous affair with anyone.
Right, you know ...

speaker_label: Ms. KAREN NARASAKI (President and Executive Director, Asian American Justice Center)
text: And they already had policies ...

speaker_label: Ms. KAREN NARASAKI (President and Executive Director, Asian American Justice Center)
text: MR. MEADOWS: As long as you work for somebody else, you have to do what they tell you to do. There is a company in Michigan where the guy said you can't smoke away from the job and that's been upheld many times and so these officers have to obey this. You know, the NBA players are not wearing hoodies anymore on the bench, they are wearing suits. They have to--these officers are going to have to pay attention to this. I think it's a nice thing that the Sheriff has passed this. We'll see whether, or maybe we won't see whether, or not it's actually getting followed.

Is this, in your opinion John, just a more specific to what many of us, particularly those of us in the media have in our contracts and that's what they call an ethics clause? Anything that they feel that the company, and they usually leave it that open ended so they can pretty much nail you on anything that you do, no pun intended, but it's often about that.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN McWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Yes, obviously it is about that. There's a place for ethics clauses in that it tamps down a certain amount of things. Sometimes when some thing is censored that keeps it from completely taking over with the assumption that it's going to happen, but in this case, the idea that we're doing something about something that might happen outside, it's very specific, it over-reaches, not to mention that it's unenforceable. It's not going to do anything. So it's kind of like symbolism.
So, Bob, what are the ideas in the juxtaposition of this and Dick Cheney. There's the fact that he is, in your mind, the Vice President, take it outside of the realm of it's a private matter?

MR. MEADOWS: That's just the society that we live in. He's a public person, whatever he does is going to be just magnified that much more and let's say Dick Cheney shot somebody. That is news. You know what I mean? That is news so, yes, absolutely it takes it very far outside.

Karen, any problems in terms of the suggestion that Bob made of not being able to smoke on or off the job, an employer suggesting that, the NBA dress code, the ban on adultery here, that we're starting to cross a line that perhaps will infringe on so many private areas that we need to take a look?

speaker_label: Ms. KAREN NARASAKI (President and Executive Director, Asian American Justice Center)
text: Well, I think it's a challenge because employees can vote with their feet, so if they don't like the employer, and generally if they don't like the rules of the employer they have a place to go, but I do think that some of these rules are beginning to get a little silly in terms of your ability to really enforce what's going on in people's private lives and then what will happen is it will be enforced unfairly and unequally and then probably used in situations where there really some other issue. But you use this rule as a way of addressing it rather than getting at the real issue.
All right, well the moral here is keep your gun in the closet and don't have an adulterous affair and that way you won't have to smoke after and you'll be safe.
MR. MEADOWS: There it is.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN McWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Keep your paychecks going.

All right. Karen Narasaki in Washington, D.C., President and Executive Director of the Asian American Justice Center, thank you so much for joining us; and John McWhorter of the Manhattan Institute and Bob Meadows of People Magazine, I thank you all for joining us. Greatly appreciate it.
Thanks. Thank you.
Up next on NEWS AND NOTES, the city of Houston welcomed evacuees fleeing the Gulf Coast after Hurricane Katrina, but a spike in crime is causing many residents to pull in the welcome mat.
You're listening to NEWS AND NOTES from NPR News.

This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Ed Gordon. On today's roundtable: was the Katrina overlooked and the crisis in Darfur spills over into neighboring countries. Joining us today to discuss these topics and more: from our NPR headquarters in Washington, D.C., economist and author, Julianne Malveaux president and CEO of Last Word Productions. Bob Meadows, writer of People Magazine, joins us from our New York bureau, and Eric Deggans, media critic for The St. Petersburg Times, is at the Pointer Institute in St. Petersburg, Florida.

All right, folks, thanks for joining us. We want to talk about what they knew and when they knew it. That seems to be the favorite question of the White House nowadays. A video obtained by Associated Press and released, a confidential government memo of a meeting, a briefing that was going on for the president, really shines a light, a somewhat different light, if you will, on Michael Brown. Maybe what he was doing in terms of defending himself was right. He suggested to the president--this is a quote: "My gut tells me this is a bad one and a big one," end quote. That is Michael Brown. A top hurricane expert voiced, quote, "grave concerns," end quote, about the breach of the levies and suggested that they might not be ready. Michael Brown again, quote, "I'm concerned about their ability to respond"--they're being disaster teams--"to a catastrophe within a catastrophe," end quote.
Let me play you something four days after Katrina hit. This is the president on Good Morning America.
President GEORGE W. BUSH: There is frustration, but I want people to know there's a lot of help coming. I don't think anybody anticipated the breach of the levies.

That's the president suggesting that no one anticipated, yet it seems very clear, based on this videotape and some other affidavits that have been released, that the president was engaged and did talk about the levies not being able to hold, Julianne Malveaux.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: You know, Ed, the breach of the levies had been anticipated, frankly, for almost a decade. The Army Corps of Engineers had been asking for more money. There was evidence that they could not withstand a category five, that a category four or three would put the city in significant danger. The fact that they had this briefing the day before and that the president talked four days after is immaterial when you look at the long arc of neglect of those levies. This was a federal government project, so all the people who want to throw mud at Ray Nagin, throw mud at Katherine Blanco, the governor of Louisiana, really have to look at the neglect that set this situation up.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: Furthermore, when the president, four days later, as you pointed out, on GMA, Good Morning America, says that help is on the way, help didn't come for another day or so, and there are those six months after the hurricane hit, who would argue that help still hasn't come for them. People are being evicted in Houston and Dallas and other places as of this week. There are tens of thousands of people who have nowhere to go. You have trailers with no one in them.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: The fact is that this is a--this is a hurricane inspired coup because now they're going to have elections on April 22, and those elections are going to be elections that basically wipe out years of reconstruction, and so this videotaped information is useful information, but it simply confirms what we've known all along.

Eric Deggans, it does put a different light, slightly, on Michael Brown. Not trying to resurrect him or absolve him from any of the problems and issues that came about, but he did go on to say during this briefing to the president as well as Homeland Security Secretary Michael Chertoff that he, Brown, feared that there weren't enough disaster teams to help evacuate at the Superdome.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC DEGGANS (Media Critic, The St. Petersburg Times)
text: It makes me sort of question where this video came from. The Associated Press got it exclusively and featured it in a new video service that it has. It distributes video to member stations and websites, and they also had seven days of transcripts of briefings where the president was also informed and Michael Chertoff, the head of Homeland Security, was informed about some of the risks regarding the levies and the hurricane, but it makes me wonder, where did this information come from because it makes Michael Brown look awful good, and we've seen this week and in previous weeks that Michael Brown is on a sort of rehabilitation tour of sorts. He's doing a lot of press, and he's trying to convince the world that he's been made a scapegoat for Hurricane Katrina, and this video speaks directly to that, which makes me immediately suspicious.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC DEGGANS (Media Critic, The St. Petersburg Times)
text: And as Julianne pointed out, the risks of the levies had been known for a long time, although they breached, which is different than what they thought would happen. People thought they would be overtopped, and that's what was talked about during this briefing that's in the video.

Bob Meadows, people want to point fingers. They want to find blame. But the reality is that it seems in all corners, and this is what we've been talking about, really, since Hurricane Katrina hit land, that all corners failed.

That's the thing we've been seeing from the reports issued by the House, by the Senate, by the White House. Everybody's been pointed at. Everybody's being blamed for these failings of Hurricane Katrina. That's exactly correct. One of the things that this does, though, is this video is almost sort of like the Rodney King video. You know, you hear about black people getting beaten, but then you finally see it happening by police, and it makes it much more immediate to you. You heard about President Bush just kind of chilling in Texas, but here you see him on this video sitting there being briefed in a short-sleeved shirt, in Texas, not asking a single question of these, of his advisors, and then at the end, finally saying, we are fully prepared. Video will always come back to haunt you.

Now, let me suggest this. The White House has released statements and sent the spin doctors out suggesting that we should not take and put too much credence into one videotape, that the President was being briefed time and time and time again, Julianne Malveaux.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: No, we shouldn't put too much credence in one video tape. We have a body of information that--we have, you know, the Republican-only inquiry that points a lot of fingers at the White House, at everybody else. I mean, this, the spin doctors need to get respun. They need to retool themselves because, certainly, none of us is foolish enough - nor is any member of the public--to simply look at this video and say, that's the beginning and the end, but we can look at the history--we can look at the people who are still there.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: That's the issue, Ed. All of this would be immaterial if indeed we would do for New Orleans what we did for New York. If we would decide that we were going to restore that place, restore those people, give them the right of return, but the fact is that we're still fiddling while New Orleans is still under water, while the ninth ward still has not been reinhabited, while insurance companies are playing with people's lives, so no, I'm not going to put any credence on a video. I'm going to put credence on what's happening in New Orleans right now, and not the benign, but the malignant neglect of our government--can't even say it, it's so bad.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC DEGGANS (Media Critic, The St. Petersburg Times)
text: Now, one thing I would put out...
All right, let me turn...
Real quickly, Ed.
Real quick for me, Eric.

...is I was in New Orleans about three weeks ago and spent some time there, and there is failure all over the place. I mean, half the street lights don't work. There is enough blame, still, to go around. They don't even know what the footprint of the city is going to be as they go to rebuild it. Local and state and federal officials can't agree, and we've had this sort of paralyzing bureaucracy for months now, and it makes no sense.

Lest we be fooled by--lest we be fooled by the pictures we saw during Mardi Gras, once you step outside of that business district into residential areas, it is still a mess and still people reeling trying to get their lives back together.

We just heard from Andy Young. I asked him about the situation in Darfur. As we know, Ambassador Young is a well-known globetrotter, and certainly understands the integral and intricate situations in many hotspots. In terms of Darfur, we see the chaos growing. Arab gunmen from Darfur have pushed across and entered Chad, stealing cattle, burning crops, killing many who are resisting. There's been a growing conflict between these countries for years and years. Here's the real question, Bob Meadows, not necessarily about the continuing crisis in the Darfur region. We've talked about that enough. Here's the $64,000 question: Does American need--have to--become involved?

Boy, the Bush administration has labeled this a genocide, so you know it must be a bad situation over there. I'm not - the U.N. wants to do some things. They want to send in more troops. I know that the President of Sudan has said it--Darfur will be a graveyard if non-Africans come in there because they don't want to have an occupation. This is a type of situation, though, that I think the U.S. has to keep up this type of pressure on the U.N. to act. I don't know if--I don't think the United States should act alone, but I think that they have to keep up the pressure on the U.N. to go in and at least, get the African Union that has the security right now--we need to bolster them. That's what really needs to happen so that they can protect these people.

Eric Deggans, I almost asked that question--almost, I underline--rhetorically because if you look at America, if you look at the United Nations, it's hard-pressed to assume that they would be able to deploy any more troops that would be viable in trying to stop any type of violence, add a resistance to any region because both of these entities, military and otherwise, are stretched very, very thin.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC DEGGANS (Media Critic, The St. Petersburg Times)
text: I think we see--we see twin tragedies here. The first is the continuing result of our foray into Iraq. We are so depleted militarily that even if we wanted to provide substantial troops to aid in Darfur, we'd be hard-pressed to find them. And we've also set this pattern in motion where Muslim countries and Muslim activists are very weary of American troops coming in to any region and trying to establish the peace. There's been fears about al-Qaida moving into Darfur and Sudan if America and western nations get more involved in sending troops there.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC DEGGANS (Media Critic, The St. Petersburg Times)
text: The other tragedy we have here is the incredible bureaucracy of the U.N. They have been so slow to act. They've known this is genocide for years. They have just now reached the point where they are considering some kind of sanctions against the Sudan. And they still haven't agreed on whether or how they will send in a peacekeeping troops, which are desperately needed, by the A.U.

So, Julianne Malveaux, what do we see? It's almost as though you sit by, as we have too frequently, and of late many of us have learned of it and watched this kind of genocide on the continent: upwards to 200,000 Sudanese have already fled for safety. And now we're looking at those who live in Chad, agonizing over whether or not they're going to be able to walk outside and live their lives as they know it.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: You know, Ed, we can't even begin to state the magnitude of this. Someone says if we go in or if the U.N. goes in it will be a graveyard. It's a graveyard already. The implications combined with the deaths, the rapes, the torture, the looting, combining that with the displacement, we're talking about millions of lives and we have known about this. The public has known about this for at least the past two years it's been going on for nearly a decade.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: The United Nations needs to step in, they need to move and the United States needs to keep up pressure. But I think more, this is a world issue and the world has all too often, we look back to Rwanda, turned its back on Africa. To say that if this were happening anywhere else in the world, Ed, it would be unacceptable. But that it happens here, we can sit around and have debate. Is it genocide or not genocide? You know, who should go there? We've been basically remiss and there are very few lobbies, even in the United States where in groups like Africa Action and Trans-Africa...
Yeah.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: ...have stepped up. But there have not been many who have stepped up and said this is an important issue. And so we're really all remiss here.

Turning out attention to a side issue to all of this in fact and that is if in fact troops were to enter yet another war zone, how would they hold up? Questionnaires filled out after troop deployment are finding that one in three soldiers and Marines who've served in Iraq later seek mental health services. We are seeing, Eric Deggans, a growing number of returning veterans needing hospitalization or psychiatric care.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC DEGGANS (Media Critic, The St. Petersburg Times)
text: I don't think that's a surprise. I mean, considering the conditions in Iraq where the insurgency can spring these deadly attacks without warning anywhere. It makes sense that we would have troops who would come back and be traumatized. And I think we're in an environment now where people are more likely to seek mental health than maybe they would have been 30 or 40 years ago, which is really the last time our American troops have faced such a deadly conflict, so you know, it makes perfect sense to me. And it's another one of these hidden costs of the war that certain presidential administrations would prefer we not consider.

What we don't see, Julianne Malveaux, is the idea of the ongoing issue of these men and women who return. Often you think well they seek psychiatric help and they get batter and they move on with their lives but unfortunately many of them do not.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: You know this is a different kind of war Ed. One of the things that we've been reading about over the past year are the number of people who come back maimed, wounded, with the loss of a limb or something like that. The numbers are much higher. Our medical technology makes it easier to save people who might have died in the past. And so you have people who will have long term wounds and long term adjustment affects and the people around them.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: In addition, the people who serve with them, who saw somebody's arm get shot off or you know their face crushed in, they have the recurring nightmares as well. The other thing about this war that's different is you don't really have a front line as you did in some place like Vietnam. You have all this stuff dispersed all over the place so someone who's simply patrolling a street has as much chance of being in harm's way as someone who is on a front line. So it really it's a much more dispersed kind of thing. And I think the one in three number frankly is low. And I think that there's no way we can begin to estimate what the long term social costs of this war will be in terms of people's mental health.

This, really identified after the Vietnam War, Bob Meadows, but we are seeing many of these soldiers come back with post traumatic stress disorder and that is something that often stays with them until they pass away.

That's one of the reasons why this program was instituted, why the military instituted this mental screening program. Because after the Vietnam War, actually it was Vietnam Veterans who said you know, really lobbied for post traumatic stress disorder to be recognized. Many soldiers because it's a macho organization, many soldiers are reluctant to seek treatment. But like somebody said this is, we're now in a society where perhaps seeking treatment is more acceptable than it used to be.

But one thing that might put a halt to all this is that although Bush's budget has a six percent increase in spending for the Department of Veteran's Administrations, this-Affairs--it hinges on a billion dollar in cuts and other programs. So veterans are actually like you know we still don't have enough money to handle all these soldiers who are going to come back with all these difficulties.

And, Julianne Malveaux, we forget the ripple effect. This not only affects the individual but their families because off times you do not come back to the same job, you're not the same person you were, and therefore do not present yourself in a way that employees might see you as beneficial.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: Absolutely, Ed, I think again you know we're seeing right now just a tip of the iceberg. We have you know, the military has begun to deal with families, what happens with spouses, what happens with relationships, what happens with children and again how people will re-integrate themselves into society. You have stories of The Post and The Times have been doing series of you know guys who are sleeping with their guns or who cannot hear anything startling without, you know not getting a good night's sleep.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: And so when we freely go into war, we underestimate what the human costs are. And our history of a macho culture has allowed us to sweep it under the rug in the past. Let's not forget also whether there are women who are also in this war. Women who have you know tremendous implications as well. We talk about the macho culture, we forget about the fact that perhaps 15 percent of our enlisted troops are women.

And in fact that is the case and letters not sent to me, I did say the men and women at war. Thank you Julianne Malveaux though for echoing that and Julianne Malveaux, Bob Meadows and Eric Deggans. I thank you very much for joining us today, appreciate it.
Thank you.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC DEGGANS (Media Critic, The St. Petersburg Times)
text: Thank you.

This is NEWS & NOTES.  I'm Farai Chideya.  One today's roundtable, a radio DJ loses his job over what he calls a slip of the tongue, and the U.S. won't allow Puerto Rico residents to vote in the 2008 Presidential election.

Joining us today from NPR headquarters in Washington, D.C., Yvonne Bynoe, author of the book Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture.  And at our New York bureau, Walter Fields, CEO and publisher of the NorthStarNetwork.com, along with Bob Meadows, writer, People magazine.

Thank you all for joining us and let's talk about this radio situation in St. Louis.  A personality at 550 KTRS was fired on the spot yesterday after referring to secretary of state Condoleezza Rice using a racial slur in a conversation.  He says he meant to say if the NFL hired Rice it would be a big coup.  Instead he used a racial slur.  We have the clip.  Let me just say it may be offensive to some listeners.

She's been chancellor at Stanford.  I mean, she's got just the patent resume of somebody that's got some serious skill.  She loves football.  She's African-American, which would kind of be a big coon.  A big coon--oh my God!  I am totally, totally, totally, totally, totally sorry for that.  Okay?  I didn't mean that.  That was just a slip of the tongue.
Just a slip of the tongue, Bob.  What do you think?

You know, when I read it, I was thinking to myself this sounds like a slip of the tongue because he was so very apologetic, but after hearing it just now, it doesn't quite sound so much like a slip of the tongue anymore.  I have to say, I guess, my attitude is kind of turned around about this.  It sounded deliberate, I have to say.  Reading it, it didn't sound that way, but hearing it, it sounds almost like - it sound deliberate.

Yvonne, there have been so many radio shock jocks, their nickname on the airwaves, like Imus, who have gone out and used racial slurs against prominent African-Americans.  And as Bob mentioned, this gentleman, who was the radio host, he didn't break tone.  He was like, oh, oh, I'm sorry, but he didn't really say, oh, I'm sorry.  Does it make a difference, his delivery, make a difference?  And what's the real issue here?  Is the issue that we, once again, are shocked that there are racial slurs on the radio?  Or is that kind of now par for the course?

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: Well, I think it's unfortunately par for the course, but I think the difference between someone like Imus or Howard Stern, you know what you're getting when you turn onto those stations.  You know that they are there to shock, and whether that's sexual content or whether it's racial content, or racial slurs, you know what you're going to get.  I think what is problematic when you turn on a regular station and you're looking to hear news or sports, and you hear this type of language.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: Now, frankly, when I read it, I just found it a bit incredulous.  You know, coon, I mean that's the term that the guys used.  Slip of the tongue, well, it had to be somewhere in your consciousness for it to slip out.  So to me, it's always a slippery slope to start thinking about what people's intent was, but he had a responsibility, just like the rest of us.  We're on the air.  He said it, and he has to pay the price for it.  So again, I think it has to be a strong message that's sent.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: And piggybacking on that, I think black Americans have another responsibility. We will refuse to really deal with people who use the N word, black entertainers, rap artists and such, so we're sending a mixed message out there in the universe, and we're going to have to get clear about our own message before we can really get stark about language and how it pertains to us.

Walter, Yvonne raises the point that really the N word has now been taken over, in some ways, by African-American entertainers.  Some hip-hop critics say that this is an attempt to diffuse the word.  Are we going to have to diffuse every racist word?  What is the appropriate response to all the many different slurs that are against African-Americans?  And of course, every ethnic group has slurs against them.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetworks.com)
text: Well, I mean, I think we should have a zero tolerance policy across the board, and I do think it's a matter of context, particularly when you're talking about news programming.  Look, I was one of the people that led the charge against Bob Grant in the New York metropolitan area because Bob Grant had had a history when he was on WABC radio, of just slurring African-Americans.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetworks.com)
text: But I think that we also have to look back--I mean, I've just listened to that clip.  That was no slip of the tongue.  You know, if that was a slip of the tongue, I have a few choice words I'd like to say right now on the air, but I know that I can't say them.  So you know, I think that we have to put things in context, but I think Yvonne is right about we have to get our own act together and determine what the standard is going to be because we are sending mixed messages when we also use derogatory terms within our own community that we then deem offensive when others use them.  So I think, you know, there is a need for clarity here.

Walter, let's move on to another topic.  The U.S. Supreme Court rejected a request to give residents in the territory of Puerto Rico the right to vote in U.S. presidential elections.  This is the latest development in a longstanding debate over the islanders' constitutional rights, and it may actually precipitate a new referendum on whether they should be independent, a U.S. state, or remain a territory.

In some ways, this reminds me of Washington, D.C. where Puerto Rico has a Congressional representative, but they can't vote.  Washington, D.C. has a Congressional representative, but that representative can't vote.  In this case, they can't vote in the presidential elections, even though they're affected by U.S. policy.  Should they have a voice?

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetworks.com)
text: I think they should definitely have a voice.  I mean, I think it is akin to what we have in Washington, D.C. where you still have taxation without representation.  I think it's almost incredible that in 2006 we have appendages of the United States where citizens are affected by U.S. laws are pretty much treated as U.S. citizens, but being told that you can't vote in a presidential election.  And I think it will drive the debate around whether or not there should be independents or whether or not there should be full statehood for Puerto Rico, as I believe, as there should be for Washington, D.C.
Bob?

Puerto Rico's voted several times and they've consistently rejected statehood.  And so I think that speaks because one of the arguments or the argument, I believe, that the government uses in denying them this right is that only states, only people who live in states can vote in the United States, in the 50 states, can actually vote for the president.  And apparently, if you're a U.S. citizen, as Puerto Ricans are, but you move to Puerto Rico from the U.S., you then cannot vote.

So what has to happen, of course, is there has to be an amendment to the constitution as which is what happened with Washington, D.C. giving them the right to vote.  And it remains to be seen if there is enough backing for something like that to happen here.

Yvonne, you know, ultimately in some ways this is up to people in Puerto Rico to decide if they even want to try to be a U.S. state.  Why do you think that there has been so much resistance to becoming a U.S. state even though it would confer extra voting rights?

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: Well, I think it's an issue about whether or not they want to retain their own individuality, and as was just mentioned, in 1998 they had a referendum and 46 percent of Puerto Ricans decided, voted in favor of statehood, 2.5 percent voted for independence, total independence from the United States, and 50 percent or thereabouts wanted none of the above.  They voted for none of the above.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: So I think that does speak to the ambivalence.  Certainly they have some limited benefits to being under the aegis of the United States, but for them, I think a lot of Puerto Ricans think it might be more of a loss to their identity as Puerto Ricans to become a state.  And frankly, a lot of the people who voted for statehood were, from my understanding, the more affluent Puerto Ricans. The working class and poorer Puerto Ricans were not particularly in favor of this.  So again, I think the argument continues to be made until Puerto Ricans make a more vigorous attempt or aggressive attempt to want to determine what their status is, that United States is not going to really have much of an incentive to do any constitutional changes or any amendments to benefit them.

Walter, let's tackle the topic of drug free school zones.  They are almost a joke in some communities because if you want to buy drugs, some folks say you just go to a drug free school zone.  But these laws have been a staple of the war on drugs.  Now some legislators and activists, are asking whether these laws are fair and effective.  The Justice Policy Institute released a report yesterday claiming that the laws have not shielded young people.

In fact, only 1 percent of the cases that come out of these laws involved drug sales to youth, but they have been disproportionately affecting blacks and Hispanics.  Should these laws be reformed and revised?

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetworks.com)
text: Well, I certainly think they should be revisited.  I mean, I think, you know, if you look at drug use in the United States, certainly we still have a serious problem, and I think there was a psychological effect when these laws first went into place that we wanted to think that, at least around schools, that there was sort of a zone of safety.  That hasn't necessarily happened.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetworks.com)
text: So I think it is time to revisit this situation, and I think there might be some other policy remedies that are more effective than this notion of creating these drug free school zones.

Bob, in fact, this is a really staggering little piece of information.  Around Yale University, the only place that is not included in a drug free school zone is the golf course, which shows how big these radiuses are.  And in some cases, these laws entail mandatory prison terms, precludes such options as probation or treatment.  They really affect how the drug offender is rehabilitated. Is that an effective way to treat the people who are offenders, the people who are incarcerated, to say, okay if you are in this specific area, no rehabilitation for you?
Saying no rehabilitation for you?
Yeah.

Well I think it's the drug user who needs the rehabilitation more so than the drug dealer. I don't have any sympathy for drug dealers. The fact that entire cities in some cases are considered drug-free zones so that you get more intense penalties, 'cause that's the thing, if you're caught selling, obviously, selling drugs is illegal. If you're caught selling drugs in a drug-free zone, you, there are mandatory penalties that go along with that, so that's really the problem here.

It, it doesn't bother me that drug dealers in urban areas who are typically selling to my people, black people, which is something I'd like to stop, I don't really mind if they're going to get stiffer penalties. If it's, maybe they should go out to the golf course and pedal their wares if they want to not face a penalty so, so stiff. So I think, honestly, I think that's a ludicrous argument, that black people face this more than any, more than anyone else.

Yvonne, what Bob is saying, really gets to a fundamental question in the black community? You many have people in the same community, you do have people in the same community who are dealers, who are users, who are victims, who are friends and family of users. What is the appropriate way to try to strategize a criminal justice policy that deals with addiction, deals with the drug dealers? What would you like to see on an urban policy level?

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: Wow, that's a large question, Farai.
I know, I'm throwing it at you.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: Well I think, I think first things first, I have to agree with Bob. I think the whole conversation about whether or not African Americans or Latinos are disproportionately affected is a red herring. I think what is more interesting, I would want to know is, are there more drug activities in this area? If there's more activities in these particular areas, in comparison to suburban areas, then I think it stands to reason that, you know, that people who are selling in these areas possibly will be black and Latino.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: And, therefore, they're going to be the people who you are going to arrest. So I think this is like an apples and oranges conversation. Who, were is the crime, and who are the drug dealers? And I think that's the number one issue that we have to deal with.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: I also, too, think that there should be certainly more drug treatment facilities for people who have addiction problems and who want to clean themselves up, but, again, I tend to agree with Bob. I'm not so sympathetic to drug dealers. I think that, certainly, if this is first time offense, perhaps you should not get the same penalty as someone who is a repeat offender. But by the same token, we shouldn't give you a slap on the hand and say, good job. I think it has to be some type of piece into, into these penalties.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: I think that children should be protected, perhaps more so than adults. So if these safety zones are not working, that that needs to be addressed, but I think that, you know, we keeping throwing race at issues a lot of times, and they are smoke screens to deal with the issues that in some areas, there is more crime. In some areas, there are black and Latinos who are committing the crime against other black and Latinos, and we have to deal with that, and stop worrying about what's happening in suburbia.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: Suburbia has their own set of issues, and that's it. If there were white people who could make money coming into urban areas and selling drugs, they certainly would do it, and they certainly are already there. So, I think we need to deal with things on the ground instead of overlaying everything with race automatically.

Walter, what about the issue of rehabilitation? Bob was essentially saying, look, I want to rehabilitate the drug users, I don't care so much about the dealers. But some of the dealers see prison as basically a school for crime. You go in, you come out with more skills, you can commit better crime.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetworks.com)
text: Well I think we have to treat the addiction side of the public health problem, and I don't think we do. I think we treat it as sort of a criminal justice problem, and I think that's part of the overall problem with U.S. drug policy right now. It doesn't make any sense whatsoever, and until we begin treating people that have, you know, addictions, we're always going to see, you know, a recurrence of behavior of the nature.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetworks.com)
text: You know, in terms of the racial overlay, you know I will tell you, you know, drugs are rampant in suburban communities. And I think it's a matter of how, you know, environments are perceived because you could probably go into any suburban community, particularly around a school, and find major drug activity. And perhaps, you know, in cities that are exempting golf courses, perhaps they need to include the golf course because I'm quite sure there's some activity going on, on that golf course.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetworks.com)
text: I think U.S. drug policy just has not made sense, period, across the board. And until we begin to really treat this as a public health issue, really determine that we're going to make sure that we put the dealers behind bars and not let them get out for a substantial period of time, and make this notion of dealing drugs, no matter where you deal them, you know, a very serious issue, we're always going to come back to this. And unfortunately, for small children who are being caught up in it, and if you go into urban communities, they are being caught up in it at a very early age, I think we do have to refocus our attention on how we protect children and young adults in this matter.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: But I think the point, what I was trying to get at, at least in terms of clarifying is that in certain communities, it's right there in your face. If you're standing on the corner, you're accosted by the dealers, and that's a reality. Where, certainly, I agree with you, there are drugs everywhere, but at least in some other communities, it is more cloak and dagger and clandestine. So I agree that it needs to be across the board penalty, but I think it's, in some places you cannot even walk down the street without being intimidated or fearful because the drug dealers have taken over, and I think to pretend that that does not exist is to obscure the real problem.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetworks.com)
text: I'm not pretending that doesn't exist.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: Sure.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetworks.com)
text: I just want to make sure that when we begin looking at this that we look at both sides. I mean, I would agree with you, but I've also been confronted, you know, in my space in suburban communities.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetworks.com)
text: I just think that we have this tendency to believe about the intensity in urban community but not understand that if you talk to a lot of parents in suburban communities, they're scared to death because this stuff is now so prevalent.
Right.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetworks.com)
text: And so public that I think we tend to always think about large, metropolitan, urban centers. We've got a problem across the board with drugs in the United States and until we really have a common sense approach, unfortunately, our children are going to be the victims.

All right, we are going to have to leave it right there, a great topic. In our New York bureau Walter Fields, CEO and publisher of the NorthStar Network.com, along with Bob Meadows of People Magazine, and in Washington D.C., Yvonne Bynoe, author of the book Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip Hop Culture. Thank you all.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetworks.com)
text: Thank you.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: Thank you.
Thank you.
This is NEWS AND NOTES. I'm Ed Gordon.

On today's Roundtable: Residents of upscale New Orleans' neighborhoods say not in my backyard to FEMA trailers. And Wal-Mart to the rescue, kind of. Joining us today, from our headquarters in Washington, D.C., Julianne Malveaux, economist, author and president and CEO of Last Word Productions, Inc. From our New York bureau, Bob Meadows; he's a writer from People Magazine. And joining us via phone today from Winston-Salem, N.C., Nat Irvin, professor of future studies at Wake Forest University. He's also a columnist for the Winston-Salem Journal.

All right, folks, let's talk first about an interesting story that hit the U.S.A. Today this week, and what we are seeing is the Justice Department now launching, what many are calling a landmark lawsuit against a county Democrat chairman in Mississippi. Here's the interesting twist here, Julianne Malveaux. It's about Voting Rights Act, but it's talking about alleged racial discrimination against whites. Many people are concerned that what the Bush administration may be doing is trying to cloud this area. What do you think?

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: Well, clearly, the injustice department has consistently has been crowding the area of--clouding the area of voting rights. This particular story is almost amusing. When you look at the fact that you're talking about a city that's 80 percent black, and the mayor is white; so where's the racial discrimination?

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: But indeed, Ed, since the passage of the HAVA, Help America Vote Act, in the wake of the disastrous 2000 election, we've seen the kind of parsing where some of us will talk about voter protection--making sure that voters well treated--the Republican injustice department has talked about so-called voter integrity, or making sure that people are properly documented as voters, and so taking a principle of protecting voters and turning it on its head.

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: And this case looks like the same thing. You've got an aggressive African-American man who is playing hardball Democratic politics. I don't see any racism there, and it's just ironic that in Mississippi, where people died for the right of black people to vote, suddenly this injustice department is deciding that white people have been discriminated against.

Well, Bob Meadows, the Justice Department says of this chairman, Ike Brown--and he's one of those old, grizzled veterans who's been around. We should note, he doesn't receive a salary for this. I mean, he's in it for the love of politics. The lawsuit suggests--and here are just some of the allegations--that Brown recruited black candidates to run in the county knowing that they did not meet state residency requirements, that he excluded whites from participating in county Democrat affairs by using such tactics as moving sites of meetings, that he attempted to prohibit whites from voting in Democratic primary elections by challenging their registrations and absentee ballots. We know that these are all tactics that were used against blacks.

They were and they are. Still, as one of his friends says, is that things that Ike is doing are things that are happening in other counties as well. These are very serious charges, and you know, Ed, Ike doesn't really seem to deny any of this. He says that he wants to only have Democrats who are going to stay Democrats, and they're not going to, all of the sudden, turn into Republicans, and I guess he means--obviously he's talking about white people doing that. I think these are serious charges. You do always have to look at it, well, this is Mississippi, of course, as Julianne pointed out, you know, where Medgar Evers was shot and Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner, etc. But still, it's something that, well, if you're looking at in this county, you need to be looking at it in every single county of Mississippi.
Nat Irvin, we should note that while he does not rebut specifics of the suit, he does suggest, as the article says here, a blanket dismissal by calling all of this bogus.

speaker_label: Professor NAT IRVIN (Future Studies, Wake Forest University)
text: Well, that would be--that would certainly be what you would expect from Ike. I think that this whole suit is mostly about style rather than substance, although as Bob and Julianne noted, or certainly Bob noted, that he has pushed the line, and perhaps, maybe has even crossed the line when it comes to how he is going about trying to bring about what he sees as justice.

speaker_label: Professor NAT IRVIN (Future Studies, Wake Forest University)
text: But, you know, I don't think, overall, that there is any movement to disenfranchise white voters in the South, which is what I think would be--I mean, that would be something serious, and for the Bush administration to get itself caught in trying to prosecute a guy, who, basically, is just a hardball politician--you know, plays hardball politics, has just, maybe crossed the line, I just--it just strikes me so odd that you would be using the Voting Rights Act to try to affirm the rights of whites to vote in this incident.

speaker_label: Professor NAT IRVIN (Future Studies, Wake Forest University)
text: It just doesn't make much sense, especially when you think about, you know, the, I guess, this 2003 case with Tom Delay and how the Republicans went about trying to recreate opportunities for Republicans to be elected in several districts, you know, even managing to--you know, not only on a state level, but on a federal level, essentially to try to create an opportunity for Republicans to be elected to Congress. I mean, when you look at that in context, it seems like--and of course, to be fair, I should say that the Justice Department and the Bush administration did have questions about that, but it just puts--and finally, I guess, I'll just say that it puts the Bush administration in an odd position to pick Ike Brown as an example of how whites are being discriminated against.

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: It's selective prosecution, and nothing but. It's simple, selective prosecution. It's consistent with these people's notion of colorblindness and the level playing field. I mean, if, as Bob said, if you're going to go through county by county and prosecute everybody, I would warrant that there'd be more white folks you're prosecuting than this lone, you know, pitbull of an African-American political activist.
But that doesn't excuse the point if in fact it's true, Julianne.

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: Well, if in fact it's, but it sounds like this guy is just doing hardball politics. But more interestingly, how much energy has this injustice department--I will continue to use the term injustice because, I mean, you know, here they're anti-affirmative action--but they can find this black man to prosecute, but how much energy have they put into keeping voters away from the polls. Why weren't they, you know, in St. Louis when people snaked around hours in line, in Ohio where polling places were closed? This is where you need to look and not at this little bitty town in Mississippi. I'm not excusing anything. If the brother's wrong, he's wrong. But it seems to me that the bigger wrong is the selective prosecution of this injustice department.

Well, but as you know, Julianne, sometimes it's easier to make a statement in a small town like this, and they just want to set the precedent, and obviously, that's what they're attempting to do. But Bob Meadows, here's the interesting point. This was the kind of tactic we saw early on in the Bush administration when Mr. Ashcroft was moving this. We saw it kind of go away after he stepped away. Are we seeing now this last gasp of the Bush administration saying, let us teach you something?

Well, considering, all that they have taught us thus far, like war is good and all that kind of thing, this is actually, I guess, is probably in line as getting back to it. And it's interesting you bring that up, because, of course, one of the things that Ike said was the reason he got so riled up was because of the 2000 election, as Julianne pointed out, where there were all these injustices going on, and people couldn't actually get to the polls and the miscount and all that kind of stuff. So here's one more lesson.

All right. Let's turn our attention--and Julianne, I'll ask you to put your economist hat on for me here--where we see--this is the headline from the Los Angeles Times: “Insurers Saw Record Gains in Year of Catastrophic Loss,” and what we are finding out is that the insurance industry made a almost 45 billion dollar profit last year, even after accounting for all the claims of policy holders wiped out by Hurricane Katrina and other big storms of 2005. Here's what executives described in terms of the profit, which was 18.7, almost 19, percent. They said it was simply a fluke.

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: Well, I'd like to be a stakeholder in one of those flukes, you know. It's fascinating, Ed, that part of the contribution to the profit has certainly been the hardball that has been played with Katrina survivors, where the--you know, the calculus of was it flood or hurricane or--I mean, I think--or wind that damaged people's homes, and people have to go back and prove that all these things do happen at the same time. But people are going to have to go back, are being challenged to go back, and prove was it flood, hurricane or wind in order to get their money. All they know is that their house is messed up.
Right. So your policy may have covered you, for instance, for flood damage, but they may have said, well, the wind caused this damage or vice versa.

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: Precisely. And so it seems that this hardball is a direct contributor this 18.7 percent, you know, profit. It's an amazing--it, literally, is an amazing rate of return, and at the same time, these insurance companies are talking about getting out of disaster relief, out of catastrophic coverage, which is absurd. So it's sort of like, let's take the money and run. They come into communities, you know, basically wooing communities, and now they want to go out.

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: This really is a--it's a cry for more regulation, and I know a lot of people don't like regulation, but clearly, this is an industry that provides a public good, and as John Garamendi from California, who's a very good, progressive insurance commissioner, says, you know, this--it's time, you know, it's really time to regulate this. Policyholders are left holding the bag. You know, insurance companies, clearly, are there to make a profit, but this rate of return is extraordinarily high.

Nat Irvin, put this next to what we saw earlier in the year and that's the oil companies that talked about record profit that they found after Hurricane Katrina. It does leave you a bit vexed sometimes.

speaker_label: Professor NAT IRVIN (Future Studies, Wake Forest University)
text: It does, Ed, and you know, and most people are just going to go look at, going to look at this and say, how in the world? And of course, the whole argument when the oil company executives went before Congress was that, look, we're not able to make a profit. We're--our investments are huge, that our refinery costs are up and that, you know, we can't find any new places to drill oil and, you know, listen we're barely making it here. And, of course, the next day, or the next quarter, you've got these, I don't remember exactly what the profit numbers were, but they were extraordinary. And then, second, you see then, not only were the profits extraordinary, but then the price of oil, the price of gas was going up.

speaker_label: Professor NAT IRVIN (Future Studies, Wake Forest University)
text: And, you know, people are starting to put some things together and this insurance company, the fact that the insurance companies are making so much money when people who, thousands of people lost their homes, as Julianne said, and then you have to have a lawyer to be able to exact a claim. And many people have not been able to get any justice at all. And what this fits into is part of what, and I don't want to blame the Bush Administration for it, but it is…

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: Oh, go ahead.

speaker_label: Professor NAT IRVIN (Future Studies, Wake Forest University)
text: …the terminology of the ownership society. You see people losing their pensions, you see companies--everything being shifted towards the individual, in other words, the responsibility of the individual. You not only have to figure out--you have to be--everything being directed toward single payer--individuals being responsible for every aspect of their lives. And you don't look for relief, even in this instance, apparently, not even from the government.
All right, Bob, let me put on my USA capitalist hat…
…and that simply says that I'm in business to make a profit and make money. And the fact that I'm in the disaster business shouldn't prevent me from making money.

Absolutely, I completely agree with you, you are in business to make money, as we all are. The--as Nat just said though, the thing that's most upsetting about this is, okay you're making profits, great. Don't then raise your rates to exorbitant levels where we can't afford. Don't scale back your coverage so that I'm paying more and getting less. Sure, go ahead and make your money, but keep your service up, don't backslide.
All right, Julianne Malveaux…

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: You know the question is…
…isn't that the American way though? I hate to say it, but isn't that the American way?
Oh, no.

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: Well, you know what? The point is that, I mean, profit maximization certainly is at the basis of U.S. capitalism, okay, now I've said it. Ugh! But the fact…

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: …you know, but the fact is that you could also contain profits and that's why some industries are regulated.
