That's why we have regulation in telecommunications industries, because we believe that people have a right to have a telephone. You provide telephone service for the poor. That's why you have regulation with things like oil, because, basically, people need energy. And what insurance companies are signaling, frankly, is that there needs to be more regulation in that industry. The--if you liken capitalism to a wolf, Ed, then we have to look at government or citizen activists as dentists, to try to file the wolf's teeth down. Because, you know, predatory capitalism…

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: …literally, I mean…

speaker_label: Professor NAT IRVIN (Future Studies, Wake Forest University)
text: Oh, that could be good.

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: …extraordinary profits at the expense of the people.
All right, let's bring the good old mom, apple pie, flag-waving Wal-Mart into this.

What we're hearing from Wal-Mart is--this week--that they're suggesting that they're going to bring 50 stores into distressed areas and help small businesses around those locations thrive. Because what they've been fighting and facing is that mom-and-pop operations suggest that when Wal-Mart comes into the neighborhood they are eliminated. So, Wal-Mart is suggesting that they are going to develop grants for nearby companies and give them free in-store advertising as part of a new economic development plan. And that they'll also hold seminars for minority and female-owned businesses, and show them how to become Wal-Mart suppliers. Is this altruism, Bob Meadows, or is this simply Wal-Mart trying to evade the fight?

Well, if it is, you know, either way--either way I'm glad that they're coming into these neighborhoods and I'm glad that their doing these types of things. I would hate it, you know, I hope they set one up right in, you know, two or three down in Detroit. I'm hoping that's what happens.

Is it altruism? You know, again Wal-Mart's in the business to make money. They hired Andrew Young earlier this year, a PR stroke, they're doing this PR stroke, great. You know, they've been accused of unfair labor practices; but again, I just want to look at--for me, the bottom line is that they're coming into these communities, they say they're going to do all this stuff--as long as they do it, then I have no problem with it.

Nat Irvin, we had Andy Young on when the announcement was made, and quite frankly he said, look, for those of us who live in suburbs and have a Wal-Mart down the street and can get in our fancy cars and drive to wherever we want, it's easy for us to say that they're carpet baggers and coming in. But for people who don't have it, be quiet and let them get in there and stabilize this community.

speaker_label: Professor NAT IRVIN (Future Studies, Wake Forest University)
text: Yeah and he's absolutely right, too. Easy for me to say, or easy for--as you pointed out, easy to make judgments about Wal-Mart when you don't have, you know--but when you're in the situation where you don't have opportunities, one for employment, or two to access--to get goods at a reasonable market, then what do you say to folks like that?

speaker_label: Professor NAT IRVIN (Future Studies, Wake Forest University)
text: I'm absolutely happy that Wal-Mart is making this move and I think that, as it, you know, as this development evolves, there will be a lot of input from a lot of community people who will, frankly, I think, help Wal-Mart to deal with some of it's other issues about how much it pays, is it able to provide a living wage and healthcare benefits--some of the practices that it's been criticized for from some of the other sectors of our economy.

speaker_label: Professor NAT IRVIN (Future Studies, Wake Forest University)
text: But I think this is not only smart, this is not only good for the community, it's a smart business sense. Wal-Mart understands that roughly, and this is a whole black community, you know, but you're looking at a trillion dollars in a couple years of buying power that comes from the black community alone. And then, when you start to think about, in terms of the employment, where will the growth come from in terms of people who can actually work, that also comes from minority communities.

speaker_label: Professor NAT IRVIN (Future Studies, Wake Forest University)
text: So they're both smart from a business standpoint, they're not saying from, in terms of their image, it does something for them. And I think they're also going to get something from listening to what community people have to say about how do you help develop small businesses, which I hope continue to grow within the minority communities.

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: You know, let me just rain on this parade…
Julianne, real quick cause we've only got about a minute left, but what about the long term of this, Julianne?

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: Well that's, you know, my brothers are sitting here with pom-poms for Wal-Mart and let's just be clear. Not, it's not about Wal-Mart being “bad,” it's about the terms and conditions of work for Wal-Mart. They're paying less then competitors are paying. They are running small business out of areas where they settle. Certainly they're blighted areas here in Washington, D.C., and New York, all over the country, that could benefit from the--from the effects of having a vibrant store there. But we have to look at the terms and conditions that they come to communities. People need to be paid fairly, they need health insurance. You're running around doing seminars, on one hand, and paying people $9 an hour on the other, is just untenable. And so we need to just, you know, let's step back a bit and make sure that activists are involved, make sure that zoning is fair, make sure that healthcare is offered, which isn't offered to everyone at Wal-Mart…

speaker_label: Professor NAT IRVIN (Future Studies, Wake Forest University)
text: Yeah.

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: …right now. Make sure that there are full time jobs and not part time. Remember, these are the people who locked immigrants up to keep them from leaving the store.
Yeah.

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: So, you know, let's not get too happy. Here's the issue, can you have economic development and economic justice at the same time?

speaker_label: Professor NAT IRVIN (Future Studies, Wake Forest University)
text: Sure, you can.

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: That's a question. Well, let's see.
All right. All right. Well, we'll have to see if, in fact, that is the case, and if I can quote the great American poet Don King, only in America.
Julianne Malveaux, Bob Meadows and Nat Irvin, thanks, so much. Appreciate it.

speaker_label: Dr. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, President and CEO, Last Word Productions, Inc.)
text: Thanks, Ed.

speaker_label: Professor NAT IRVIN (Future Studies, Wake Forest University)
text: Thank you, Ed.
Thank you, Ed.
Up next on NEWS AND NOTES, NPR senior correspondent Ron Williams wraps up this very busy week in Washington with his panel of political insiders on our weekly installment of “Political Corner.”

This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Ed Gordon. On today's roundtable, more on the New Orleans mayoral race and mental illness in the military. Joining us to discuss these topics and more from our New York bureau, Bob Meadows, writer with People Magazine. Joining us via phone today, Robert George, editorial writer with the New York Post. And also with us, Callie Crossley. She's a social and cultural commentator on the television show Beat the Press seen in the Boston area, and she joins us from member station, WGBH, in Boston or Cambridge or somewhere thereabouts.
All right, folks, let's talk a little bit about what we just heard, and that's the interview with Ray Nagin. Robert George, what did you think of what you heard from Mayor Nagin?

speaker_label: Mr. ROBERT GEORGE (Editorial writer, New York Post)
text: Well, you know, I wish Mayor Nagin had been a little bit more, I think, forthcoming in his own role and his own culpability, I think, in the tragedy--what is still the ongoing tragedy with New Orleans. I mean, he says that he saved lives and so forth, and that may be true, but it seems to me that there was a large failure of leadership, whether it was--obviously, it wasn't just his fault and it wasn't just the governor's fault. But it seems that he seems to minimize his own role in the overall disaster, and I would be a little bit surprised if he wins reelection. But I know enough not to predict elections in Louisiana.

Callie, here's the interesting dynamic in all of this: it seems to me that all of the entities that were involved really are minimizing their role in the disaster, whether it be Ray Nagin and the local government, state, federal. No one really wants to say we weren't ready for this.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (Social and cultural commentator, Beat the Press)
text: Absolutely. And particularly facing the hurricane season coming up, he almost has to do that. Because to now say, listen, some of the decisions I've made were not good ones makes him very, very vulnerable in his upcoming campaign. Remember, he's facing Mitch Landrieu, who is a homegrown boy and who knows what happened there. He was there on the ground as well in a different capacity.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (Social and cultural commentator, Beat the Press)
text: So you know, he's going to have to be made to stand behind everything that he said. And everything that he said, a lot of people have problems with. So at the same time, though, I have to say I'm surprised that he made it this far, so I don't know what to predict.

Well, that being said, Bob Meadows, here's the interesting point, and it always--and I say this all the time--depends on which prism you look through. While he was not a favorite of the African-American community during the first run, Ray Nagin made points in the African-American community when he stood up and got mad. Some will say that he lost the decorum that many politicians have. But many African-Americans said they liked when he got up and demanded the federal government get their act together and get down there and used a couple of curse words here and there.

We noted that the book that is written by Mr. Brinkley suggested that he was holed up in the Hyatt Regency, yet former police chief Eddie Compass told us on this program that Mayor Nagin, particularly the first couple of days, was out in the streets with him dealing with the situation. So, it all depends on what side of the fence you sit on.

Sure, he made… He was passionate at a time when you needed passion. You didn't need decorum. You needed somebody to actually stand up and say the things that he said, especially right at the end of--right as Katrina--in the days after it.

And one of the things that I did like that he said, Ed, while you were talking to him. He said, I take full responsibility. That is one thing that I want to make sure that we remember. He did say that, I take full responsibility for what happened.

Sure, he's going to tout his programs. And again, I was in New Orleans right as Katrina was coming, and I remember he said, get out. He said, don't come to the convention center. I remember all that stuff. People went there anyway. The exact--the evacuation plan may not have been what it should have been, but again, 90 percent of the people in New Orleans did get out.

Here's the biggest problem, Callie, and I asked the mayor this. I've asked others, who are dealing with New Orleans, this. The problem is the levee system. He suggested that they were running into a few problems. The Army Corps of Engineers has suggested that it's not going to totally be ready June one. Heaven forbid if we have a huge hurricane system go.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (Social and cultural commentator, Beat the Press)
text: Absolutely. There are some pretty decisions coming up, including whether or not to get rid of all of the housing that's remaining in some of those neighborhoods--to get rid of that. I think that, maybe voters will go in and think--some of them, anyway--who can bring the political muscle here? Who can negotiate with all the powers that be--whether you're mad or not, whether you think it's unfair or not--to at least put us in a position to maybe start attacking those levees and making them be repaired in the way that they should be?'

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (Social and cultural commentator, Beat the Press)
text: Some people, I think, may think that, well, maybe Mitch Landrieu can. I think that while it was appropriate for--maybe some may think it was appropriate for Ray Nagin to get mad--the question is, what kind of political damage did he do, so that he can't work across the board to bring the muscle that needs to happen there, to bring the resources that need to happen there, to really make that city safe again?

speaker_label: Mr. ROBERT GEORGE (Editorial writer, New York Post)
text: I guess…

Let me, Robert, because I've got to move us along, take us to another embattled politician. That's one that takes to the airwaves tonight, and that's the president of the United States, in what we don't see often--and that's a rare prime time address from the oval office--particularly with this president.

He's going to talk about the immigration, quote, “problem,” and talk about how he--Bob Meadows--is bringing the National Guard in to secure the Mexican border. Some will say that this is just window dressing.

Well, other people say that it's militarization of the border, which many people do not want, as you've mentioned. As you mentioned, that the president of Mexico, Vicente Fox, wants to talk to Bush about that. Bush says this is going to be temporary. I don't believe it. His temporary things tend to run a lot longer than just temporary. And it's really a question of, is this what we want? I mean there are plans, in Congress, to build fences--The Senate, across the board--to keep out illegal immigrants.

But I do think, you know, last month, when we had all these rallies--despite all the rallies, despite all the hundreds of thousands of people who turned out for them—still, I think the majority of Americans--they may actually support this kind of thing where you send the military down there to keep people out. Because people don't mind if people come, they just want them to come legally.

Robert George, here's the problem: many people are suggesting that we are, as we've seen our military stretched, stretching the National Guard. And that if, for instance, we have another problem during hurricane season on the Gulf Coast region, oft times, National Guard troops are deployed. We are going to see them now deployed elsewhere. Are we stretching the National Guard, now, too thin?

speaker_label: Mr. ROBERT GEORGE (Editorial writer, New York Post)
text: I think that is a--I think that's a very strong possibility. However, the president is caught really, right now, between two opposing forces. I mean, he's got a conservative base, which possibly more so than anything--even including the out of control spending--is really up in arms over the immigration issue. And he wants to show--show that he's got some control on this. And by bringing out the National Guard, that's one--that's one way of doing this.

speaker_label: Mr. ROBERT GEORGE (Editorial writer, New York Post)
text: On the other hand, you've got governors who are also feeling, literally, overrun by having to deal with the immigration problem. But Governor Schwarzenegger, in California, and Governor Richardson, in New Mexico--both of them have said that they have really practical concerns about whether they want to allow their National Guard forces to be turned over to the federal control, because they've also been deploying them to deal with the immigration problem, themselves.

speaker_label: Mr. ROBERT GEORGE (Editorial writer, New York Post)
text: So, I think that the main point about the Guard being overstretched is a serious concern. But right now, you've also got the president with a 29, 30 percent approval rating, feels that he has to do something to affect the issues that are eroding his base.

Callie, interestingly enough here, what we're seeing with all of this is a precarious dance by Republicans--who often, if they're not on one political end of the spectrum or the other--finding not really, knowing where to land.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (Social and cultural commentator, Beat the Press)
text: Well, and President Bush is the prima ballerina. This really is a toothless tiger situation, because what you do by putting those National Guards there--and we've been told according to sources--that they're there for surveillance, not enforcement. So what you have is a federal minute man situation. You know, that volunteer, you know--group that's going out there, saying, we're watching. We don't have the authority to arrest anybody.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (Social and cultural commentator, Beat the Press)
text: So, what good does that do? You know, you really are--I mean, he really is dancing around the issue. And you have the governors, as was pointed out, not happy with that. And I think what's interesting about this, is that he has refused--or they have not allowed those governors to know--exactly what the plan is for the National Guard troops, which makes that a little suspect. I've got a feeling that if…

Something very interesting coming out of--coming out of Connecticut. Let me move to the next topic, because we'll continue, obviously, to watch this and talk about it tomorrow after he actually gives the speech. But this from the Hartford Courant, that's suggesting that--they received information obtained under the Federal Freedom of Information Act--that shows that U.S. military troops with severe psychological problems have been sent to Iraq or kept in combat. Some service members--who eventually committed suicide--have been kept on duty, despite clear signs of mental distress--sometimes after being prescribed anti-depressants and given little or no mental health counseling. Bob Meadows?
You know, that's actually a great segway from the previous one. Your original question was, are we stretching our troops too thin? I think this is a sign of that.

As I said, the Army's having trouble recruiting, they can't get new soldiers in there, so they have to use what they have. You can't really blame the commanders. The president ordered them into this war, so they have to follow him. They have to use the soldiers that they can.

But I'm a little surprised, because I remember, and I think we discussed it on this show a couple months ago--saying that, for post traumatic stress disorder, more soldiers were actually being treated and diagnosed with that--because the Army was much more alert to these symptoms now. So, I'm a little surprised by this coming out, which is kind of saying the opposite, that they're ignoring it.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (Social and cultural commentator, Beat the Press)
text: Yeah, but the thing about this story is that the commander in chiefs, according to this story, are the ones making the decision about whether somebody is competent enough from a psychological perspective to stay in the field.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (Social and cultural commentator, Beat the Press)
text: I mean, I think that's dangerous. They are not competent to make that distinction. That's the work of a medical person. So, you know, that all… it's scary to think about.

speaker_label: Mr. ROBERT GEORGE (Editorial writer, New York Post)
text: Well, indeed. And obviously, they're not just endangering the specific troop--this specific individual, the person who's suffering under this--they're also endangering the efficiency and decorum, and so forth, of the entire battalion or troop--troops there.

speaker_label: Mr. ROBERT GEORGE (Editorial writer, New York Post)
text: I mean, you don't want to, obviously, have somebody that is psychologically unstable, armed, lining up with other men in service. And so, I mean, think it's a really disturbing, it's a really disturbing report, and it's something that's going to have to be addressed.
Bob.

Exactly. I can't agree more. This is something that is very dangerous, as Robert just said. And also, I think that we really have to look at what's going to happen to these soldiers once they come home. That's really one of the keys. I mean, not just that they're in battle now, but what happens when they come home? We have to make sure that we're taking care of them.

All right. Let me quickly get to the last topic of the day, and that is: California State Senate passed a bill last week, that would require textbooks in public schools to instruct students on contributions by gay and lesbians, in the state's development there, in California. Also, a contribution of transgender people. They believe that it will win--at least Democrats do--support in the General Assembly, and then we would see that move with real legislation.
Robert George, do you see this as an important move that may work it's way across the country?

speaker_label: Mr. ROBERT GEORGE (Editorial writer, New York Post)
text: I certainly hope not. I mean, of course, if you've got certain individuals who, and sort of specifically identify themselves as gay and lesbian and have made contribution, there's no--I have no problem in terms of putting them in the basic curriculum.

speaker_label: Mr. ROBERT GEORGE (Editorial writer, New York Post)
text: But if a lot of this is sort of an ex post facto identification of--this person was gay, and that person was lesbian, when that was never a specific aspect of who they were or how they identified themselves--I think it just becomes of this sort of kind of historical feel goodness, which I think helps--may help the gay rights lobby, but I don't think it really helps us in learning. Helping students learn anything, really, about the history of California or the history of the United States.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (Social and cultural commentator, Beat the Press)
text: I think it's interesting…

Callie, one would believe that the gay community, as in years past African Americans fought to make sure that our contributions were put in historical context. One would believe, that those support this legislation, would say the same.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (Social and cultural commentator, Beat the Press)
text: Possibly. But this would be the first time that you have a group of people who are really, you know, held up because of their sexual orientation as opposed to their cultural orientation. And what the gay rights movement was--as I understood was--that we, as gay people, are bigger than that. We are more than our sexual orientation. That's how I read what had always been stated by advocacy groups. So this to me feels a little bit like going backwards.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (Social and cultural commentator, Beat the Press)
text: You know. So, I'm not quite sure about that. I will say--add this: Here in Massachusetts, there are parents filing suit because, as you know, same sex marriage is approved here. And in one of the classrooms, a teacher did a story in which two characters, this was a fictional story, were married. And that seemed appropriate because in Massachusetts, this is legal. But parents were saying they were not alerted. So at least that will be avoided in California because everybody will know that this is happening.
Bob, one of the--one of the state senators who is the first openly gay member there in the senate suggested the bill would “help shape attitudes of what gay people are really like,” end quote.
Yeah, she says that it will ease tensions between gay and non-gay students.

You know, I'm kind of up in the air on this, I have to say, because I have no trouble with people advocating for what they want. You know, if she wants this and people have passed, the assembly has passed this--you know, I think it's great.

I don't know if it has much of a chance of passing Governor Schwarzenegger, once it gets to him. I know that--in whatever I've read about this, parents of, you know, the usual--the conservatives are completely against it. And parents are coming out and saying, you know, they hope it doesn't happen. And you know, that this is something that they should discuss in their house--things like that.
You know, I do look at it in a way, you know, as, would I want this for black people? You know, if, you know, if you want black people noted.
But again, it's kind of like, as long as gays are out of the closet, then, yes, recognize what their accomplishments are.
We should note, interestingly enough, that a spokesperson from the governor's office says that the governor has not taken a position on this quite yet.
Alright, Robert George, Bob Meadows, Callie Crossley, thank you so much. Greatly appreciate it.

Just a quick note to the listeners. If you'd like to comment on any of the topics you've heard on the round table today or any of the stories that we give you here on NEWS AND NOTES, please call us at 202-408-3330 or you can email us. Log onto npr.org and click on contact us, and please be sure to tell us where you're writing from or calling from and how to pronounce your name.
Alright, folks. Thanks so much. Appreciate it.

speaker_label: Mr. ROBERT GEORGE (Editorial writer, New York Post)
text: Thank you.
This is NEWS AND NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya.

On today's Roundtable, Illinois Senator Barack Obama says Democrats need to court evangelicals and the fight for fair housing continues in New Orleans. Joining us today to discuss these topics at NPR headquarters in Washington, D.C., economist and author Julianne Malveaux, President and CEO of Last Word Productions. And, in our New York Bureau, Bob Meadows of People magazine, along with Pedro Noguera, professor of education at New York University.

Welcome and let's get right to it. So yesterday, the Supreme Court handed down a decision about the Texas Congressional map engineered by former House majority leader Tom DeLay. The court ruled that most of the map will remain as is, but a section was thrown out because new boundaries didn't protect minority voting rights. Bob, what are the implications of this decision?

That remains to be seen. I think one of the things that the Supreme Court did, of course, by upholding this matter, is that it could open the door to the majorities - party majorities from different states from just redrawing districts any time they want. This is something that, obviously, people are very concerned about, especially the minorities in the various states.

Georgia Republicans have already done it. Colorado Republicans are trying to do it. Perhaps Democrats in New York, Illinois, wherever, will try to do the same thing. So, obviously, like I say, this is something that the repercussions of it, immediately, in Texas, is that what they redrew two years ago after what they have redrawn six years ago is going to sort of stay the same, but it might be changed a little bit, but it may have huge repercussions down the line.

Well, actually, the ruling says you can redraw the lines whenever you want, you just can't do it this certain way. And what I found interesting, among many other points, is that the kind of opposition among the justices was on the basis of civil rights of Hispanics. It says, you know, Justice Anthony Kennedy, writing for the majority, says Hispanics do not have a chance to elect a candidate of their choosing.
So this voting rights law that really started out in the African-American interest has now been used for Latinos. Pedro, what are your thoughts on that?

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: Oh, I think that's a wise decision, given that, you know, the Hispanic population is growing not only in Texas but elsewhere, important that there be representation - adequate representation in the Congress and in the state legislature.

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: I think the real question, though, with respect to the Supreme Court decision is the fact that it opens the door for this kind of manipulation of elections at every state. And I don't think that's a good thing for voters and I don't think it's a good thing for the overall health of democracy in this country.
Julianne?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Farai, you know the Voting Rights Act was extended to include Hispanics, actually, when it included the states of New Mexico and Texas back in - I think the first amendment - so the first amendment of the 1965 Voting Rights Act. So the Voting Rights Act has been cognizant of the interests of other minorities all the while. It did start out, clearly, with the African-American push for equal rights, but it did include others very early on. So I think that's important to note.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: This decision is horrible, and we need to look at it in light of what's happened now with the Voting Rights Act. In fact, the very authorization of the Voting Rights Act has been tabled for now, because Congress people in Texas and Georgia do not like the fact that their states are held out as special. But you see that this case, in terms of the Hispanic voting rights issue, makes it clear that Texas should still be held out as special.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: So when you look at the Supreme Court, combined with what's going on in Congress, I say that people of color have a lot of work to do to ensure that our voting rights are maintained. If, any time, one party gets a majority they get to go in and draw lines, we will have utter confusion at the Congressional level. And the inability, especially of Representatives of color, perhaps, to maintain seniority.

And in this case, Tom DeLay, of course, who's given up - or giving up the political life - he had such a profound impact on Texas politics. And basically, what he engineered is going to remain. Pedro, what do you think of the implications of Texas going from 17 to 15 Democratic majority in the legislature - now it's overwhelmingly Republican?

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: Well, that, I think, is a real issue. If you look at the history of Texas, Texas was always a state that produced several very significant Democratic Congressmen and Senators. And that's going to be increasingly less likely to be the case not simply because the politics of the state have shifted, but because the lines have shifted.

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: And Texas is becoming increasingly diverse. You look at cities like Houston, Dallas, San Antonio, these are majority minority cities. To not have African Americans, Latinos, represented there, I think represents a grave miscarriage of justice and a real sign that the Democratic rights of those citizens are being violated.
But...

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Farai...
Julianne.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: ...the word gerrymandering is one that we need to never forget. Gerrymandering was what was used, essentially - and one of the reasons why we had the Voting Rights Act - to divide people. What I think is going to end up happening here - and I'm very, very apprehensive about the fact that, as Pedro said, you have these majority-minority cities, but you have these majority white suburbs. And you basically see lines being drawn in ways that will pit African-Americans and Latinos against each other in some elections but preserve the suburbs for white Republicans.

You know, I want to turn to Bob with another topic. It's time that the political parties are starting to go head-to-head around the 2006 midterm elections, precisely the Congressional districts we're talking about. Senator Barack Obama criticized his fellow Democrats yesterday. He said his party did not "acknowledge the power of faith in the lives of the American people." Now he's urging Democrats to woo evangelicals and other churchgoing folk so his party has a fighting chance in 2006. What do you think of that?

I thought it was - I remember about a year ago, Republicans were saying that they need to target blacks through religion. And, obviously, TD Jakes helped out George Bush by supporting him. This is something that, yes, the Democrats do need to do.

And it - Barack's speech the other day was very impassioned. This is something that he said has been bothering him since he was debating against Alan Keyes back in the 2004 campaign. Alan Keyes accused him of not being a Christian because Barack supports gay rights, because he supports abortion. And Barack was saying that, listen, the conservatives have taken over this by pretending that white evangelicals only care about gay rights, abortion, prayer in schools, things like that.

But what he's saying is the Democrats have to tailor their message. They have to - to these people, and that they can't just avoid or dismiss this issue. They have to attack it head on. I think it's brilliant.

Pedro, you know, Bob was just saying that this is something that was very passionate, this speech. And, in fact, during the speech, Obama says, kneeling beneath that cross on the South Side of Chicago, I felt I heard God's spirit beckoning me. I submitted myself to his will and dedicated myself to discovering his truth. He has not spoken in those terms before. And in some other nations, like Europe - many European nations, religion is kind of a non-topic in most of politics. But is this a case of sincere emotion or a case of if you can't beat 'em, join 'em?

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: You know, I'm really concerned about it. I think that matters of faith should really be left up to an individual. We don't elect politicians to run for religious office. We're electing them to represent us. It's one thing to appeal to people of faith and to appeal to the humanitarian interests and concerns. It's another thing to say you're going to appeal to evangelicals, many of whom are very committed to very conservative causes, and which would alienate another part of the base.

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: I'm concerned that Obama is pandering to a segment of the country that has no interest in support of the Democratic Party at all. And it really concerns me because I see this kind of approach from Obama in a number of areas - around the war, the fact that Lieberman is now his mentor - I see it as a very bad sign.
Julianne?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: I agree with Pedro up to a point. I do think that Obama is basically straddling a middle ground very, very carefully. And I think that that's problematic when, clearly, he has other views. I think with this faith thing there is something for Democrats, especially African-American Democrats, to begin to deal with here, which is how you spin the message of economic justice in the context of faith. And that's what we need to do.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Faith is not just about gay rights and abortion. It's also about that which you do to the least of these, you also do for me. So if you really want to talk about faith, how do we have so much hunger in this country? How do we have so many people who are still earning the minimum wage?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: You know, I would have had more respect for Brother Obama if he had brought some of the social justice issues in to segue them with faith. Because I think what you've seen is this wedge and it hasn't impacted African-American voters. You look at Ohio, when you just start talking about abortion and gay rights.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: But there's so many other things that are said, that are spoken to in the Bible, including the issue of fair wages. That is biblical, I mean, if you want to play faith. So, you know, if you want to play the faith card, play it in a way that works and that really is humanitarian.

Julianne, Bob, whoever wants to jump in, what about this whole issue of whether or not this is a lost cause. You know, the president's poll numbers have been dropping. His evangelical support isn't even as high as it was. Does this mean that the Democrats have a perfect opportunity, or that, you know, they shouldn't waste the - the Democrats shouldn't waste their energy?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Oh, Farai. Don't say perfect opportunity and Democrats in the same sentence, because you know they're going to mess it up.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: You know if they had a perfect opportunity they'd mess it up. The issue is not Mr. Bush. The issue is his party. I mean, the reason why Barack Obama is speaking up is because about a quarter of the Republican Party are hard-line Christian conservatives. You cannot even talk moderate Republican unless you acknowledge that fact.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: So take Mr. Bush off the table and look at the future of this party, and you can see why it's appealing for a politician who's straddling the fence to try to talk there.
Bob, do you think that - I mean, Barack Obama gained prominence for being, I guess, only the second or third black Senator since Reconstruction...
Right.
...and it's tough out there. It's tough out there for all politicians, but when you have that broad of a constituency, does he have any choice in this whole straddling the line thing?
Well, certainly he has a choice. He has a choice but he - well, okay. He has a choice, but I guess, perhaps maybe not if he wants to be reelected.

He does have to appeal to this wide range of people. He's a Senator, he's not a Congressman. He's got to appeal to a lot of people to get reelected. He has to - he's a black man and I imagine next time his candidate - the candidate the Republicans run against him is not going to go down because of sexual charges or whatever it was. So he really has to appeal to this group. He's got to try to at least.

That's why I think it's a brilliant strategy. That's why I call it brilliant. I'm thinking in the context of him winning, not so much how it's going to help the greater masses. But if he just wants to win, if the Democrats want to win, yeah, they've got to go after this base.
All right. Well, I'm going to turn, reluctantly, because I think there's a lot more there, to another topic.

A coalition of advocates says a federal plan to demolish four public housing complexes in New Orleans is discriminatory. A lawsuit filed this week alleges the demolition plan violates international laws that protect people displaced by natural disasters. In this case, that means mostly poor African-Americans.
And, Julianne, I know you have been aware of this case. Can you give us a little more sense of what's going on?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Well, half of New Orleanians have returned already. But of the people who lived in public housing, only 20 percent have returned. That 30 percent gap represents a gap in public policy. Those who have the means can come back, but those who don't can't come back.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: HUD is literally playing games here when they say they're building for a more prosperous time. Well, what does a more prosperous time mean for poor people? In other words, you're not planning to provide public housing, subsidized housing, for poor people. You're writing them out of the future of New Orleans.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: The lawsuit, I think, is actually quite brilliant, to use Bob's word, because I think it does put it in the context of international law and the right of return. And those are the key words that many New Orleans activists have been using to talk about future plans.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Now, Nagin's back in, but he still hasn't come up with the plan as to how to get people who've been dispersed, you know, this New Orleans diaspora, how to get them back to the city if they want to come. Some don't - but many do as you talk to them, and the issue is there's nowhere for them to come. This really does speak to the politics of income, because those who have are able to move and those who don't aren't.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Renters, apparently, have no rights. Public housing tenants apparently have no rights, and this is what...
Let me, yeah...

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: ...is being pushed to the court.

...let me just get Pedro in here. Do you think that using international law in this context is really going to make a difference, because the U.S. has a kind of tense relationship with international law?

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: Well, it may not make a difference in the U.S. courts. It does, I think, resonate politically within the United States and beyond, because the world saw what happened in New Orleans, saw that - how the greatest, you know, power in the world turned its back on very poor people during a time of crisis. So I think there is an embarrassment factor to be weighed here.

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: But the other side about the public housing, that we all have to keep in mind, is New Orleans was a city that was in terrible shape before the flood. It had such intense poverty, and we should not be seeking to recreate New Orleans as it was. The real question - and HUD actually has some fairly innovative programs, there's a program called Hope Six, which is a program designed to bring mixed-use housing - the real question is, can you bring those who were there back, but under better conditions, with better housing, in cleaner, healthier communities? That's the challenge the mayor faces.
And you know that Hope Six was on the chopping block, in terms of federal funding...

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: I know.
...but it was saved, for the moment. Bob, let me ask you.
Sure.
How could America make a promise to New Orleanians that we will get you back home, and will this country make that promise?
Well, you know, America is so good at, you know, keeping its promises to minorities. I mean, just look at all those treaties with the Native Americans.

It's very easy, you know. Who - there was a Congressman, Richard Baker, I think he was quoted as saying something along the lines of, you know, we, God did what we couldn't do, finally cleaned up public housing after Katrina. I honestly think that's the mindset that is here.
Wow.

I have to say that. They don't - as Pedro said, as Julianne - you know, they don't want these people back. They don't want it the way it was. You have a power structure in place, and a lot of these people are black, who, sure, sure, you're going to build it in the future, you're going to build it down the line. It's not coming now. People are desperate. They're living in abandoned homes. They don't have - because people are there, as Julianne implied, but they don't have anyplace to go so they're living in abandoned places. There's no electricity. There's no running water. This is - it's a complete travesty, as far as I'm concerned.

Well, you know, we at NEWS AND NOTES went down right after Katrina. We went back six months later, and what astounded me was just seeing the Ninth Ward and other areas just block upon block upon block of homes that were just molding. You know, and could be - I mean, it is just mind-boggling.
Julianne, I guess the last word to you. Should America make a promise? And what would make that promise real?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Well, America, as Bob has said, has made lots of promises. I think that it is unconscionable that Americans have not risen up, and especially our organizations like the NAACP, risen up and demanded that these people are replaced.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Pedro, with all due respect, these so-called innovative plans that HUD has have to be balanced again HUD's inability to execute. They have been unable to execute for the past eight months, and I basically do not believe they're going to be able to execute in the future. The AFL-CIO's work offers us some hope, but the fact is Americans of good conscience must rise up and say this is unacceptable.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: What if it happened in Washington, D.C., Farai, or in Los Angeles, or in San Francisco post-earthquake, or somewhere else? Why is it acceptable in New Orleans for poor people where most of them are black?

All right, we're going to have to leave it there. In Washington, D.C., economist and author Julianne Malveaux, President and CEO of Last Word Productions. And, in our New York bureau, Bob Meadows, of People Magazine, along with Pedro Noguera, professor of education at New York University.
Thank you all.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Author; President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Thank you.
Thank you.

And, as always, if you'd like to comment on any of the topics you've heard on our Roundtable, you can just call us: 202-408-3330, or you can send us an e-mail. Just log in to npr.org and click on Contact Us. Be sure to tell us where you're writing from and how to pronounce your name.

Next on NEWS AND NOTES, NPR Senior Correspondent Juan Williams follows up on FEMA spending on this week's Political Corner, and the inspiring story of an immigrant who worked as a janitor before becoming a U.S. college president.

This is NEWS AND NOTES. I'm Ed Gordon. On today's Roundtable, a program offers rewards to the poor for doing the right thing, and a raid on Congressman Jefferson's office is ruled okay. Joining us today to discuss these topics and more, from our NPR headquarters in Washington, D.C. - Mary Frances Berry, professor of history at the University of Pennsylvania. From our bureau in New York City, Bob Meadows. He's a writer for People magazine. And Roland Martin, executive editor of The Chicago Defender, joins us from member station WBEZ in Chicago.

All right, folks. Let's look to what we have been talking about for a number of months, since the raid in May and the search of Congressman Jefferson's office. And this is U.S. District Judge Thomas Hogan who put down a ruling, suggesting that, in his words, members of Congress are not above the law. He has rejected the request from lawmakers, as well as Representative Jefferson, to return materials seized by the FBI during that raid.

The suggestion, and these are the judge's words: “Congress' capacity to function effectively is not threatened by permitting Congressional offices to be searched pursuant to validly issued search warrants.”

All right, Roland Martin, here we have it. This judge - and interestingly enough, this is the judge who approved the FBI's request to, in fact, conduct the overnight search of Congressman Jefferson's office. What say you?

speaker_label: Mr. ROLAND MARTIN (Executive Editor, The Chicago Defender)
text: Well, I certainly agree with Judge Hogan in every respect. I've always contended that a member of Congress does not have the right to simply do as they wish.

speaker_label: Mr. ROLAND MARTIN (Executive Editor, The Chicago Defender)
text: I certainly understand separation of church and the powers, but clearly, they had a well laid out subpoena, a search warrant, that they wanted executed. And so again, you're talking about possible crimes here, and so I don't care whether - and I'm not going to play the race card. I don't care if he's black. I don't care if he's white, female, Hispanic, Asian. It does not matter. He is not above the law.
Mary?

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Well, I think, Roland, that's all fine and dandy, but - and the people I talked to in New Orleans are only concerned about the apparent corruption that Jefferson apparently has been engaged in, whatever the legal issues are. But there's something a little suspicious about this. I mean, when the - Hogan approves the idea - Jefferson's private lawyer, House counsel, and the Capital police were not able to observe what they were taking from his office, and there may have been materials there having to do with his functions as a Congressman and his constituents.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: There was nothing wrong with letting him observe it. I can imagine if Congress went and got a subpoena from some judge - and you can always find a judge to issue a subpoena - to go to the White House and to pick up materials in connection with some criminal, supposed-criminal matter - say the Abramoff matter - and to not let the White House counsel or anybody at the White House to tell the guards, the Secret Service, that they're going to break in if they don't let them - this would be ridiculous. So I think the way in which they did it raises some concerns, and I'm not surprised that since Hogan issued the search warrant, obviously he would uphold his search warrant. We'll have to see what the Supreme Court says about it, but I think that there should have been a better way to go about it, and not to raise all of these questions.

Bob Meadows, here's what's very interesting in all of this. This angered members of Congress so much that some quietly suggested, and some a bit loudly, that they were going to retaliate by perhaps tinkering with FBI and Justice Department budgets.

The President stepped in and said, hey, let's cool this thing off, find out what happens - can you work out a compromise? Otherwise, we're going to see what the ruling will be from Judge Hogan. And suggested that the Justice Department would not seek to regain custody of the materials until this was ruled upon. So clearly, this has raised the ire of many - not just Congressman Jefferson - on the Hill.

And thus far, no compromise has still been worked out. This was actually something that actually brought Republicans and Democrats together when this came out. They said it was a breach of constitutional boundaries, that Bush has again overstepped his authority, the broad executive authority that he adheres to. People, like you say, were outraged about this. And it remains to be seen what this is going to mean for New Orleans, of course, because Jefferson has been bumped off - the Democrats went against him.

They bumped him off, forced him off the Ways and Means Committee. He's up for re-election. One of the things that he's been touting is how much aid he's been able to bring to New Orleans post-Katrina, so it remains to be seen. What is he going to be able to do now?

speaker_label: Mr. ROLAND MARTIN (Executive Editor, The Chicago Defender)
text: You know, Ed, first of all, the judge really agreed with the point that Mary made in that he said that the way it was executed was not properly administered, and so certainly that is an issue. But I think again, the ruling was very specific as to whether or not it was proper to execute such a warrant on a member of Congress' office. So again, how it was administered and whether or not it was permissible I think are two separate things.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: We'll have to see what happens on appeal.

speaker_label: Mr. ROLAND MARTIN (Executive Editor, The Chicago Defender)
text: Right.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Ultimately, these records will be looked at by the FBI. They will either be looked at with some judge overseeing it, like they did in Watergate, where the judge oversaw the looking at the tapes and listening to them and so on. Or it will be seen just by the FBI under an order.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: That will ultimately happen. One could argue, though, that members of Congress - in a bipartisan way - were concerned not just because of the legal issue, but because there have been many issues raised about some of the other members of Congress.
Well that's it, Mary.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: They might be worried about somebody coming to their office.

That's the crux of the argument, and there are those who are upset about this in this way: they believe that the whole question of the separation of the branches was brought out not because they felt that Congress was trying to uphold that stalwart thinking, but it is the ability to protect themselves -those who might not be doing the right thing - for fear that they might be the next raided.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: And there have been many examples in the Congress of people from DeLay to Cunningham, that guy out in California. There have been many examples of this, of wrongdoing, by people in Congress. So there may be - and the Abramoff thing isn't settled yet. And it has - there are many byways involved in that. So I don't think that - when people start raising constitutional issues, it's like quoting the Bible. They don't always do it for the purest of reasons.

All right. Let's turn our attention as that story continues - and we'll continue to watch it as we have - to take a look at something out of Chicago. And here's the interesting point: you know the points you earn for perhaps using your credit card or using your frequent flyer miles that earn you either trips or little trinkets that you can go to catalogues and receive? Well, in Chicago, residents in low-income neighborhoods are earning rewards points for paying their rent, getting their children to school every day, and seeking work. And the points can be applied even if they attend PTA meetings, and can be applied for gifts like DVD players and the like.

This is from the Pathway to Rewards Program, which is run by a non-profit organization called Project Match. They have awarded about $19,000 in prizes to 130 people since the inception a year and a half ago.
Roland Martin, should, in fact, people be getting rewards for what many would considered to be doing the right thing?

speaker_label: Mr. ROLAND MARTIN (Executive Editor, The Chicago Defender)
text: Well, sure. I mean, look. I don't have any problem with it, because, again, if you also step outside of individuals receiving welfare, you know, you have other cases like that. I mean, I don't see the particular issue. The question is, you know, we're going to - we can always find something to complain about. We can always say that well look, you know, you're on welfare, or you're in public housing, you know, you shouldn't - if they're giving you free bus passes, you shouldn't be getting that. You can at least pay for something.

speaker_label: Mr. ROLAND MARTIN (Executive Editor, The Chicago Defender)
text: We can always come up with something - hey, look. If they are going to PTA meetings and got kids in school, that's great. You know, what the heck? The quicker they can get off of welfare, that's great, and they can build the momentum. So, you know, look. I have no problem with it whatsoever.

But the assumption there, Bob, is that this will move them off of welfare and suggest a new way of thinking for many of these folks. Others will argue that this is simply the idea that many people hold, misguided albeit, that you have to give incentives for these folks to do the right thing.

You know, they may have that - what you first said, yes. That is the hope, that these people, that the people in these positions will develop a new mindset so that they're doing right, the right thing. They're trying hard, they're just, they're striving all the time. But I have to piggyback on what Roland said. My first reaction to this was sort of a negative thing. And then I remembered, you know, when I was a kid, my father used to offer money for A's and B's. That didn't necessarily make me do well, but it was definitely a nice incentive.

This is private money that's being given out here. It's not coming from the government, it's not public. These are people who want to do this, the project. These are people who want to do this; this is not coming out of any taxpayer's pockets or anything like that. I'm all for it.
So, Mary, I'm going to show my age. This is no different than, I think it was called S&H Green Stamps. I remember people used to collect those and go get an iron or whatever.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: You're an old man. You're older than...
I am an old man.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: You're older than I thought you were, Ed. Doggone.
I don't know what you're talking about.
So is this to some degree the same thing?

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Here's what I think about it. First when I heard about it I thought, now what is it, dogs doing tricks, and you know, you give them a treat? And then I thought, well, there's nothing wrong with that. It is like all these things that we've been discussing, the different kinds of rewards. So I see nothing wrong with it if, in fact, there is some kind of support network to make it possible for people to do the things they need to do, and if someone - I don't know who it is in this program - is taking into account whatever problems these people are.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: These people are in hardcore poverty, who are the ones who are left after a whole lot of people have already gotten off welfare and into work, and so on. And these are people who have a lot of different needs. So if there's some framework for this to make it possible for everybody to do whatever it is, whether its to get a high school equivalency or whether it's to get a job if there is a job, then its something that I'm all for it. But if it's simply making promises or getting some people to do something and leaving the others behind then I'm not. But, overall, I'm for it.

All right. Well, here's the bigger and larger and longer argument in some people's minds of getting something for nothing. Others will say that this certainly is something for atrocities, and that is the growing question of reparations for African-Americans, descendants of slaves.

Of late, we've seen this movement change from a fringe movement to scholars and historians picking up the mantle and running this race: one of the major proponents of it, Charles Ogletree, a friend to this program and a Harvard law professor, one of the leading legal minds in this country.

What we have seen of late are small victories across the country, including the Moravian Church and Episcopal Church both apologizing for owning slaves and promising to battle current racism. The Episcopalians even went as far as to launch a national yearlong probe into the church's links to slavery and to decide whether the church should compensate black members.

Roland Martin, I remember, again, years ago, when people talked about reparations, there was this thought of this larger umbrella, if you will, that every black descendant of slaves would receive money, probably, and preferably in some people's minds, from the government. Here we see these small victories. Is this isolated, or do you believe this is a way to show the growing thought and movement of reparations to black Americans?

speaker_label: Mr. ROLAND MARTIN (Executive Editor, The Chicago Defender)
text: Well, I think the great thing is the people who are advocating reparations are getting smarter as to how they approach this. The problem with the whole reparations debate is we went from looking at the history of racism and jumped all the way to, well, how much am I getting, without actually dealing with a process. And so, again, when you begin to advocate on behalf of those African-Americans in Tulsa, when you begin to go look at those very individual cases, that's how you build momentum. You simply don't just have a conversation going from, you know, A to Z, and everything is fine.

speaker_label: Mr. ROLAND MARTIN (Executive Editor, The Chicago Defender)
text: And so, when you - and also when you begin to force people to confront the reality of American corporations that have grown and benefited as a result of slavery, when you begin advocating it that way, it's a whole different picture. Everybody always wants to focus on, well how much money. Well, I'm not giving -those negroes don't deserve any kind of money whatsoever. But when you begin to force them to say, wait a minute, this particular church, this corporation, this institution, was built on the backs of slaves then it changes the view of people, because you can really quantify something.

speaker_label: Mr. ROLAND MARTIN (Executive Editor, The Chicago Defender)
text: So again, that was a very smart move to do it that way versus that whole emotional issue, because, sorry, you were not going to win that debate.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: I wanted to make two points about this, Ed. One is that I was pleased that the book I wrote about Callie House and the 1890s reparations movement was very important and these people have been, who are in the movement, have been reading about it because they didn't know that blacks, at least those blacks who were alive and in being had asked for pensions and reparations; and that this brings into being a new legal approach, I mean, because they asked for it while they were alive.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: But the other point I wanted to make is a woman named Deadria Farmer-Paellmann is one of the leading lawyers who has brought most of these private corporation cases that I talked about in the article, and she was the one who first decided to go after the private - the corporations, rather than just focusing on the government. And I think what Ogletree and the (unintelligible) and the people who are an (unintelligible) and the other people involved, they have done, with looking at Tulsa and looking at getting legislation, is important.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: But I think the most significant thing that has happened is that when white folk, like Mrs. Brown(ph) and the Brown family that's been in the story that was in the news and white people in the churches and elsewhere, have decided, look, I don't care what the debate is among black people about whether we want reparations or don't want reparations. As far as we are culpable and as far as we have connections, we want to assert that something ought to be done.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: So I think the movement is gaining momentum, and the piece that's missing is in responsibility for reconciliation and reparations for our government, which John Conyers has been pushing forever. And that's going to take, I think, some time.
Mm-hmm. And Mrs. Brown, we should note, is a member of the Episcopal Church who screened a documentary focusing on white culpability in all of this.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Right.
All right, Bob Meadows, we should very quickly get your thought on this, and whether or not you see this as a up-tick in the idea of more people joining the fight for reparations.

More people joining the fight. You know, I'm not really certain that there will be more people, necessarily, joining it. I mean, people may jump on a bandwagon if it gets really rolling. But I think, as Mary says, you have some really good people on it, like Deadria, who are really working on this and, of course, Roland said, going about it with a new tactic by going after private corporations. And really, going after them is like a puzzle, because a lot of the organizations, companies that did that, 150 years ago, had been bought, sold, merged, into different things and they may no longer exist. So it's really, really an intensive research project too.

Well, Bob, one thing I can promise you, you may see some people if this thing really gets rolling, you will see some people jump on board if this thing really gets rolling. I can promise you that much. I don't know much, but I know that.
All right folks, thank you so much. Greatly appreciate it.

Next up on NEWS AND NOTES, getting out the vote in poor communities. The working poor could be the decisive vote in this year's election. And black athletes and the community; the author of a new book says they could be doing more to give back.
You're listening to NEWS AND NOTES, from NPR News.
This is NEWS AND NOTES. I'm Ed Gordon.
On today's Roundtable, Kofi Annan calls the Israel strike on the UN deliberate. And polls show pessimism.

Joining us today from Georgia Public Radio in Atlanta, economist and author Julianne Malveaux. She's president and CEO of Last Word Productions. And from our New York bureau, Walter Fields, CEO and publisher of the northstarnetwork.com. And Bob Meadows, writer for People Magazine.

I welcome you all. Before we get into what we were going to discuss, I can't help but want to get some idea of what you thought about segment A's discussion, and that is the legacy of Condoleezza Rice and particularly how she's handled the course of the last couple of weeks with the problems in the Middle East. Julianne Malveaux.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Well, I think that it was a really great discussion, and Phyllis Bennis really hit it right on the head when she talked about the issue of legacy. Her legacy is going to be the deaths of these innocent people in Lebanon.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: But, you know, this notion, Bill Fletcher's notion that she's an accidental Black person, all African-American people do not have to be liberal in thought. I kind of bristle at that. She is an African-American woman who is wholly wrong about foreign policy.

Walter, the idea that some might think it's a little strong to assume that this will be her only legacy, as she's done a number of things, but certainly this will go high in the bio when you read about her down the line one might believe.
Well, I think she's just singing from the neoconservative songbook. I mean, she's consistent with how neoconservatives have positioned themselves on the issue of the Middle East.

And I agree with Julianne. I mean, I think you can be ,lack and conservative, but you can also be black, conservative and wrong. And I think she just happens to be wrong. You know, there was a funny skit in the Dave Chappelle Show where they had a racial lottery and she was given away as sort of a free choice along with Colin Powell. I think for many black Americans that's probably going to be, you know, the perception of her legacy as we move forward.

Yeah. Bob, it's interesting because we are as a people quick to jump up and yell and talk about we're not a monolith. And sometimes it's difficult for the community to accept different thought down the line.

That's absolutely true. I mean, you look at people like Condoleezza Rice and - you know, you can go - there are many, many people you can name. But all Condoleezza Rice has to do really is just go to a black church and she will be accepted as if she has never left us.

Honestly, like everybody said, I hate to hear somebody's blackness questioned, because, as a black person, you can't hide in the closet and pretend you're not who you are. This is how Condoleezza Rice has grown up and she is representing - I think her legacy will be as the first black woman in such a high power, position of power.

I agree. All right. Let's turn our attention to the latest NBC News/Wall Street Journal poll. The findings are very interesting, some of which aren't surprising. Sixty percent of the people polled are doubtful that the Iraqi War will come out for a successful conclusion on the United States' side. Eighty percent say that America has declined - the pessimism we see is a long-term decline they believe.

But here's what was interesting to me, Walter Fields. Sixty-five percent of those polled feel less confident that the lives of their children will be better than the lives they've led. And as we know, that has been, almost since the beginning of this country, the American dream. That juxtaposed to 2001 when this question was last asked to respondents, only 49 percent believed that to be the case.

Well, you know, in many ways it calls to mind my memories of growing up, you know, during the period of the Cold War and how, because of this supposed Soviet threat, many parents were very fearful about the possibilities of nuclear war.

And I think we're back at that point in this country. Where, if you look around the world, there's not a corner of the world where you really have stability. And I think for many parents looking at their children - and I look at my 7-year-old daughter - I am very concerned about what type of world she will grow up in. Because as we look, we're beginning to see not only the issue of sort of military conflicts, but we're also beginning to see a destabilized global economy. And the fact of the matter is is that most Americans are very concerned that their children will not even have the type of life that they had, which is a very scary thought.

Bob Meadows, here's what's interesting in all of this. It seems to me -and this is just my observation - but it seems to me that if these polls are to be believed, that many people have almost resigned themselves to that fact and are doing little to try to change it. Whether it's through voting, because we still see abysmal numbers of voters turning out, whether it's becoming active in the streets and protesting, whether it's participating within your neighborhood to try to better the block, we just don't see it.

A lot of times when things really seem so bleak and you can't have any influence over it whatsoever - such as your vote doesn't count or your representatives don't vote in the way that you would like to see them vote -you drop out. I can't honestly say that people are going - you know, parents are still doing the best they can for their children, they're trying to instill them with values and things like that to make them be better.

And also you have to let them know that, hey, this isn't the world that I grew up in. You're going to have to do better, you're going to have be better and you're really going have to make your voice heard. So parents have to lead by example by making their voices heard as well.

Do you believe that to be the case, Julianne Malveaux? That the majority - of course, there are people out on the frontlines; of course, there are parents that are intricately involved in their children's lives - but what about a generality here if we can allow that for the Roundtable. Do you believe that to be the case that people are in the mindset that they can make change?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: You know, Ed, the thing that I've been talking about a lot when I'm running around the country speaking is a theme that I call the end of imminence. It's what is happening to the United States once the imminent world power, the dollar, will soon be overtaken by the Euro.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: As Walter said, we do have a destabilized global economy. If we want to look at children, at young people - there's a young woman, her last name is, I forget. Anyway, her book is called Generation Debt, and it talks about how 20-somethings have it so much worse than 20-somethings 30 years ago. We are investing less in our children collectively, although individual parents may be doing their best.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: When I graduated from college, I had $2,000 in debt. The average young person now has $20,000 in debt. And so we really are not investing in our young people. We're not investing in our infrastructure. Ed, Europe is turning out more engineers than the United States is. India and China turning our more engineers than the United States is.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: This pessimism is, quite frankly, very justified. But the challenges, as you said in introducing this issue, what do we do about it? It seems to me that too many people have accepted it.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Another big part of this is the fact that our population is shifting in ways that this administration and others have been wholly insensitive to. So as you see more Latinos, more African-American people. So who's going to take care of old people? Who's going to do the work? Who's going to be - but we going to invest in those people in terms of education. We see ourselves cutting back, especially K-12 inner cities.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: So when you look at some of this, you have to say the pessimism is justified and it's very unfortunate.

And, Walter, I don't claim to be the great economist that Julianne is, but I do know one plus one is two. And the idea of individual debt is one thing but the mounting debt this country is taking on, particularly each day this war goes on, eventually that has to be paid for.

Without a doubt. But understand that these deficits were also a conservative strategy. I mean, during the Reagan administration, they piled up huge deficits then turned around and built up the military and said we don't have money for social programs.

They purposefully have bankrupted this country, and people need to understand that; that what you're beginning to see is this notion of a shift. You have a small group of neoconservatives now who are creating this New World Order. And it is about the end of imminence, because if you look across the world and the opinion of the United States is in the toilet right now.

And part of it's because most of the world is beginning to understand how the United States is beginning to try to lay its footprint all throughout the globe. And there is this really angry reaction right now, particularly in the Arab world, about what's happening in the Middle East. Because they see that as part and parcel of what they U.S. went into Iraq.
So this notion of a destabilized world order is really the function of a small group of neoconservatives and conservatives who have basically decided to reshape the world.

It seems to me, Bob Meadows, that this country would go into some type of anaphylactic shock or something like that if in fact we're knocked from our perch as the world police, the big guy, the number one country. While that is, one would believe, generations off, we are seeing almost a sea change in how the world looks at the United States.

We have not really won a major - we haven't won a war since - I mean, granted, we won the Persian Gulf War, but that was a different - we had a different agenda at that time. It hasn't happened since World War II, that's 60 years ago. We can't just throw our weight around like we used to because people realize they can't fight us.

Nobody can really fight us, but what you can do is you can keep pecking away. And all you have to do is keep surviving. So what does that do? It just makes us look weak. It makes us look ridiculous for going into all these different situations.

The army right now, the military, rather, is stretched so thin we can't even take on another project. We can't do anything in Sudan. We can't do anything to help Israel out. We can't - or whoever - we can't do anything because we're so stretched.

What we really need to do is just go find Osama bin Laden. Everybody would have supported us for that, forever, because they understood. But instead, we're in a situation where now we have major, major egg on our face. And yeah, our reputation all around the world is shot.

Yeah, you talk about the Sudan. Tomorrow we'll have an interview with the president of southern Sudan and the vice president of Sudan, and that will be interesting. I conducted that yesterday, so we'll ask that folks tune in and listen to that.
All right. Let's turn our attention now to Pennsylvania...

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Ed, if I could just jump in for a quick second. Just one quick second...
Uh huh.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: ...because you say it's going to be generations. It's not going to be generations. It's going to be a couple of decades.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: If you look at what's happening with China and population and the economic pressure that they're putting on the world, in addition, as they industrialize and westernize, as cars go there and the impact on gas prices - in addition to the way that they're investing in education. I think it's around the corner, to see us knocked off our perch, if we haven't been knocked off it already.
