All right. Well, I'm the ugly American. So I'm holding true to two generations, doggone it.

All right, Julianne. Now, let's turn our attention to Pennsylvania and the race for governor there. Lynn Swann really stumbling, some might say. Others will suggest it's simply that he's outmanned dollar-for-dollar by Governor Ed Rendell there, the Democrat. But we are now seeing the president headed this way.

We should note that Lynn Swann, the former NFL All-Pro wide receiver was hand-picked by the White House to make this run. The president is coming in for a $10,000 per person dinner - an opportunity to have photo ops with George Bush.

Walter Fields, does it surprise you at all that we are seeing candidates not necessarily disassociate themselves - that happens a lot from two-term presidents who find themselves in different kind of quandaries, historically. But what we are seeing in some peoples' minds is not the kind of traction black candidates thought they might have, i.e., Lynn Swann, Kweisi Mfume, Mr. Steele, et cetera.

Well, the problem with Lynn Swann, I mean, the president is radioactive right now. And many Republican candidates, you know, are sort of dis-inviting the president. Lynn Swann - I saw Lynn Swann at the Republican National Convention, and I tell you, he was an isolated soul. I mean, it was very stark to see Lynn Swann and Mike Steele in Madison Square Garden, because they just stood out like, you know, it was incredible.

So I think the problem that black Republican candidates are going to have is, how do you position yourself vis-à-vis this White House? And how do you articulate a vision, that the stench of this administration isn't hoisted upon you?

I mean, Lynn Swann is going to walk a very difficult line here, because he's against a well-financed Democrat incumbent, Ed Rendell. And the chances of Lynn Swann winning this race are really almost zero to none. They picked him because, of course, he's a former Pittsburgh Steeler, high name recognition. But after you get beyond that, you can't run away from this White House. Even if the president doesn't show up, believe me, the Democrats in that race are going to paint George Bush all over Lynn Swann.

Here's what's interesting, Julianne Malveaux, the idea of a Michael Steele having enough money in his coffers to, in some degree, disassociate himself with the president. Lynn Swann is trying to do it without being quote, disrespectful, because he needs the president to come in to build these coffers.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Two very different candidates: two very different kinds of appeal.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Mike Steele is a pro. I mean, I disagree with him on virtually everything, but you know, it's interesting to see how he has gone in and peeled away layers of Democratic support. Dorothy Bailey, for example, a woman, sister, who is a former Prince George's County Commissioner, is supporting him. You know, lots of visible Democrats are supporting him because he goes to our churches, he does our thing, he, you know, he's thoughtful and all that. You know, he's wrong, but he's thoughtful.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Swann, on the other hand, is a political novice who doesn't have nearly the appeal or the charisma of a Michael Steele. And from that prospective he probably needs radioactive Bush much more than Steele does. He also, you know, Steele has been in politics. Swann is just sot of coming out there. It's a fascinating kind of thing.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: He - of the three African-American men who are running on Republican tickets -he could be easily called the sacrificial lamb. Republicans go out and pick somebody but then they don't really, can't do very much with them. Ken Blackwell looks good in his race. And Michael Steele, it'll depend what happens with the Mfume-Cardin primary. But in this case, this brother is just out there, you know, being Forest Gump. He's there.

Bob Meadows, though, it's interesting to see, when you line all of these men up who are running for state-wide office, the governor seats in these states, the differences. And also, the idea that I don't know that we've seen the excitement - even on the Democratic side with Kweisi Mfume - from the black community that many people thought would certainly be perhaps higher in volume right now.

Well, I would imagine it's - you know, some of it, as Walter said, you know - once you get past Lynn Swann's name and connection with the Pittsburgh Steelers, there's really not much there, necessarily, to get excited about. And so that's got to be it, that there are not exciting candidates. It's not Barack Obama, you know, from two years ago, that people can really rally behind, like that. So, you've got to imagine that, you know, black people aren't just, you know, you see a black face and you get excited. It's not like that anymore. You really have to come to the table with something. And that's something that Swann and the others, you know, they're not necessarily providing.

You know, its interesting that Bob says that, and while we don't, Walter, run to the television every time a black face is on - as we did in the 60s and early 70s - there is still this sense of pulling for the black contestant on a game show, or the black person in a race. And it is an individual, I guess, whether its charisma or a situation that, particularly on the political side, either excites you or does not. And as I said, I just don't see the excitement across the board for any of these candidates. Are we just too far away from Election Day, or is there something here?

I think we're a little too far away from Election Day. And I will say I still do run to the TV when I see a black person on. Particularly on the news and they're not, you know, they aren't the news - they are actually delivering the news. I find that real exciting.

But I think we are far from Election Day. And I think Mfume's race is going to be very interesting. Because, despite the issue of non-excitement, if Kweisi is able to take Prince George's County and Baltimore City, and Democratic Baltimore County, he will probably win that primary. And that's when I think the excitement will kick in. When it's a Steele versus Mfume race, then I think you're going to see some real excitement.
Yeah. Yeah, that'll be some...

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Absolutely.
...with 30 seconds, Julianne. That'll be exciting if indeed you see two black candidates vying for that seat.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: And if Mfume is able to pull that off, high kudos to him, because, you know, Cardin has basically out-funded, you know, outraced him like, by a factor of three or four.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: But, you know, I think its, we are too far from the elections. In Ohio there is a lot of excitement about Blackwell.
Yeah.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: It's very exciting. I was in Cincinnati a week or so ago, and although - and he's like a lightening rod on either side.
Yeah.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: I think in Pennsylvania Swann is, he's a football player. With all due respect.
All right. We'll see - all right, we'll see. Bob, Julianne, Walter, thanks so much. Greatly appreciate it.
Thank you.
Next up on NEWS AND NOTES, NPR's senior correspondent Juan Williams recaps the weeks' headlines from Washington in our Political Corner, and the a cappella sounds of Take 6.
You're listening to NEWS AND NOTES, from NPR News.
This is NEWS AND NOTES. I'm Ed Gordon. On today's Roundtable, the president admits his frustration with Iraq, and do we now have an ending to one of America's great mysteries?

Joining us to discuss these topics and more from our bureau in New York City, Pedro Noguera, professor of education from New York University, and Bob Meadows, a writer of People magazine - or for People magazine I should say. And from our NPR headquarters in Washington, D.C., economist and author Julianne Malveaux. She's president and CEO of Last Word Productions.

All right, folks. We woke up to a face that has become all too familiar for the wrong reasons to all of us, and that is little JonBenet Ramsey. A suspect now has confessed to killing JonBenet, saying that her death was an accident. A former teacher, 41 years old, saying now that he was in love with the child beauty queen. He was captured in Bangkok and will be extradited to the United States.

We don't know enough details to discuss this particular portion of the case truly, Julianne. But what we do know is this is one of those cases, now that we see someone who may be - and I underline may be - the murderer of this young girl, it shows us the idea of rush to judgment that Americans - and really the world - made in this case and often other cases. So many people thought it was the brother or the mother or the father who immediately said it had to be.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: You know, Ed, you're very right about the notion of rush to judgment. We've seen that in so many cases. But I think that's connected to this 24-hour cable cycle that focuses on certain kinds of cases and elevates them far beyond proportion.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Of course, the death of any child is a tragedy, but I would ask how many children's death have not had that kind of coverage? If you look at our community, the African-American community, at the number of poor children who are found dead that never get the attention or even the acknowledgment of a JonBenet Ramsey, whose death dominated the media for nearly a year.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: I feel very badly, of course, for the family because they basically operated under the cloud of suspicion with Patsy Ramsey even being accused of killing her own daughter, albeit perhaps inadvertently. But we have to look at what news has done about elevating cases disproportionately and how reporters who, you know, rush to scoop each other, come up with these crazy, half-cocked, far-fetched, you know, kind of theories that then become part of this spin cycle.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Just this morning there was a piece where they had three court-type - Court TV-types or legal lawyers - you know what I mean. Well, they had them again speculating. Like, why are they speculating? We don't have enough information. We the public need to demand that people put a period on that, that they stop it.

Bob, it's interesting. You worked for People magazine and that was a story that People covered back and front. When you think back 10 years ago -it's hard to believe she would be 16 had she lived - when you think back, as Julianne suggests the constant coverage of this, there were many of us in the media who thought that even at that point, you know, we were going too far.

You know, I really don't know if that's the case here. I mean one thing I do want to say is that most times when children are killed, it's by somebody that they know. That's a fact. So it's not really completely out of the question that people would think that the parents or the brother - maybe not the brother - but the parents had something to do with this. There was a lot of evidence…
: When I say too far, Bob, I just want you to understand I mean just about the amount of coverage we gave it, that's all.

Yeah and you know - I mean, but it happened and people bought it. So I don't really know if we - if there was - you know what I mean? Yeah, to me it's like okay, enough. But just the nature of the business itself, you know, people kept reading about it. People are going to read about it now, they're going to be fascinated. OJ Simpson, boy that was coming out of my ears. I couldn't wait for that to be over with. But people kept watching. People kept reading. So yeah, is it too much? Well, as you know, don't pick up the magazine. Change the channel. Do that type of stuff.

Here's the interesting point with JonBenet, Pedro, and the idea that you had videotape, as Julianne said, with the advent of 24-hour news we're so used to seeing, seeing, seeing. Had there been no videotape of this young girl on stage, had she not looked 13 or 15 rather than whatever age she was at the time - 6, I guess - you know, we would not have seen all of what we saw. The fact that she was a beauty queen really helped elevate all of this.

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: Absolutely, and I think the point that Julianne made earlier about the large numbers of deaths of children across the country and the fact that this is not an issue that we raise, it really speaks to the disservice that the media often plays in sensationalizing these kinds of cases and preventing the public from understanding the larger issues involved.

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: We have many children in America today whose lives are in jeopardy because they don't have secure homes, they don't have parents who can look out for them. And these are the bigger issues that Americans are not grappling with. Instead, what we get are these kinds of cases where these glamorous children and their wealthy parents are - occupy the news for long periods of time. And Americans just continue to not really understand the deeper issues that really affect the quality of our lives in this country.

You know, I've got to say, though, it's not even really just wealth parents. You know, that girl in Utah, Elizabeth Smart, her parents weren't wealthy - it's just white kids. That's really what it is.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Well, you…
Let's just be real.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: And what we ignore is the foster care system and the number of African-American children in the foster care system. There have been a couple of recent cases in New York that, to its credit, the New York Post had covered somewhat extensively. But that - those cases are like the tip of the iceberg. Our children are in trouble and folks are running around talking about JonBenet without talking about, for example, the oversexualization(ph) of that child and the extent to which, you know, sex and sexuality play a role in the exploitation of children.

Yeah, and say what you will. One of the things that happens when you see and hear people talk about something every day - the idea of the brother being suspicious or the parents being suspicious - even for those who are investigating the case, it does plant that in your mind. And sometimes you will react because you hear something day after day after day and start to believe it even in your subconscious. So it is something that we have to be careful about.

All right. We'll move our attention now to the president. We are finally hearing through cracks and crevices that the president - as he made clear in a private meeting held this week - is concerned about the lack of progress in Iraq and frustrated about the new Iraqi government.
Pedro, this really cannot come as a surprise, yet it's interesting because usually this president holds cards very close to his vest and would not let something like this out.

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: Well, it's amazing that he's finally concerned.

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: I just finished reading the most recent issue of Time magazine; journalists just describing the carnage, the constant carnage in Iraq, the civil war that's going on nonstop, the total inability of the Iraqi government to address any of it and the irrelevance increasingly of the American troops there. It's a total mess. It's a quagmire. They have no way out. There's no strategy. And Bush has created a mess of immense proportions that the American people and the next administration will have to try to figure out.

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: The fact that he's finally realized that maybe he made a mistake is quite amazing and disconcerting.

Here's what's interesting to me, Bob Meadows, the idea - and we can recall in the early days of this war when Rumsfeld and - the Secretary of Defense Rumsfeld and Dick Cheney, the vice president, suggested that we would almost see parades in the streets by people being freed from the oppression that they knew, and now the president is saying that he's shocked by not seeing greater public support for the American mission.
Yeah, it's - right. They thought…
…from the Iraqi people.

Exactly. People would be singing the praises. And you know - a lot of people, sure, they were happy once Saddam went down. But the thing is, when you knock down somebody's government, whether they're elected or not, there's going to be turmoil and instability that follows. The other thing about it is, can you imagine if some other country came in here and - you know, I'm not a Bush fan - but if some other country came into America and actually got rid of him somehow? Even I wouldn't be too happy about it. You know, it's like this is the person leading my country. So no, you can't expect for people to just throw rose petals in front of you. That was so incredibly naïve.
All right. Julianne Malveaux, have at it.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Take Bob's analogy, because I love it; it's a great one. And actually I would have a different reaction. But take Bob's analogy of someone came and got Mr. Bush. But not only did they do that, then they decided to reorganize our Congress.
Right.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: They decide to reorganize our Senate. They decide to pick who they like to be in charge of whatever. I mean, people are outraged. In addition, let's say that they - you know, Iraq is just about in civil war, and so let's say that this governing group came in and decided to fan our attentions, you know, so that maybe we had a North-South war or a race war, something like that. Yeah, people are upset.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: You know, this administration is an utter disaster around this issue. We're going to spend a trillion dollars, we're - you know, but we can't fix New Orleans. I know that's an aside, but you know we're going to spend a trillion dollars on this mess. We can't figure a way out of it. The people do not want it. Our actions there have inflamed extremists in the rest of the Middle East, and so now we have other drama that we've got to deal with. We don't have the troops to deal with it. We don't want to pay our troops. And this man runs around, you know, on a motorcycle in Pennsylvania yesterday, you know, touring the Harley-Davidson plant without a clue.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: We - the problem, though, is that Democrats aren't a heck of a lot better. And we are in desperate need of leadership in this country. And though Democrats have talked about things, they've talked about them very softly. They have not talked about what is wrong and what an alternate plan is. And certainly we can't just get up and leave. As Colin Powell said in the beginning: if you break it, you're going to have to fix it. But we have not figured out how to fix it.
But, you know, it's funny you - yeah, you stole my thunder there, Julianne.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: I'm sorry.
Because that's what I was going to give to Pedro - the idea that lest we forget the words of Colin Powell, they're really starting to ring true here, Pedro.

He quietly - and then, toward the end, not so quietly - tried to tell those in the administration who were for this war and moving fast and moving quick that there has to be a new way to talk to people that we've not talked to in the past. And if, in fact, you break it, you buy it. And now it's bought.

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: But fixing it is not going to be easy. And as we saw with Yugoslavia, when you have a dictator in place who's holding together a country that's historically been divided, when you remove that dictator what you often get is civil war and years of bloodshed. It's unlikely that you're going to be able to find a regime that can pull together the Shiites, the Sunnis, the Kurds, into a regime that was - that leads to a coherent Iraq now. And so fixing it I think is a very complicated proposition, and I'm not sure what that's going to entail and how easy it will be.

Perhaps another trip by the White House - this from words from the vice president last week - and people really started to kind of pay attention this week, and that's the question of whether or not voting for or against Joe Lieberman was aiding and abetting the war in Iraq and those who are opposed to American standards. What was said by the vice president is that the Democratic primary was giving the al-Qaida types exactly what they wanted. Julianne?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: You know, Dick Cheney needs to get off the Kool-Aid. This is so ridiculous. I mean these folks have abused the word terrorism, the notion of terrorism, the concept of terrorism, to try to bludgeon people into voting for them. And so to come out of that Connecticut primary with that kind of a statement is typical Republicanism. They used this war from the time it started - they used September 11th from the time it started for political purposes. And this is nothing more than political rhetoric, which fortunately, finally, the American people are beginning to see through.

How much, Bob, can this be said to be, rather than political rhetoric, Republican rhetoric, just the idea that we all don't see through the same prism in that there are a load of Americans who really believe this?

There really are. There are tons of them. And Bush was applauded yesterday because he actually - he didn't say this, he didn't bring up al-Qaida and he didn't say Democrat, but he said something that implied the same type of thing and people were applauding him.

They were like - he said, you know, there are some good people out there but they think we should cut and run, and we can't do that. This is what he said when he was speaking with Lynn Swann. And he got - he was, like I say, he got an ovation for saying that.

This, though, it is politics, because let's not leave out Joe Lieberman in all this. He said the same exact type thing about Ned Lamont as well after the loss. And you have to realize Ned Lamont only won the primary. He's still got to repay - face a Republican candidate, Alan Schlesinger. So they're just still fanning those flames so that Lamont will lose.

Mm-hmm. All right. Let me move quickly to a subject that has been talked about for quite some time, and it became a phenomenon in inner city and with inner city children about a decade or so ago. And that is the high cost of gym shoes and the want for many African-American. And now we see suburban children buying $150, $180 gym shoes. The difference is, oft times those in the inner city cannot afford these.

InStep's NBA Superstar Stephon Marbury, who is now suggesting that its time to stop this high priced gym shoe. He is putting out a line that he will wear himself during this upcoming NBA season, Bob Meadows, of a $15 gym shoe - the Starbury.

I think it's great, nothing wrong with it. I'm sure that the kids will add it to their collection. It won't be the only sneaker they buy, unfortunately. But I think it sends a really good message that we have to -that we as black people especially have to slow down on this just rampant consumerism. Save your money. Don't spend it on - don't spend $150 on sneakers. And actually, you know, of course, this has been going on for generations...
Yeah.

...since the Jordan's came out in 1984, so it's not a new thing. I don't really blame the kids for it. But I think it's a really positive move by Stephon who got a ton of bad press last year for the Knicks. So hopefully this will get him some good...
Yeah, that's, we know that's certainly part of it.

With about a minute and a half to split between the two of you. Pedro, this is something that you have to talk about the parents as well, those who know they can't afford to buy the expensive gym shoes who have often made a way somehow.

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: No, you're right. And too many parents fall, you know, prey to the advertising and to the pleas of their children to buy these very expensive sneakers. I have some kids myself who are putting pressure on me for the (unintelligible), so I understand those pressures.

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: It'll be even more significant when we see Nike and these companies that produce these sneakers come out with cheaper products and take a step similar to Marbury's in reducing these inflated prices. So I think it's a good step; it's a small step, but hopefully it's a step that others will follow.

And, Julianne, very quickly, put your economist hat on for me. I've not seen this shoe yet, though I'm told we'll get a look at it next week. But I am told that it is not a, quote, cheap shoe. It doesn't look cheap. And this really shows you the idea of the profit side of these kinds of gym shoes, that you can make a quality shoe and sell it for $15.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Absolutely. I mean these shoes are produced in China. They're using the same material that they use for all these other shoes. And so what you're really saying is that Nike Swoosh, all these other folks via stars like Michael Jordan and others, basically was extracting $130 worth of profit. You know, take a couple dollars out for the advertising budget, take a couple dollars out for Mr. Jordan or whomever, but, you know, $120 worth of profit per pair of shoes.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: The thing is, you know, one of my nephews had his shoes taken from him on a bus in Oakland about five years ago. Somebody stole his shoes. Pulled a gun on him and said give me your shoes. And so I just want to hug Stephon Marbury. I think this is just such a wonderful move. And I just would like to see more of these stars step up and connect their own economic success to the success of the community that has empowered them.
Yeah. All right. Well, Bob, we see it's already working. Stephon is turning that image around. He's getting a hug from Julianne Malveaux today.
Exactly.
All right. Julianne, Pedro, and Bob, thanks so much. Appreciate it.

speaker_label: Professor PEDRO NOGUERA (Professor of Education, New York University)
text: Thank you.
Thanks, Ed.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Thank you.

(Singing in foreign language)
You're listening to NEWS AND NOTES, from NPR News.
This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Ed Gordon.
On today's roundtable, a new poll says most Americans believe bin Laden will strike again, and the television show Survivor starts its season with teams divided by race.

Joining us to discuss these topics and more, from our New York bureau, Walter Fields, CEO and publisher of the NorthStarNetwork.com. And Bob Meadows - he's a writer from People Magazine - he's also there. And from our NPR headquarters in Washington, D.C., economist and author Julianne Malveaux. She's the president and CEO of Last Word Productions.

All right, folks, now that our science course is over - my head is still spinning on that one - let me take us to what we see in a CNN poll, that nearly three-fourths of the respondents there believe that we will see - as we're coming up on the fifth anniversary of September 11th - another attack from Osama bin Laden. That is the belief of many of these people polled.
Bob Meadows, this is not surprising, but it begs the question whether or not we will ever return to what the president liked to call normalcy.

You know, I did actually find it a little surprising, Ed, because I wonder what the other 25 percent of the people thought. What we just saw in London with the airplanes, that was probably an al-Qaida plot that happened to be thwarted. Bin Laden struck before September 11th, not necessarily in the United States but he was responsible for a lot of terrorists and bombings overseas.

So this is something that they're not going to stop. What I know that authorities believe about al-Qaida is that they often have these slow developing plots that are going to, that want to be huge spectacles, as well as the smaller acts of terrorism. So, yeah, absolutely, they are going to strike again, and, no, we will not be returning.
But really, you know, this world wasn't very safe before September 11th. I think that people are just more aware of it now.
Walter, what we've seen too is the United States catching up with the rest of the world in terms of terrorism on our grounds.

Well, I think that's the real issue. You know, in my mind, what September 11th really did was it unnerved the American public. You know, we finally realize just how vulnerable we are as a nation. Americans had pretty much settled into a comfort zone, thinking that they would never, ever see that type of terrorism on our soil.

And I think people now realize - when you begin to think about how open this country is; and how much access you have in this nation; the fact that most of our borders, people just slip through without any problem - I think that's the real issue here. Whether or not bin Laden or some other factor actually attacks the United States, what's really happened is that we are now a less secure country in the minds of most Americans.

Here's what's interesting, too, in the numbers, Julianne, is that the percentage, albeit high, had dropped from the 2004 same question. Sixty-six percent of the poll respondents said it was likely at that point, and even higher, of course, closer to the actually event, the year of - was 76 percent.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: And you know, Ed, what's even more interesting than that to me is that African-American people have never experienced significant security in these United States. Even before September 11th, so many of us were always waiting for the other shoe to drop one way or another. In the wake of September 11th, Cornell West said to white America really, welcome to the world. In other words, now you know what it feels to be like us.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: And indeed we would watch these images of bombings in Israel or Bosnia or Rwanda, and it wasn't about us. It was so distant. But also the images in our own communities of drive-by shootings and other things where, you know, people don't know any security of life.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: And so this concept of security is one that I find at least somewhat amusing. Who has ever had the luxury of thinking security? If white America ever thought security, then we go stirring the pot in the Middle East. Not just with our invasion or Iraq - looking for Osama, finding Saddam - but also with what we're now doing in Iran. And we literally have heightened the risks by our intemperate actions around the world that the rest of the world simply does not support us in.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: And so these numbers do not surprise me. I would've been interested in a racial breakdown. But I would have been even more interested in knowing who in black America, especially post-Katrina, has ever felt secure.

Walter, it's interesting, because Julianne brings up that point. And I can recall being in the barber shop talking about the attacks, and a brother saying, hey, you know, you didn't have to wait to worry about someone attacking you at your job or your home. Just think back to Philadelphia and the MOVE incident. So as Julianne says, African-Americans have often been, felt, or have felt besieged.

Well, you know, historically we've always lived under the threat of violence. That's what supported White supremacy all of these decades and centuries, so I think Julianne is right. But I will say, I think that even for African-Americans, I think there was a shock value about 9/11.

Particularly if you lived in a major urban center. Because the notion that in one fell swoop you could have that many people eliminated. And I think we felt it again with Katrina. I think there's something about these cataclysmic events that sort of sends a chill down your bone. Because in this country, even if you're African-American, I think was always this sense that it will never happen here in terms of the type of terrorism that Julianne described as happening around the world because we felt that we were impenetrable.
Bob, if we can continue to break that down, though, it may be a question of shock, yes, surprise, no.

No. I think everybody was surprised by September 11th. I think there was surprise to the government's reaction after Katrina, because people, you know, you thought that the government - you hoped that the government had its act together a bit better than it performed. A lot better, actually, than it performed after Katrina.
And to see, obviously - to see that TV, yeah, that was completely shocking, as you say, to everybody.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: You know that…
All right. Real quick, Julianne, and, Julianne, clearly we've been going to a few more dashiki meetings than they have.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: You know, in my book, The Paradox of Loyalty, a young woman did an essay where she interviewed an older black woman - a young black woman -about this. And the older sister kept saying, you know, we knew this was coming but when. My mom said, she said, you know - not saying it should've happened - but what took so long?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: The hubris that the United States had shown in the rest of the world. We, you know, baby boomers and Gen Xers may not have seen it, but all the black people were saying the world is not going to put up with this. So, obviously, people are inconvenienced, obviously, nobody saw the world, you know, the World Trade Center…
Yeah. No one thought the magnitude but no one was surprised - well I shouldn't say no one…

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Exactly. Well, people were…
But there were people who were not surprised with the attack…

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: People were sitting there saying…
On the United States.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: You know, this was coming, this was coming. We were just wondering when it was coming.

All right. Let's turn our attention to another study. This done by a Minnesota-based life insurance company contracted to find out - and, Julianne, let me start with you, put your economist hat on for me - this of women. Ninety percent of women said that they felt financially insecure. And this was even - 46 percent of women overall and 48 percent - and here's the surprising part to me - 48 percent of those with an annual income of $100,000 or more felt insecure. Almost half of the respondents were troubled tremendously by the fear that they could potentially become a bag lady - this is the language they used - at any time.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: The bag lady myth is a big one for women around financial planning issues because women don't feel they know enough about money. Women, especially of a certain generation, were taught that, you know, this guy was going to come take care of them - whatever. But they were taught that and so therefore they didn't learn.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Many married women don't know what their husbands' total assets are. Many married couple squirrel money away from each other. Women also tend to be the ones who are caretakers. When you look at the data on who takes care of elderly parents or these, you know, what do they call them, boomerang children who come back home at age 25 to stay. It's women who are putting the resources into that.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: So so many women fear I'll give so much there'd be nothing left for me. Also rising life expectancy. And the fact that if you look at poverty rates among women over age 65, they're nearly double those of men. So these are reasonable - well, they're not reasonable fears - but they're fears that come out of fact. And what women have to do to combat those fears is really just to educate themselves about money, about investing, about saving. Many women are afraid to, you know, do the risk thing.
Yeah.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: You've got these uber-guys who are on Wall Street, and you've got these women who've got their money tucked away somewhere making one percent.

Though, Bob, what we did see in this study is women have been listening to their mammas, grandmammas and aunties as they are twice as likely as men to have a secret stash on the side; just in case those men are not acting right.

Well, yeah, I've heard about that. And that was - well, yeah. I mean they're twice as likely because, as all the things that Julianne pointed out, you know, men have traditionally - although, you know, it's been so long, you know? I mean in the black community especially, black women have been leading households for generations. So I'm not even going to go there.

But, yeah, black women have - or women have a stash on the side so they don't -so that the husband doesn't find out what they're spending. And also so that if they want to go out and buy a handbag, some shoes, something like that for themselves, they don't have to explain where that money came from. It's their secret stash.
Yeah. Walter...

But I think what this poll also - I want to say what this poll also speaks to is just the uncertainty of the world today. Healthcare, jobs, Social Security is failing. People know that there's not going to be - there may not be anything left for them by the time they reach retirement age. And as Julianne pointed out, poverty rates among women are so high that this is a fear that is tangible.

Walter, it was still very surprising to me to hear from women who were making $100,000 or more, which actually puts them into the top 2 or 3 percent of wage earners in this country, I believe, Julianne. And, Walter, that was so surprising to me. It really does speak to the insecurity that women in this country feel financially.

Oh yeah, and I think it speaks to the larger issue of gender disparities. I mean I think part of it is when you see someone who has an annual income of, you know, $100,000 or more that feels that way, it suggests that there are some other things going on and not necessarily related to income, that it's a general sense of insecurity about their place in society.

So I can completely understand sort of that response on the survey. But I think what's really interesting here - I think for our community this is critically important when you look at the role that women are playing in households today and that we need to understand this a little bit better. Because when you look at who's raising, you know, many of our children, when you look at who is leading households in our community, we need to understand that part of our civil rights struggle has to be this issue of tackling these gender disparities. If not, it's going to overwhelm our community.

This on the heels of a special coming on on ABC this evening. The late Peter Jennings, his last special, which looks at AIDS in the black community. Out of Control I believe is part of the title there.

We see the black gay community in New York City in alliance with some New York politicians to unveil new billboards, a billboard campaign which hits Harlem and some of the transit area in New York, which is reminding African-Americans that gays are a big part - a large part of the black population.
There is this sense now from black gays of the need to fight back and be recognized. Walter Fields?

I can't tell you how important this is. I mean I've lost three college friends and fraternity brothers to AIDS, my best friend 15 years ago. And I think part of the challenge in the black community is that we need to have an open conversation about this. Because if not, it will always be discussed in the backroom.

So I applaud this effort, because I think, you know, it's a human rights issue in my mind. I think we've got to get to the point to understand that, you know, whatever your sense of what is natural may be, the fact of the matter is is that we have an incredible diversity of humanity in our ethnic group and that we need to embrace all of it and not make people feel as though they have to live in such a way that they can't be who they are and fulfill, you know, their promise.

Bob, there is this push by these groups to suggest that what they also want to do is get away from what has been tagged by the media as this down-low mentality - homosexuals trying to lead a heterosexual life and endangering not only themselves but their family members - as well as the denial that the larger community has - in particular many of, not all, but many of the black churches - that have fueled the fight against homosexuality and many people say have continued to cause the problems we're seeing in the community.

You know, black people tend to be very socially conservative on a lot of issues, gay marriage probably being at the top of the list. And, yeah, the churches often speak, you know, pastors leading the charge against it as an unnatural act. It's Adam and Eve, not Adam and Steve, is often the saying that you hear.

So this type of movement to counteract that is really - it's an uphill battle pushing a boulder and being dragged by a chain to get against that mentality the black community has. As far as the down-low phenomena, I've often wondered, you know, how big a phenomenon is that? Is that just a media creation or a media-hyped creation? But yeah, if you are gay, be gay. Don't hide in the closet. There's no need. You're already black. You've already got prejudice against you. You may as well just come out and take it all.

Yeah. Julianne, it's interesting to see taking this to the streets, so to speak, and actually putting it up on billboards, making people face the reality of it on a day-to-day basis in a huge way, in a very large way, literally.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Well, I think it's been an issue - if there is a war against racism, we need every soldier in that war. We need women, we need gay folks, we need every African-American person to fight in that. And we have fallen for this socially conservative hype that comes out of the Republican Party about gay marriage and abortion. Well, my line has been standardly(ph): if you do not like gay marriage, do not marry a gay person. When they ask you, just say no, thank you, and keep on rolling.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: The real issue is that so many - this down-low phenomena, first of all, I think has racial overtones. When white boys do it, they don't call it the down-low, so they want to make it a black thing. It's not a black thing. It's a phenomenon, the stigma against gay people forces men into relationships with women to hide themselves. But that puts our communities at danger. And our community, the black community, is already in so much danger and we really can't afford that.
Though black America really tagged it the down-low, Julianne.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Well, yeah, but white folks - when the down-low gets the front page of The New York Times, Ed, you know, what else that black people do gets the front page of The New York Times. Come on! I mean...
Well that I agree with, yes.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: ...anything that's pathological in our community, folks will try to trumpet. And the down-low thing is seen as something that's self-hating, et cetera. It is something - does the name Oscar Wilde mean anything to you? I mean, come on, you know, white men have done this from time immemorial, so this is not a black thing.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: But more importantly, I do think that our community has to come to terms with the fact, you know, as one of my colleagues said, that we are a diverse community. And we - if we let social conservatism trump our economic interests, which I think we've done far too often, we end up worse off.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: I mean Jesse does this thing that's brilliant. He gets you in a room and he says, who's unemployed? And, you know, half of us raise their hands. And who needs healthcare? And, you know, people raise their hands. Who's in a gay marriage? And you get two hands raised. Now maybe three people are hiding, but the fact is that this isn't - this should not be the wedge that separates our community.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: I think, as Walter said, we need to have some open and honest conversation about this, and these billboards are a first step.
Yeah, the billboards, and we should also note the encouragement of watching the ABC special tonight that Peter Jennings put together before his untimely death.
All right, Bob, appreciate it. Julianne, appreciate it. And, Walter, appreciate it.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist, Author, CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Thank you.
Thank you, Ed.
Thank you.

Next up on NEWS AND NOTES, senior correspondent Juan Williams and his political roundtable give us an insider's view of the latest happenings inside the Beltway. And the smooth jazz group The Rippingtons celebrate 20 years of making music.
This is NEWS AND NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya.
On today's Roundtable, a last goodbye to former Texas Governor Ann Richards, and CNN's Nancy Grace in the midst of a firestorm. Did her interview about a kidnapping go too far?

Joining us today from our New York bureau is Bob Meadows, writer for People magazine. Laura Washington, Chicago Sun-Times columnist, is in our Chicago bureau. And from Nashville, Tennessee, Jeff Obafemi Carr, host of the radio show Freestyle, is at Spotland Productions.

Thank you all for joining us and let's go straight to the first topic. Mourners from across Texas and the nation said their formal goodbyes yesterday to the late former governor of Texas, Ann Richards. About 500 people, including Democratic National Committee Chairman Howard Dean, actress Sandra Bullock, entertainer Lily Tomlin and U.S. Senator Hillary Clinton attended the funeral.
During the service, Senator Clinton shared a portion of the conversation she'd had with Governor Richards as she contemplated running for the New York Senate seat.

Ann said to me one day, she said, well, do you know yet whether you want to run? I said, well that's what I'm trying to decide. She said, well it has to be from deep inside you. Do you want to do it? Do you want the responsibility? But don't make the decision because you think it would hard. That goes with the territory. Make it because you want it. Ann Richards sent out a message to young women that is reverberating today: Set your own course, dream your own dreams, go places where you want to go even if nobody has gone there before, but never forget you're no better than anybody else.
Jeff, when you hear someone like Hillary Clinton talking about Ann Richards, what does it conjure up about, you know, how female leadership has progressed in American politics?

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Well, I think it conjures up a good feeling for me in a number of ways. I think that Ann Richards' legacy is well established. She was very fearless, quite a remarkable woman. I know many of us in the African-American community really point to women in our own families and communities who are strong and fearless but who never got an opportunity to be recognized.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: She represents a woman who was recognized in the mainstream as such a remarkable woman, a person of conviction who wasn't afraid to put herself out there. Some people say we don't need that anymore, but that's exactly what we need. We need polarizing figures that define American politics.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: She had some great one-liners; she created a legacy for minorities and women in the state of Texas during her short tenure as governor. And I think she was a role model for women, love or hate her positions that she took at times.

You know, Laura, it strikes me that polarizing figure is something that applies to Ann Richards and also to Hillary Clinton. Ann Richards was beloved by many but not by all, and she eventually lost her seat to George W. Bush, who, of course, now is our president. If women are controversial, sometimes they don't get the same leeway that male politicians do.

What is your sense of how an accomplished, strong figure like Richards, a no-nonsense figure like Richards, who always talked about women having to do the same things men do but backwards and in high heels, how did she affect American politics?

Well, I think that the message there is that she learned - she came along at a time when it was really tough for women to be assertive, tough for women to be pushy, tough for women to be tough, which was something that you had to do to get to where she was, she got to. So obviously she was extraordinary.

But she was always - the message was always don't try to out-boy the boys. Don't try to, you know, do what the boys do, because you are going to be vulnerable to criticism in a way that men are not. And there was always - she was also able to overcome this nagging reluctance that I think we continue to have to accept women in high administrative positions in government.

It's one thing even for them to be Congress people or senators, as a Hillary Clinton. But when you start talking about running a state government, when you start talking about running the White House, there's a lot of reluctance there. I think she continues to be a role model for how you can overcome that.

She was also vulnerable. As you note, Farai, she had her enemies, she had her critics. She was a recovering alcoholic; she had personal problems in her life. And that made her I think even more larger than life and even more of a role model for young women today.

Bob, you know, there are so few women even now in the House and Senate - you know, roughly 14 percent - compared to women being 51, 52 percent of the country. Have we really come that far in terms of female leadership on the national level?

Well, I think we'll really see in two years when Hillary perhaps declares her candidacy for the race. Condoleezza Rice is actually being considered. She's somebody who Republicans may even consider to be a viable candidate on their side. I think that's really when you're going to see.

You don't necessarily see it when the pioneers are doing what they do. What you see it is when the seeds that they planted start to grow. So we'll see if some of her seeds that Ann Richards planted begin to grow and take fruit, especially in 2008.

One thing that I do think about Ann Richards, though, she was really known, as people have said, for her wit. That line against George Bush the senior about how he was born with a silver foot in his mouth. But what I really wish is that she had been able perhaps to be a more popular politician in Texas, because she was a really popular person, but she wasn't really that popular a governor. She only served one term.
And had she been more popular perhaps she could've staved this George Bush the second attack that came and we're under now.

Bob, but do you think that being more popular for a woman requires being more deferential, being more feminine? You know, Ann Richards was a bit brassy and aggressive. And, you know, what people call in men assertive, people call in women aggressive.

Well, you know, I do believe that at the time, as Laura pointed out, the time she was coming up, Ann Richards was not a born politician. This wasn't something that she aspired to when she was younger. She was actually a teacher and then she was a homemaker for quite a while when she was married.
She didn't understand, maybe, that you had to kind of duck your head a little bit. And so she was brassy, she was pushy, but that enables Hillary to be pushier than she may have been 15 years ago.

The thing I think is interesting about comparing Hillary and Ann Richards is again that vulnerability. Hillary obviously has a lot of negatives, but a lot of them center around her personal life, and we know what that's all about. And some women and men criticize her for not standing up to her husband and to all his flaws. Some folks empathize with her.

And I think this is a time now - and we'll see again in two years - but this is a time now where it's okay for women to not be perfect and to have these vulnerabilities and for that to be even an attractive quality.
I'd like to think so. I'd like to think it's an attractive quality - forgive me for cutting you off, Farai.
No, no, please.

But I was just adding that it's got to be a unique conundrum that women find themselves in. I think it's a conundrum that I as an African-American man have found myself in coming from generations of having people who want you to assert yourselves but having certain situations where you say, hey, don't look a guy in the eye if you get pulled over by a policeman. This is how you have to act. I find that women, by and large, are relegated to having to act like that too.
It's a shame because - and I often get in trouble for saying this - I say that women are smarter than men, and the number one way they prove that is by making us think we're smarter than you all.
Thank you very much.

But it's such a good psychology that we end up being tricked. As men in a male-dominated society we end up thinking that we are, in essence, smarter. So we lock out opportunities, and some women buy into that. So that when you see a Hillary Clinton or you see a Governor Ann Richards or you see a Condoleezza Rice sometimes, you often hear other women saying that she ought to sit down and shut up and I'm not going to vote for a woman to be president.

So I think we still have a ways to go before we break out of the notion of women needing to being relegated to being beside or behind a guy to be a leader. I think they have to continue to find creative ways to open up those doors so that we can see that it's best to, you know - just like when you go to the club, it's best to go to the where the women are, because they're smart.

You know, one thing that I believe Gloria Steinem said - and I may be misquoting - is that I've never heard of a man ask how to balance work and family. That is something of a feminist saying. So I think that women in politics may be held to a higher standard about how they comport themselves in their personal life. Laura, do you agree with that?

Absolutely. Ann Richards, again, is a symbol of someone who was able to meet that standard. And there's - you know, I think that's true, but I don't think that that really matters in the end. Because, you know, men are expected to be more macho, men are expected to be tough in ways that women aren't expected to be.

So I think that extraordinary people like Ann Richards, like Hillary Clinton, that they get to this level - the balancing act is - it may be an unfair challenge for them, but it's a challenge that they've got to meet if they want to get ahead.
Let's do a little bit of, you know, fantasy political football. If there were in 2008 or beyond a Hillary versus Condi match, who do you think would come up on top? Bob first.

Well, I'm going to say Hillary because she's white. Hillary is an extremely polarizing figure, but I think if you put a black woman up there, I think a lot of Republicans would have a very, very difficult time voting for her; and I think Democrats would support Hillary. So I'd have to go with Hillary.
Laura?
A lot of black folks would have trouble supporting a black Republican woman. That's why I agree for the same reason, for that reason.
Jeff?

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: I'll add to that. I wouldn't stray. I think that, yeah, I think that for a lot of the same reasons that Hillary would be the candidate.
No love on the Roundtable for Condi, or at least…
There's love, but...

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Oh, I love Condi now, don't get me wrong.

I love her as a human being but the reality is, you know, the way people perceive things. And people vote these days on perceptions and whose got the most yard signs and has the best image. They don't necessarily look at the best policies.

Well, on that, I want to turn to another very hot topic. Former prosecutor turned talk show host Nancy Grace has really gotten into hot water after a woman she interviewed, some would say interrogated on the air, committed suicide. Now she says she's not sorry for her aggressive approach.
The woman was being questioned on Grace's show about the disappearance of her son. Here's a clip of the CNN interview.
Why aren't you telling us and giving us a clear picture of where you were before your son was kidnapped?

speaker_label: Ms. MELINDA DUCKETT (Mother of Alleged Kidnap Victim)
text: Because I'm not going to put those kinds of details out.
Why?

speaker_label: Ms. MELINDA DUCKETT (Mother of Alleged Kidnap Victim)
text: Because I was told not to.
You're not telling us for a reason. You refuse to give the simplest facts of where you were with your son before he went missing. It is day twelve.

speaker_label: Ms. MELINDA DUCKETT (Mother of Alleged Kidnap Victim)
text: I'm (unintelligible) with all media. It's not just here, it's for all media. Period.

The son is still missing. The woman committed suicide at her grandparents' home. The husband, who was estranged from his wife, does not blame Nancy Grace. But some other people are blaming her. Laura, what's your opinion?

Well, you know, some people are, as you say, saying that Nancy Grace's interview might have contributed to her suicide. We'll never know that for sure. There was never, as I understand it, there was not a note or something that said I did this because. You can imagine what kind of pressure this woman, Ms. Duckett, was under. And Nancy Grace might have been a contributing factor to that.

But I think the other thing that concerns me is just that little bit of a, that clip is just, not only - when you bring, you know, regular people who are in trauma on a television show up against someone who's a very skilled interrogator, it's a complete mismatch and there's no way that that woman could present herself well. So maybe she shouldn't have been on that show.

She's just not used to that kind of scrutiny. She's not used to being interrogated in that way. She's an unsophisticated person, and that's why Nancy Grace should have been maybe a little bit more respectful. There's nothing wrong with asking some tough questions, but did you pick up on the tone of those questions, the accusatory tone?

She wouldn't even let the woman finish making what - it sounded to me like she was trying to say was a reasonable argument was that the, you know, the police don't want me to reveal these details. You know, I'm mainly concerned about my child.
But you didn't get - but again it was just such a mismatch that it would, there's just no way she could win under in that situation.
But Nancy Grace is known for that, Jeff. I mean, you know, this is her trademark. You know, former prosecutor, tough as nails, her trademark is doing these kinds of attack interviews.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Yeah, of course it is. And when you allow your trademark or your image to define who you are, sometimes you actually believe it and so you end up going a little bit too far.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Two questions in this scenario. One, did it contribute to the suicide? And two, did she go too far? I've been in talk radio for 16 years, and one thing you learn I learned probably the third week into my first year doing talk show, that all of the callers aren't necessarily playing with a full deck. I learned four weeks in that all of the guests aren't necessarily playing with a full deck.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Present company excluded.
I've done call-in radio, too.
Right!

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Present company excluded. And you have to be careful when you're dealing with people who are under duress for any number of reasons. And so when you're in a place where you actually start to believe the hype, then you start to push and you start to go a little too far.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Melinda Duckett said I was told not to. Obviously there's been conversation that said that there was an investigation going on so she's not supposed to reveal certain things, to put them out in the media already. She continued to be pummeled by Nancy Grace. So I think, did it - did she go too far? I think she did go too far. And did it contribute? We're still not sure. But I think when you're talking about dealing with somebody who might be stressed, any number of pieces of hay might end up being the straw that broke the camel's back.
Now, Bob, you're at People magazine, which does a mix of celebrity/public figures…
Right.

Mm-hmm.

Well, this conversation will continue, and we will certainly keep track of whether or not the boy is found, which may bring some light to the other issues surrounding this case.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)

At least we think not.
That's right. They could have a card that we don't know about.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)

So it doesn't surprise me that you have these whiteness studies popping up. Actually, it's very interesting. I mean if it's done in a way that is an honest discussion, it could really shed light on this issue of privilege. But for the longest time - I've always said - I think there's need to be a full discussion of this issue of white privilege. White people need to understand and experience the flip side. And the only way you can do that is understand your privileged position.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)

West Philadelphia, born and raised, as the Prince of Bel Air talked about. You know, I was thinking about this story about the hair-braiding. I mean my hair is short cause I like to keep it simple. But I've thought about my son who's a college sophomore, and he gets his hair, you know, braided and all this stuff that the young people do. And people come over to the house and they sit down and, you know, either they listen to music or they go into the kitchen or wherever and it takes hours and hours and hours from people who just do this as a way of making money. speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: But Cornrows and Company - the brother and sister have a great place - and police came and told them they needed to be licensed because they were cosmetology but they use no chemicals. speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: And they have on their Web site all this stuff about just literally what's going on. And what emerges from here is this really is about cosmetologists trying to get in our Kool-Aid. speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: So then they've come up with - many states have come up with a limited license, as Philadelphia is suggesting - 300 hours. But they have no curriculum, no one to teach it, not tests. So, again, it just seems to be a nuisance. And in many of the states that have imposed the 300-hour requirement, they can't enforce it because they don't have anyone to teach these classes. So…

But what about this? What if you go to have someone do your hair, cause, you know, the price is right. You know, so and so knows somebody who knows somebody who knows somebody. And yet the person does it and they've yanked your hair and they start pulling it out on the sides because they didn't know what the heck they were doing…

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Get up out the chair. I mean it's real simple. You get referrals - I don't think that the state - I mean certainly, and I think this organization talks about issues of training and sanitation and safety. They produced a sanitation and safety handbook. And there are a couple of issues, including sanitation, including the issue of alopecia, the, you know, scalp disease. There are issues.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: But here's the deal: if you're going to regulate, you have to have something that's connected to the regulation. And having someone go to classes with hair dye and all that is not going to do it. So if the state wants to regulate, make it relevant.
Well, guys, what do you say about that? Do either of you - do you have your hair…
Yeah. I have dreadlocks.
Yeah. So tell us.

But I used to have short hair, of course, and my hair has been many different lengths. I got to tell you, I'd like to be in an out roar over this but I'm really, really not. Here in New York, you know, they have licensing for all these different hair techniques.

Something, right. Okay.

Make sure they make the razors in it and the blades in every time they cut somebody's hair. When I started getting my hair locked, again, you know, you just look for that license. You know that.

That's right.
...that can happen. I mean that's very, very important.
That it is. Walter, what do you...

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)

What did you say?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)

They have the limited licenses here in New York.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)

If I go to a barber who's not licensed I have to assume the risk if he jacks up my hair.
Mm-hmm.

So I don't have a problem with them being licensed. Because I think there are some public health issues. I think there are some professional standard issues. And I think if you're going to operate a business you should be willing to be licensed. I don't see a problem at all with this.

I think part of this is is just trying to create an environment where the consumer has some degree of confidence that the person who is working on their hair is skilled, is paying attention to health standards, and that there will be no problems going forward. I think you can make the license cheap enough where it's not onerous. I think you can put the training together with very little issues. All these people who are braiding hair can certainly be part of the regulatory process if the state so chooses to involve them.
So, you know, on a surface level, I don't see a problem with it at all.

Well, let me just throw this one little bit into the Kool-Aid with the three of you, and that is how much of this is concern over the fact that there may be some other folks who are not black who could jump into this business and just start making all of the money.
You know something? I hate to say this, but hair is hair. I mean we went through this with the hair care products companies...
Mm-hmm.

...when larger white companies began to buy those black hair care products. And companies - and mind you it was the black hair care products companies that made the decision to sell those businesses off. You just have to provide the best service possible, and it's going to be up to the consumer to determine whether or not they go to person A or person B. All right. Let's go on to our last topic, because we've only got about four minutes left. And this is actually, this is important. I mean hair is important too, but, you know, we all fly, and...

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Well, it ain't the most important thing, but...
Well, yeah, right. But I'm concerned about who's watching that screen when I'm up in the air. And there's an issue now between the FAA and the air traffic controllers.

Did you know that this group of controllers, who came in after Ronald Reagan got rid of the others 20 years ago, they're starting to retire now. And what's happened is the contract that they had has come to - they've come to an impasse where the FAA is saying, look, we need you to be at that screen longer than two hours. And the air traffic controllers are saying, look, that's a dangerous situation. They point to what happened in Kentucky a couple of weeks ago with that air traffic controller situation down there.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: I think we should be extremely concerned. I mean this is insanity. The four hours that they're accustomed to is a significant amount of time. To take it up by five and a half hours - you don't even have these TSA people who are sitting there screening your baggage doing anything for more than 30 minutes at a time because of eye fatigue. And if they have eye fatigue just trying to look for something in your pocketbook, I mean what kind of fatigue do you think people might have looking at planes that potentially will collide?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: It seems that the FAA has been very petty here. The other thing they're spending a fair amount of time doing is imposing a dress code. I don't care what these people wear. I mean what they wear is less important than how accurate they are in steering planes. And so if they're dressed casually I don't think it's a problem.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (Economist; CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: I think that what we're dealing with is an economic issue, an industry that's in some trouble and the FAA's attempt to extract the very last dollar and the last amount of effort from these folks.
Do you fly a lot, Bob?
I - yes, I do, actually.
So this is an issue for you too, yeah?
Oh, sure. Absolutely. It's an issue for anyone who flies the friendly skies. You know, there's, what, like 14,000 controllers in this country, and the issue is of course it only takes one mistake.
That's right.

You know that's the tragedy here. What happened in Kentucky was that controller only had like nine hours between shifts and only got a couple hours sleep. When they came back, the planes collided - or the plane crashed, I'm sorry.
Right.

And, so yeah, it only takes one mistake. And this is, as Julianne pointed out, this - I believe, yeah, this is a money issue. Because all these people have been on the job for 10, 20, 25 years and they make a decent, you know, pretty decent salary.
A hundred thousand dollars. Yes.

I read total compensation is about $165,000, including benefits. And so yeah, it probably is a situation where the FAA is trying to push these people to the brink so that they will retire voluntarily and so that they can hire in people making less money.
But isn't it a responsibility, Walter Fields, of the FAA to try to do this in a cost effective and efficient manner?

I'm not so sure. I mean my first private sector job out of college was with a start-up airline for three and a half years as a ground manager at Washington National Airport. And I will tell you, if the public really understood the dangers involved in air traffic control, I think you'd have many less people traveling. Most of the incidents that happen never get reported, number one, and most of them occur on the ground.

We have a real problem in this country in two areas. One is the controllers and the other is air space. That particularly around large metropolitan areas we have so much congestion that we have overtaxed the system. I think these controllers are making some legitimate claims in terms of fatigue, because it's a very difficult job to sit in front of that radar screen for over two hours watching blips go by. And I think there is an issue of fatigue.

I think the government has sort of shirked their responsibilities ever since Reagan dismissed all of the air traffic controllers, and they're trying to squeeze more out of individuals when actually what they probably need to do is add more controllers. I don't care what you pay them. When you think about the cost of not paying them and not having people who are fresh on the job, it's tremendous.
So I think this is something that the public really needs to pay a lot of attention to, because in some parts of the country we have maxed out on our ability to handle air traffic. We...

And let's start with Wal-Mart. Wal-Mart responded to the report in a statement received late yesterday, and that read, in part: A small number of our associates, only 3 percent, are at or above the maximum pay range, and no associate's pay will be reduced. We created more than 240,000 jobs over a three-year period. The majority of our associates are full-time, mid to low 70 percent.

So, Julianne, let me start with you. The basic controversy here is whether or not Wal-Mart is, in essence, trying to lower its employment cost by putting more people on a part-time schedule and putting wage caps. Is this even -should this even be a big issue, or is this just business as usual?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Well, it absolutely should be a big issue, Farai. It's been the issue of legislation; not regarding Wal-Mart, but in general during this Republican administration.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: You've got two competing issues here. One is the issue of employer flexibility, the question or whether or not you can have workers work at any time. And the other is the issue of worker rights. How can people schedule their childcare, their doctor's appointments, their worship services. What kind of rights do they have in sort of an at-will, free-flow labor market.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: We had a piece of legislation that came up in about 2002, the Worker Flexibility Act, that would have allowed employers to schedule people any 80 hours over a two-week period before they paid overtime. speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: This Wal-Mart policy, if it is indeed a policy, seems a way to get around that and essentially to disempower workers. So we should be very concerned, and there is the possibility of legislation to contain this kind of activity. And I hear Michael Meyers clearing his throat.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: You're right.
Go ahead, Michael.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Look. I do not have any stock in Wal-Mart - and excuse the pun -but look, department stores, like any other business, should pay prevailing wages. speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: So I'm not going to be one to pile on Wal-Mart, because I know this is a pile-on-Wal-Mart season, particularly as the holiday season comes up. And although Andy Young has lost his position, I know that he gave it his best shot; he messed up. They need a spokesman. Call me.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: You could get a promotion, though.
You could get a promotion, you're absolutely right. Thank you, thank you very much for that, Mike.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)

Wal-Mart was the place to be because they have all these great savings. And even people who will say yeah, I don't really like it, but they find themselves there.

Obviously, here in New York, since we don't have them, it's not much of an issue. But yeah, absolutely. When you get to these small towns - and the other part of it, Wal-Mart has said that they're going to make this commitment to come into more urban areas, which I'm still waiting to see when that happens.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Let me just jump in a quick minute, Farai. A couple things to Michael's point. They have a right to flexibility, but why not give people evening schedules then?
