speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Isn't everybody business trying to cut its costs?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Just a minute. Just a moment, Michael. And the reason why consumers, Bob, don't care - it's not so much that they don't care. They're getting good deals. Wal-Mart is the biggest thing in town. They are getting scale economies when they buy all over the country. They have stuff that's being made specifically for them, that you can't get anywhere else. speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: The issue is that workers should have some rights, and it seems to me - and I haven't seen their response - but it seems to me that this company systematically seems to downgrade workers rights. The wage cap is the most ridiculous thing I've ever heard of.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: And I say that…

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: And you say you want a job. You already put yourself out there. Brother, you go, brother. You have no more credibility…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: No, I didn't say I want a job, I said…
All right, folks. Well, before we go back to Michael…
I knew I wasn't going to get to talk today.

No, no. We're going to get to you, Bob. But, Michael, let me throw this at you. Wal-Mart says they're doing what Sears and Target already do, so is this simply, you know - is Wal-Mart the one, the company that has to wear the flak jacket because everything that goes on in retailing sort of ends up being blamed on them?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: As I said, this is pile-on-Wal-Mart season. Everybody piles on Wal-Mart. It's a business. I don't know any business that doesn't want to cut its costs, and cost cutting is part of the business.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: That's why we have labor laws.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Excuse me, Julianne. Excuse me, Julianne.
Okay, folks.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: I said that I agree with labor laws, I agree with wage and hour laws. I agree with anti-discrimination law and anti-age-discrimination laws, (unintelligible). But I also believe that businesses don't need an economic czar, particularly Julianne Malveaux, looking over their shoulders…

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: They just need you as a spokesman? I can't…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: …telling them every decision they make is anti-worker.
All right, guys, you're getting too much back-and forth. We're going to move on to another topic. And, Bob, you are going to get to go first.
Yes!

It's about another Bob. Bob Woodward's new book, State of Denial, criticizes the Bush administration's handling of the Iraq war. It claims Laura Bush and former White House Chief of Staff Andrew Card wanted to dump Donald Rumsfeld, the defense secretary. Woodward also claims that two months before 9/11, Condoleezza Rice ignored warnings of al-Qaida attacks from former CIA chief George Tenet.

Now in some ways Bob Woodward's previous book to this was considered favorable to the administration. This one is seen as an attack. You know, how important are books like these that have a lot of inside access to our look at the political process?

Well, they're very important because the Bush administration's been so incredibly secretive about what's been going on. They haven't been forthright. Everything that they've - pretty much everything that they've said has turned out to not be true, whether it's, you know, looking for the weapons of mass destruction, whether it's not the Iraqis are going to welcome us with flowers once Saddam is gone, and by the way, how long this war would last and how much it would cost, too.

So yeah, you need books like this. I'm a little - yeah, you're right. Bob Woodward's first two books about Bush were very favorable. Why is he now - what made him switch? I'd like to know the answer to that. People are of course saying well, it's because the president didn't talk to him for this book. So I really want to know.

And I'm also wondering, why was he so late to the party? These are - most everything he's saying has already been put out there in plenty of other books. Why was Bob Woodward so late to this? It's like all of a sudden he's just realized that oh, by the way, this war isn't really working out.

But, Julianne, even though he's late, he is a celebrated author whose books always manage to shake things up, you know. So in a way, whether or not he is late to the party, he is someone whose word is being taken seriously.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Well, this may well be a case of better late than never, especially given his first two books that, as you said, Farai, were favorable.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: The big news here, there's a lot of stuff that was not news. It was interesting, I watched the Larry King interview last night and a woman called and said some of this should have been on the front page of The Washington Post, not buried, you know, in the pages of your book. And I agree with that. So there's a little conflict that I think a lot of people who are journalistic experts have talked about in terms of the roles that he plays.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: But I think the stuff on Rumsfeld, especially right now heading into an election season, is interesting. Some of it is news. Poor Tony Snow can't spin this if he wants to. I mean he's trying like heck, but it's just not working.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: And the fact is that Rumsfeld has been a controversial figure who has not gotten along with the others on the so-called defense team. He and Condoleezza Rice clearly have been at, you know, loggerheads for quite some time. He apparently - you've seen this in the body language, and now it's confirmed - does not respect her, did not return her calls. So some of this is news. It gives us a sense of an administration in disarray while now more than 3,000 Americans are dead.

Michael, I think that what Julianne mentioned was actually what I was most struck by, the allegation that Rumsfeld doesn't really talk to Rice. Most people know that the former Secretary of State Colin Powell was frozen out, but Rice seems to be very much in the loop. How do you parse out that situation between the defense secretary and the secretary of state?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Oh, I watched the Larry King interview as well. What is it - Bob Woodward now is a gossip columnist? This obsession with calling for Rumsfeld's resignation, it is, to use an ex-Congressman Foley word, childish. Childish. Rumsfeld is…

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Oh…

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: oh, my. That was low.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: …Rumsfeld is doing George W. Bush's bidding. Bush has reiterated his confidence in Rumsfeld. The man is not going to resign.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Now look, as far as Tony Snow is concerned, yeah, I agree with Tony Snow. We've read this book before. By the way, I love the fact that we have a White House spokesperson now who doesn't even sound robotic. He can actually think and say what he wants to say.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: But the Bob Woodward book, this last one, you know, it's All the President's Men again, part two. There are no crimes here, however, except for war crimes and the like. And that's George Bush's situation and not just his underlings.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: So I suspect that the question that the American people want to hear is, do we really expect President Bush, and his men and women, to tell the truth about Iraq or to be in a state of denial? And the answer is, we expect them to be in a state of denial - the title of the book.
All right. Well, we're just going to leave that topic and point out that this is all people's opinion. Moving on…
…moving on to…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Informed opinion.
Informed opinion, of course. Moving on to black colleges. We've got a couple of minutes left.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Oh, God! Is it my turn?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: To go first?
Okay, Michael. I love how everyone now is petitioning to go first.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Oh, you know…

Let me get, let me get - it's kind of a couple of interlocking topics. One, HBCUs in and around Atlanta are pumping millions of dollars, you know, actually $10.8 billion, into the state of Georgia. But they're having a harder time drawing students, according to the U.S. Education Department.

Black students choosing to attend an HBCU fell from 18 percent in 1976 to just under 13 percent in 2001. Now obviously white schools, or predominantly white schools, have opened up to black students but, you know, I guess, Michael, is this sort of the death now for HBCUs or is this just what we should expect.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, there's been a death knell for HBCU schools for a long time. I say, and I'm not a religious person, although I am, if there's the death knell, God bless them. Good. Racial law - race and racial…
What - explain this.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Because race and racial loyalty is not what it used to be. We don't need black colleges. We don't need white colleges. That's just old hat. We need nonracial institutions of higher education. We have to see that race identifiable colleges are anachronistic.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Of course black students are going to the better schools, to the best schools that they can get into. Just like whites, just like Hispanics, just like Asians. Nobody is running to a black school because it's a black school anymore. That's just old-fashioned thinking. This is a marketplace of ideas, and we need critical thinking. We cannot guilt black students into going to black colleges anymore. Period.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: We shouldn't have to guilt them.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: And I say, thank God.
Julianne?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Michael Meyers, shame on you. We should not guilt them…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: I have no shame and no guilt.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: I know that. That's very clear. You know, we should not have to guilt them into anything, but we still do need HBCUs.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Farai, if you look at the landscape, obviously Michael's…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Who's we?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: …right about one thing. Students should go to the best place they can get into. In some cases that is an HBCU. If only 18 percent of our kids are going to college, that means that, you know, you know, there's another 30 percent who could go. There are kids in community colleges who could be in four-year colleges.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: The fact is that some of these HBCUs are offering an excellent education, and some of them are also offering a diverse education that includes an…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: (Unintelligible) survive.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: …outreach to Latinos and to whites. And so these schools need to be saved. But here's the deal. The people I have ire with are these HBCU alums that aren't giving to their schools.
That's it.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: If you look at the records of HBCU alums, you know, they -Princeton has a 66 percent alumni giving rate. Morgan State shows up as N/A. In other words, not applicable. In other words, not enough people to count. Now that's what you call a shame. So if people who are decrying the death of HBCUs are upset about it, they need to give to these schools. The physical plant needs to be improved. (Unidentified) has gone to Bennett and doubled their alumni giving rate in a four-year period. But we still need these schools.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: No, we don't.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: They're an affordable option for young African-American people. And, Michael Meyers, just go somewhere.
Okay, guys. Guys…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: I'm not going to an HBCU.
Bob's got the last minute.
Yeah, well, you know, I have to say I actually agree with Julianne. But I actually, I Googled each of us on this panel and I know none of us went to HBCUs.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: You've got that right.
So…
But my cousins did, and my friends did.
So, I do - hey, my wife went to an HBCU and I'm not trashing them.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: I tried!

But, you know, I think one of the reasons we have to remember, you know, black men aren't going to college the way they used to. That's one of the things that's a problem. I also think A Different World isn't on anymore. That sent a lot of kids to black colleges back in the day.

But you're right, exactly right. Where are the black college alum giving back to their schools, supporting their schools so that they're not so rundown? Man, I went to Morehouse back in the day and couldn't believe how rundown it was. Those dorms were atrocious. Not every school has a Bill Cosby waiting to give them $20 million.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: A Different World isn't on anymore, but we're living in a different world. Race isn't what it used to be. Goodbye, black colleges…

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Race is still a factor, Michael.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Goodbye, white colleges.
All right - all right, guys.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Goodbye!

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: It's still a factor. And if you continue to ignore it, it's still a factor.
Okay. On that note…

In New York, Bob Meadows, from People Magazine; Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition. And in Washington, economist Julianne Malveaux, president and CEO of Last Word Productions, Incorporated.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Thanks, Farai.
Thank you all for this spirited discussion.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Thank you.
Thank you.

(Singing) I like that. We don't need no lawyer, Sam, because there's no trouble there. But I like it all because I'll be free from my cares. (Unintelligible) Going where I won't be (unintelligible). Going where I won't be (unintelligible). A place like that, a place like that, they got a place like that somewhere on the other side.
You're listening to NEWS & NOTES, from NPR News.
This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya. On today's Roundtable, a rise in casualties in Iraq, and the GOP has lots of obstacles to leap before the November election.

Joining us today from our New York bureau is Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition, along with Bob Meadows of People magazine. And from NPR headquarters in Washington, D.C., we've got Yvonne Bynoe. She's author of the book Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-Hop Culture.
So thanks, everybody. And I have to start with these numbers on Iraq. I mean there's been so much going on geopolitically. We could talk about Korea, but let me start here.

That the number of U.S. soldiers wounded in Iraq is at its highest monthly level in nearly two years: 776 per month. And right now we've got GIs fighting on this block-to-block level in Baghdad, and some military experts are saying that it's really important to look at the number of people wounded versus killed because body armor and new technologies are really keeping people from dying, not necessarily from recovering.
So I think at this point, as we look at these casualty numbers, what is it doing to our perception of the war, Michael?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Until the so-called soccer moms, security moms, scared moms get scared for their young children in Iraq whose lives are being killed or wasted, spent, whose bodies are being wounded and who will have to be taken care of when they get back to the United States - if they get back to the United States - until they elect the right kind of leadership, until there's opposition from the right kind of politicians to this war in Iraq, you're going to have casualties. War is, as some general or president said - yeah, general - hell. That means death, it means wounding. It means that the United States is going to be a police force in Iraq now as opposed to winning a war, because even President Bush accepts that he cannot win this “war.”

Yvonne, you know, Michael just mentioned the soccer moms, but in some ways, at least as it's spun in the kind of political world, soccer moms are a bit more socio-economically secure that perhaps some of the mothers who have sons in Iraq or daughters in Iraq, because it is very much a mixed force.

We're talking I think still primarily in the military about working-class families who may or may not have the same sway when it comes to getting the ears of politicians. Does class play any role in how these discussions go on?

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: I think they certainly do. For the most part - there have been some studies done. And you're exactly right, Farai, that a lot of the military is working class, whether you're black, white or brown. The military is still an avenue of access of economic advancement, if you will, for young people who may not be able to go to college for financial or academic reasons.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: So certainly whether or not they are patriotic and believe in the cause is less interesting and less relevant than whether or not they have any political power in terms of where this war is going or any future war. In the past, the sons of the elite were fighters, so there were different calculations made as to whether or not we were going to put our sons in harm's way. Now the elite run from battle, and they leave these - the people on the ground are the poor and working-class folk.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: So I think that there is something to be said as to who bears the brunt of these conflicts. But I think there's something else that we need to go back to. The perception of the war, frankly, hasn't changed for the people who didn't believe this was a good case to begin with. We still have not heard what the benchmarks are for pulling out. What we are hearing are these high death rates. What we are seeing are people coming back, as Michael said, who are wounded and mangled and will probably be so for life. But I don't hear the Democrats, either, getting a backbone and actually saying: Beyond pulling out, what are the benchmarks? What is success? What are we willing to do here?

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: I hear the stay-the-course on the GOP side, and I hear very little on the Democratic side. The Democrats need to get a plan and be realistic. We can't pull out tomorrow, but we need to start ratcheting back and being clear what that is going to look like because the Iraqi police is not standing up, as we keep hearing. They're running. They're still polarized. So this is - Bush didn't want to be in the nation-building business, but that's exactly what he is in now. And this could take decades, I mean 50, 60 years for this to look like some sort of democracy that we're familiar with, and I just don't think we have the will to be involved in that.

And, Bob, you know, that really leads into, you know, some of our upcoming conversation of the GOP. But there was this big debate this weekend between Allen and Webb in Virginia, one of the most hotly contested races with, you know, intimations of racial bias and all sorts of talk of all these other issues. But really when it comes down to it, it was a similar situation to what Yvonne was saying, from what I learned of the debate, where Allen, who is the Republican, said, you know, stay the course, and Webb, who's the Democrat, said well we're not - you know, we need to do something, but it wasn't exactly clear what he wanted to do.
So, Bob, how does this play - you know, how does the Iraq war play in to the these upcoming elections, do you think? I mean is anyone scoring any points here?

Well, that's the very sticky, sticky situation that we're in. Everybody is of the mindset exactly what those two candidates say. Well yeah, we can't just jump out, but oh I really don't know how to get us out. That just shows the complexity of what you have going on here.

Iraq right now is a situation where it is on the verge of a civil war. If we just pull out, it's going to be complete and total chaos. I think for the American people it really boils down to - and I have to say, you know, 68 percent of the people have said that all the Republican shenanigans that are going on will not necessarily affect how they vote, and as Yvonne said, people who felt one way before the war still feel that way.

A lot of the people who felt we should be going into Iraq, they also kind of still feel that way. So nobody really has - despite everything that's happened, nobody has found a solution, nobody has found a way out. How is it going to affect the voters? I think Iraq is going to be a very big topic come November 7, but along with many other things like North Korea, the economy and Mark Foley, for instance.

Oh yeah, Foley. Foley remains a large story with, you know, I think something like four dozen subpoenas going out for this probe of it. And, Michael, let me get you to react. Because you've got Foley, you've got, you know, these figures coming out of Iraq. You also have this other race in Pennsylvania with a representative who had an affair and was alleged to have strangled his mistress and, you know, that's a big fight. This is the Republican candidate.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Yes.
Then of course you have Allen and Webb with all of the racial drama around that. Are the Republicans really vulnerable in terms of losing the House or Senate?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: I must say I'm astonished, because I thought the October surprise was going to be the discovery and the capture of Osama bin Laden.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: And now it's the discovery and the capture, and the outing so to speak, of Representative Foley. And it will continue to be the capture of the other hooligans who knew or should have known what was going on in Washington, D.C.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: I just don't believe that there's only one congressman who is in Washington, D.C., who's going down, so to speak.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: So, you know, for me it's a failure of both leadership and memory. Hastert doesn't remember anything. He has a short-term memory loss; it's always the first to go. But once the memory is gone, I think some of these other people have to go. Hastert has to go.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: And the Congress is in real trouble now, those incumbents and people who get into these sticky messes. The people, the electorate, have got to stand up and say we are tired of this immorality. The Republicans stand for “morality.” Now I don't care if you're a Democrat or a Republican. If you're doing this kind of sticky mess, they've got to go down.

Well, Yvonne, you know, you have a situation where the president called Hastert to commend him for his leadership on this issue. Do you think that's something that the president might regret if it's proven that the speaker of the House actually knew about this years beforehand?

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: Yeah, I think Bush regrets this whole situation. I think, however, he was between a rock and a hard place. If he pulled his support from Hastert, it really is going to set the whole thing on its head. And as we all know, Michael is exactly right. There are a lot of people who had to know about this guy. There are people in Florida who knew at least that he was gay. That was an open secret. Him being gay is not the problem. The problem is if he was having these inappropriate conversations with these young pages, he couldn't have been the only person who knew. And, you know, in Washington it's that, you know, I don't recall, I don't remember. You know, that's become a cliché.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: So I think that overall, when we look at this situation, Bush has no choice. His mentality seems to be, you know, as we've heard over and over and over, staying the course. At this point, their best bet is to hope that Hastert can weather this storm and that they can get through the next set of elections.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: But after the midterms are over, who knows what'll happen. He might get kicked to the curb after that point because he will no longer of service to Bush. So we just have to wait and see.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: But real quick, back on Iraq. I'm always curious because people keep saying, well if we pull out it's going to be a catastrophe. It's already a catastrophe. And looking at Israel and the Palestinian conflict, that's been over 50 years and that's still a catastrophe. So I really don't think that that's a, you know, a real cause to say we can't pull out. We need to find a formula and a plan to pull out, but we need to get out.

Well, I want to turn to violence of a different stripe - school shootings. There's been this spate of shootings at schools. There was another case just recently where a kid fired a gun in a school and intended apparently to shoot some of the fellow classmates and teachers, but the gun jammed.
Now this is a very weird proposal. I just want to hear what you guys have to say about this. A Wisconsin…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Hmm, it's weird.

…lawmaker says that teachers should arm themselves, that all teachers should carry guns; and that if you look at Thailand and if you look at some other countries, teachers are armed. Of course, it's been pointed out that in many of these cases there are guerrilla warfare going on in certain regions that make it a little bit more imperative perhaps to carry guns.

But, you know, on the one hand you have the mayor of Boston and the mayor of New York joining together with a coalition of dozens of other mayors to try to really prevent guns from getting into the schools. But then you have someone else saying, you know what, just give the teachers guns.
Michael, you've got to have something to say on that.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: I certainly do. Look, in New York City we have police in schools. They carry guns. The teachers don't carry guns. I'm, you know, it's very difficult. You know, you've got to remember you have a gun culture in the United States. In New Hampshire, Maine, Montana, all those whiter states, people can get guns legally, lawfully. In New York City it's very hard to get a license for a gun.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Now I could get a license for a gun because I'm a controversial figure and I'm always threatened. But I don't want to get a gun because I'd use it. And so I think you have to be…
Michael!

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: …you have to be very, very careful about public policy. And I don't' think arming people, arming teachers, is the answer to anything. You have to have less guns, fewer guns, particularly in schools. But again you have policemen in schools. We lost that fight. But the police are armed and dangerous.
Bob, I mean is this just sort of a stunt, or do, you know, are we supposed to take this seriously? It sounds like the lawmaker is serious.

Well, it's coming out - of course this representative is in Wisconsin. They just had this principal who was killed by the student. So he's responding to that, and he's probably very emotional at this point. But yeah, it's not a stunt; it's just crazy and ridiculous because, no, you can't have the teachers packing.

And as you implied, Farai, the examples he pointed out are situations where teachers are being included as part of the government in Iraq, so therefore they're being targeted; or there's a guerrilla war and teachers are being targeted. Teachers in Wisconsin, teachers all over the world - teachers in our country rather, they're not being targeted like this.

These incidents of school shootings are very - or relatively isolated incidents. But yeah, the key is to not give more guns. It's to take the guns out. If this kid had - you know, if these children had been armed with, say, knives or something like that, they wouldn't have been able to cause all this mayhem because people would have been able to jump on them instead of just fleeing away, running away.

So no, that's not the solution. And I actually - the mayors going up against these illegal guns, I applaud it. One of the opponents in this story, for some reason, says it's political grandstanding. Well everything in politics is grandstanding and it's all political. But no, actually I applaud this effort and I hope that it's successful - far more than Representative Lasee.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: It won't control illegal guns.

Yeah. Well, Yvonne, you know, at this point when you look at an issue like school shootings, which seem to go in waves, you know, and in fact psychologists analyze it as kids who were already disgruntled sort of feeling empowered when they hear about another school shooting to go out and do a shooting themselves. So they do go in waves.

But what really is the solution? I mean it's a very difficult problem to legislate away, because it's a very difficult problem to even identify, you know, why certain children are going out and shooting their classmates. Why there are adults entering spaces like the Amish school. I mean it's a very disparate problem. So how can - what kind of solution would you want?

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: Well, I think first of all we have to get over the notion that crime only happens in urban school communities. If we look at the vast majority of these school shootings, they have not been in any urban community. They've been in schools that have a majority white population. A lot of them have been rural or way out in the sticks.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Yes.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: So I think that we really have to come to grips that there are a lot of kids of all colors that really need help. And I think, frankly, I'm for school security. I know it's not the best situation, but I think that we need to start looking more across the board of having more deterrent measures, be that metal detectors or whatever. And I am for having some type of security force, and I mean real security, in these schools.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: But as long as we keep saying, oh, it's in southeast D.C., oh it's in the Bronx, oh it's here, there's no real measure to address these issues in a comprehensive way. I also think we need to talk about counseling. Again, as long as it's just violent black youth, we don't have to really have real conversations about how to identify students who are at risk mentally before they get set off and bring to school a gun.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: I also think the parents have to be held more accountable. In a lot of these school shootings these were parents who had guns in the home and that children had access to, or the kids got guns and the parents were clueless that they had any. So, you know, I think that if your child is a minor, they're living in a house with you, you bear some responsibility, particularly if they go out and shoot somebody with your gun or a gun that was housed under your roof.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: So I think that we have to look at these things in a broader fashion. But we have to start acknowledging that white kids do shoot, white kids do get guns and white kids are killing people. And I think once we can get that on the table we can have a more effective conversation about how to curb this youth violence.

Well, that's going to have to be the end of our conversation for today. We've been talking with Yvonne Bynoe, author of the book Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership in Hip-Hop Culture; along with Bob Meadows of People Magazine and Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition. Thank you all so much.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism, Leadership and Hip-hop Culture)
text: Thank you.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Thank you, Farai.
Thank you.

Next on NEWS & NOTES, a pro-choice women's movement taking part in a controversial campaign to have their voices heard. And from dice to online betting, gambling is a global business. A new book looks at gaming from ancient times to the present.

This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Tony Cox, in for Farai Chideya. On today's Roundtable, the Pentagon tries to reinvent its public image. Also, a new ad uses sex to lure voters to the polls. And John Kerry steps back into the campaign fray.
Joining us today from our New York bureau is E.R. Shipp, professor in journalism, Hofstra University School of Communication. E.R., nice to have you.
Professor E.R. SHIPP (Journalism, Hofstra University, School of Communication): Yes, hello.
And Bob Meadows, writer, People Magazine. Hello, Bob.
Hello.
And in Nashville, Tennessee at Spotland Productions, Jeff Obafemi Carr, host of the radio show Freestyle. Jeff, nice to have you back as well.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Good to be here, Tony.

Listen, damage control. That seems to be the theme of our Roundtable on this slightly abbreviated version today. First up, the Pentagon, they're trying to do a facelift, I guess you could say, starting with beefing up the public relations staff and trying to set the record straight as they see it with regard to coverage of the Iraq War.
So here's my first question, Jeff, to you: what is the first step? And before you get to it, don't say dump Rumsfeld. That was yesterday's Roundtable discussion.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: That's every week's Roundtable.
What's the first step?

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Well, we look at this Pentagon PR issue that's come up. Now regardless of the company line that we hear is being presented here, I think it's pretty obvious for those of us who have been in the media to varying degrees and talk radio, news reporting or publishing, whatever it is, what's really going on.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Although coming short of referring to it as an official information operations program, anybody that reads about the structure of the approach that the Pentagon is now taking is going to argue that it's precisely that. They have the rapid response departments, surrogates that are going to be hired to blanket the media to present all of the good and wonderful things that are coming out of the Pentagon's efforts.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: But I think it's important to realize that if we don't buy, or if we buy the company line that it's not a propaganda campaign, then they've done their job and they've done it well. So we are at war. It's a shadowy, unclear, ill- defined and quite amorphous war, but nonetheless it's war. When you're at war, the propaganda machine will roll out full-fledged on both sides.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: And in this case, the Pentagon's launching a PR campaign to try to sway the population to believe in this war, as well as convince our enemies that we're righteous in this.
Well, E.R., do you think they can do it?

No. They can try to do it. But I think we can see from polls how people in this country are not supportive of the war at this point. So no amount of public relations activities is likely to significantly change that. Even I believe Mr. Rumsfeld gave the department a D plus rating some months ago.
Yes, he did.

And what they're now trying to say is we're trying to do better than a D plus. So they know that they are not convincing the American people, and they definitely aren't convincing the rest of the world, obviously.

Well, you know, Bob, I'm wondering if you're trying to do something new and trying to get the public to look at you with new eyes, do you tell them, hey, I'm about to put some makeup on so, you know, pay attention?

Well, I think that probably is what we'll get news media to report on what you're trying to do. But the truth is they can put out as many photos of Iraqis planting flowers and traipsing through fields as they want. It's not going to matter when you have dozens of Iraqis dying everyday over there, when you have just had the, I think, the third or fourth highest month for American soldiers dying over there.

This war is so extremely unpopular, it doesn't really matter what type of PR the Pentagon is going to try and put out there. Because that story is so tragic of what is happening in this civil war that is now happening in Iraq.

Speaking of damage control - we're going on to our next topic - how does, E.R., John Kerry manage to do this? Insert himself into the campaign in a big way a week before the election? Or do you disagree that this is a big blunder?

Yes. It was a blunder. But let me start by saying this: politicians should stick to their day jobs. They should not try to crack jokes. He essentially got in trouble by saying that if you don't do well in school, you'll end up in Iraq.

That wasn't the way the punch line was supposed to go, apparently. He was supposed to say - and I'm quoting - “do you know where you end if you don't study, if you aren't smart, if you're intellectually lazy? You end up getting us stuck in a war in Iraq. Just ask President Bush.”
So the punch line was supposed to focus on President Bush, but it came out sounding as if he were demeaning the troops.

So he botched this. Having said that, though - having said that, though, the president is really using this as a distraction. Because right now, a lot of Republicans running in tight races are distancing themselves from him. So he's trying to put the focus on Kerry, as opposed to what's happening in this own party.
Absolutely, but that's what he should be doing, shouldn't he, Jeff? I mean, that is the correct strategy for something like this, isn't it?

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Well, of course it is. And I think that what's happened is Kerry did bring this issue up. And he did make a flub, and the Republicans are going to make him pay. We're down to the wire, and any opportunity they have to take a seam and to rip it open into a wide-open doorway in the Republican's favor, they're going to take.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: You have to realize - as E.R. said - what your strengths are. Now Bill Clinton, he could've pulled that joke off without reading off the paper. Maybe even Jimmy Carter in his own deadpan manner could've done it. But as a general rule, if you're not a funny guy, you shouldn't tell jokes -or at the very least you should practice the joke. And no matter what, never takes your eyes off the script, and so he…
Off the cue card…

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Never take your eye off the cue card. And when you do that, if you're not an experienced comedian, this kind of thing could happen. And I think at this point he's explained enough that it was a flubbed joke, and I think it's not that big of an issue anymore. But the Republicans are going to continue to press this.

Well, you know, I wonder about that point that you just made, Bob Meadows, because - I mean Jeff made the point, but I'm coming to you, Bob Meadows - that, you know, Kerry has just begun to sort of resurface a little bit more as we look towards 2008, you know? And to have something like this sort of crop up reminds people of some of the missteps that were made, you know, in the presidential election last time around. So does this hurt him in the longer run?

It hurts Kerry from the standpoint of, yeah, if you can't tell a joke - he was, back in 2004, he was seen as this aristocratic guy. Even though he went to Vietnam, he was still seen the aristocrat and George Bush, for some strange reason, was seen as the common man.

Having the ability to tell a joke, have a beer, shoot back, you know, shoot back and shoot the breeze with people, that's one of the things that you have to be able to do. He's already showing, you know what? Not only am I an aristocrat, not only do I have this jaw, but I also cannot tell a joke. I cannot remember a punch line.
So, yeah, it takes that away from him again.

All right. We've got another one to talk about, although this time, it's not exactly damage control. But it is putting a new face on an old institution. A new media campaign launched by the group Women's Voices, Women Vote is raising eyebrows for the way that they are trying to entice voters to the polls.

Now they are calling the ad campaign, quote, “Remember Your First Time,” end quote - now remember that - and have enlisted celebrities like actress Regina King to talk about their, quote, “first time,” but it's not the, quote, “first time” you may be thinking about. Here, let's listen:
I was the last one of all my friends to do it. What would my mother say?

After I did it my first time, I told everybody. I had such a big mouth about it. You got all that energy flowing inside and you go in and commit. It's a beautiful thing. I will do it again and again and again and again.

Well, the ad says 20 million - and she's fanning, you know, if you've seen it, she's fanning - the ad says 20 million women did not vote in the last presidential election. E.R., does this make you want to vote?

Well, I always vote, so we'll put it that way. I won't tell you about my first time. But anyway, I had not even known of this statistic, first of all, that 20 million women - most of them unmarried women - did not vote, and that's what this campaign is really aimed at.

And I think the thinking seems to be that if you're an unmarried mother, you're so busy raising your children, working and all of that, that the last thing you have time to do is to go and go to the ballot - to go to the booth to vote. So I think the campaign is rather clever, and it does get your attention because you don't know where these people are going.

Particularly, you've got Desperate Housewives involved and all of that. But I think it's good, because they're raising issues that - some of the main issues that women should care about are healthcare, education, opportunities for jobs, equal pay, social security. We should all be considering that. But if there is 20 million women out there who aren't voting, then this is a good campaign.

Well, you know, Jeff, I saw it and I had a couple of different reactions to it. Obviously, it's funny and it's cute. But I was wondering whether or not it's seemed clever or desperate. Which does it seem to you?

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: It could be one or the other. I mean, there are always two sides of this coin. When you interject sex in any way into the discussion, it makes people perk up in their seats. I mean, I could say, I'm so enjoying being here with the group, sharing.
Watch out, now.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Interacting is so stimulating. And instantly, people who are flipping through the channels would pause and say, hey, well, what are they talking about?

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: So I think it's kind of innovative on the one hand, but it also can be used deviantly, as in the case of the Senate race that's on fire here in Tennessee - particularly here in Nashville.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Harold Ford Jr. - he went to a Playboy Super Bowl party that at first, he had denied going to. And then it was found out, and they played that up on commercials and all over the place. Then when he was confronted about it, his reply was, hey, I like football and I like girls. And they played that up, too, but that may have registered with some of the male voters who are out there saying well, yeah. You know, I like football. I like girls, too. I like that guy.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: So as a result, the Get Out the Vote campaigns are blistering now. You're standing in line forever just for early voting. And it's anyone's guess on how it's going to shake out now. But it injects something new to the discussion.
Well, you know what, with the Ford campaign, what makes that really controversial is that the ad plays up a white woman…

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Yeah.
Yeah, right.
…a blonde, winking and cooing and saying call me up, Harold, kind of thing. So that plays into the whole racial history that we have, particularly in the South.

Well, you know, Bob, sex sells. It sells cars. It sells soap. It sells all sorts of things in the American culture. So why shouldn't it be able to sell voting as well, or at least participation in voting?

Sex does sell, but you often - you have to remember, the American public is among the West world, we're like the most squeamish when it comes to sex. This may actually turn some people off. But as far as the desperation of getting people out to vote, there are many tactics. You have to remember in Arizona right now, they have this measure being voted on. They're going to give $1 million every two years to a random voter. I can't really argue against these things that are trying to get people out to vote. I know I would be out at that poll in Arizona if I was there.
How long do you have to be in the state to order to register to vote?
Well, you know…

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Yeah, right. I can't…
E.R., you can't move to Arizona.
I think it's too late this year.

You know, I am confused about by one thing, and maybe you can sort of explain it to me. In listening to the Regina King ad and understanding that the target - as I understand it - is women voters, why they would use, you know, that sexual innuendo to reach women voters?
Well, it's not just Regina King's part - all of the women were playing off of that whole thing. Somebody had a clever idea.
Okay.

There are probably other ways you could've reached women. There probably are, in fact, there are other ways that people are doing things. We can't forget that organizations as old as the NAACP and the Urban League and as new as Rock the Vote are out there trying to attract people to the polls.

They're using various means, whether it is just going around to churches and that kind of thing to talk to people, or whether it's having concerts to invite younger people. So there are many ways that we are trying to get people to participate. Think about it. In this country, more than half of us don't vote, period.
Yeah.
So this is just one other effort.
This is our last topic. We only got about a minute or so left, unfortunately, because we got caught up in talking about Regina King and sex. I mean, how could that happen? But it did.
The Red Cross is also trying to do a little damage control post-Katrina - reorganizing, overhauling, trying to put a new face. Can they do this successfully, do you think, Bob?

Well, I think what the Red Cross is doing, truthfully, is coming into the 21st century. They're going to, I guess, slash their 20-member board now to 12. They're going to try to diminish the influence of presidential appointees. The thing I wonder about, though, is they're going to do this over a period of six years. It seems like they could do a little bit quicker than that. And, of course, this is all in response to Hurricane Katrina and the criticism that they faced, how they couldn't play nice with others and were kind of slow to react to a lot of things. So I guess it remains to be seen.
Bob, I mean, Jeff, do you, what do you think?

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Yeah, I think it's - I think it could be speedier, as Bob said. I think that in the relief efforts that I participated in, I heard all the criticisms from slow response to lack of coordinated, informed volunteers and the like. And in reality, you cannot have an 8-Track approach in an iPod world. And anyone that has ran an organization with the board knows that it can be hard to run with the board involved in day to day operations. And traditionally, things like fundraising and a long-term visioning is the board philosophy for even the largest most successful non-profits. So it only makes sense that the same rule would be true for the Red Cross.
Unfortunately, E.R. we have run out of time, which means that when we get together again, you get the first word, because I'm taking away the last word from you today.
Oh, well.

E.R. Shipp, professor in journalism, Hofstra University School of Communication. Bob Meadows, writer People magazine. Jeff Obafemi Carr, host of the radio show Freestyle. Thank you all for a very good Roundtable today.
Thanks.
Thank you.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Thank you.

This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya. On today's Roundtable, Prime Minister Tony Blair of the UK offers an olive branch to the axis of evil. And major shakeups at The Washington Post, the L.A. Times and Philadelphia Inquirer raise questions about the future of newspapers.

Joining us in our New York bureau is Walter Fields, CEO and publisher of thenorthstarnetwork.com, along with Bob Meadows, writer for People magazine. And we've got economist and author Julianne Malveaux, who is president and CEO of Last Word Productions. She's at member station WGBH in Boston, Massachusetts.

Welcome everybody, and let's go to Tony Blair. He was the one stalwart in the international community that President Bush counted on to have his back. And now he's saying, you know what? Let's meet with Iran. Let's extend the olive branch. Let's try to be magnanimous. Who is this good news and bad news for, Julianne?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Well, it's good news for Iran and it's bad news for Mr. Bush. And it's quite interesting, it's quite a turn of events. As recently as October 28, 2005, Tony Blair had talked about a military option in Iran. But I think that in his last year of his prime ministership - this week he gave his last Queen's speech, you know, to the Parliament - and he's got some 30 security-related measures that he plans to introduce in this last year of his term.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: And I think he's looking at the long haul, which unfortunately Mr. Bush has been unable to do. And looking at the long haul, how much war can the planet really, you know, stand? So he - I don't think he's capitulating to Iran and Syria at all. I think that what he's doing instead is saying, look guys, there are options. You can be isolated or you can come in with the rest of the world and talk about ways that we can reduce some terrorism.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: But it does make Mr. Bush, it isolates Mr. Bush further, and puts him on a limb all by himself. And that means isolates the United States further. We cannot afford this.

Bob, in this situation, is this kind of a thumb in the eye to the Americans after Bush kind of - excuse me - Prime Minister Blair followed us around rather blindlessly, according to some of the members of his own party, the Labour Party.

I think what it really is, is that for Tony Blair legacy trumps friendship. He wants to be remembered. As Julianne pointed out, this is his final year. He is now aiming for his legacy. He wants to be seen as somebody who facilitated a peace process in the Middle East as opposed to someone who is known for his merely following, blindly, President Bush.

So, I think that's really what he's working on. And honestly, this is what the American people are ready for. How can we get out of this situation? It doesn't necessarily matter how we get out. All people really want is to get out of there. And discussion, wow, what a concept - talk to Iran and Syria. Bush is doing the same thing right now over in Asia. He's asking China and Japan and South Korea, hey, you guys, you talk to North Korea so we don't have to come in here and handle this. What a concept to get the neighbors to take responsibility for this.

Walter, let's take a look at the specifics of this partnership. Mr. Blair said that he could extend the olive branch if Iran stops supporting terrorism in Iraq, gave up its nuclear ambitions. And he said again that Syria and Iran can choose partnership or isolation. Are those terms that Iran today, which has been, you know, pretty much ostracized by the U.S., would be willing to meet?

You know, I don't know. I think Iran has certainly made it known that it will not be bullied into a position. And I think that we have yet to really explore all of the options through diplomacy. So, I think it's a good start.

We need to understand that Mr. Blair is not doing this on his own. He is under tremendous pressure. His continued leadership of the UK was really a negotiated compromise. Because his Labor Party wanted him out. So I think, you know, what Bob suggested is exactly right. Is the fact that he's trying to preserve his legacy right now. And I think he'll do anything to try to leave office on a good note.

But clearly I think most people understand that when you look at that region of the world, Iran has to be part of the solution. You cannot isolate them this early on without offering them an opportunity, but a part of a situation that allows them to have a say in how the final resolution in Iraq takes place. Because you need them desperately to be on your side.
So I think it's a good start. And we haven't really tested the diplomacy waters with this country yet.

Now I want to go to the people who cover the news. Yesterday, we talked about the launch of Al-Jazeera International. Today, the topic is newspapers. A little bit more than a week ago, Dean Baquet was forced out of his position at the L.A. Times over cost cuts. High level African-American employee in the newspaper business.

Now Leonard Downey, Jr., executive editor of The Washington Post announced shakeups that would shrink his newsroom. It's being kind of marketed as, oh this will be great for new media, but I doubt that a lot of folks in the newsroom are kind of feeling that interpretation. And the Philadelphia Inquirer has been tightening up. There's been the whole sale and, you know, kind of disbundling of Knight Ridder and the Tribune Company is up for sale.
Should we be concerned that American newspapers as we know them just aren't going to exist anymore, Bob?

Well, they're definitely changing. There's, of course, the death mill for newspapers has been around for generations now. But, I think the difference now is that there was always until you can take a laptop into the bathroom you're always going to have newspapers. Well, you know what? You can take your little handheld anywhere you want.

I spoke with a couple of people at the Post, though, yesterday about this. And they're in that mode of worried by still kind of confident as to what is going to be happening. Because I was in newspapers for only seven years and I went through three of these shakeups. So this is not an extraordinary thing. This happens all the time.

But really what they're getting at is the only way for newspapers to really distinguish themselves now is on the local level. National news - TV covers that in an instant. And, by the time it hits the newspapers - it's done. So they really do have to focus more on the local level and, of course, on the issues that TV can't get to.
What about the economics, Julianne. I mean, a lot of these companies are profitable. They're just not as profitable as their owners want them to be.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: You know, when you look at people getting a 10, 15, 20 percent rate of return and they say that's not enough, the question has to come up what is enough? Because, literally, that was considered a respectable profit at a point in time.

speaker_label: But the other piece of the economic equation is this
text: They have less advertising; you have the blogosphere. Many of these papers are online and they are different kinds of models as to how you extract revenue from an online kind of model. So you are looking at some change.

speaker_label: But the other piece of the economic equation is this
text: My concern is that will we reduce the coverage especially of international news to the electronic media, especially television and radio? Well, we end up with us a kind of shorthand that basically, short circuits in-depth thinking, if you will. The minute and a half to three-minute piece that you see on MSNBC or CNN, frankly is no substitute for the kind of in-depth analysis that you've frequently seen in newspapers.

speaker_label: But the other piece of the economic equation is this
text: What Len Downey said is that people are going to have to justify now the link of their stories, and I'm not quite sure what the means but lots of people are fearful that you're talking about sort of more McNews, more nuggets of news as opposed to news analysis. And I think that that would be a big lack.

speaker_label: But the other piece of the economic equation is this
text: A lot of people think there are a lot of information sources out there. But the blogosphere is not reporting. It's regurgitation. It's opinion. And the issue is where will the real reporting come. Farai, already, if we look at the coverage of the African continent, for example, it's woefully inadequate. And with these kinds of cuts that you see you can expect it to get even worse.

speaker_label: But the other piece of the economic equation is this
text: There are all kinds of industries and other issues where there is a major inadequacy. And I don't see anyone else stepping up to sell that point.
Well, you know, Walter, you're working in online media. Is that going to take over the function?

Well, I think what we're seeing is a change not in the newspaper industry but in the media landscape. And what you're beginning to see are many papers understanding that new media has to play a role, a significant role, in the marketing of their product. And a good example to look at is the New York Times.

About three years ago, the chairman of the New York Times gave a speech. And he basically said the New York Times is not a newspaper company anymore. We're a media company. And it doesn't matter what the distribution portal is. It could be print, it could be radio, it could be television, it could be the Internet. But we're going to use all of them.

So, when you look at The New York Times and their partnership with the Discovery Channel. The New York Times now does incredible pieces with Discovery Channel in investigative journalism. That's the new model that newspapers are going to start pursuing. And I don't necessarily think it's going to be a bad thing. Because oftentimes when you look at today's newspapers, much of it is filler and much of it is wire service copy. There are very few papers in this country that are doing original reporting because the cost of it so tremendous.

It's the main reason why you have broadcast television networks that don't really have foreign news bureaus anymore. CNN still has probably the widest reach of any American television broadcast network. But that's been cut back years ago.

So as you begin to see newspapers make the shift. And also you have to understand that borders and barriers of news coverage have gone down. So now you do have the BBC in America providing a different perspective. You have Al-Jazeera in America providing a different perspective. So I'm not too frightened about it. In fact, I'm very excited about it because I think for American citizens you may finally get a different type of news coverage that we've never been privy to because our news coverage has always been from the perspective of the American newsroom and a very narrow perspective.

So I enjoy getting a feed from the BBC, and I've always read Al-Jazeera online. I'm looking forward to seeing their cable network, if anybody will pick it up in the U.S. So I think it's a real interesting time in the media landscape.

So you're up for the pick and choose? So we'll take from that and move on to another sobering study. The Census Bureau reporting that racial disparities and income, education and homeownership persist and in some cases are growing between black Americans and white households.

Decades after the civil rights movement, African-Americans are still fighting the basic issues of how do we put food on the table? Where do we live? Are we facing things like mortgage redlining? At this point, do we need a change in strategy, Julianne?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: We need a change in strategy, but we also need to enforce the civil rights laws that are on the books. And I think that government certainly, among others, have a lot of do to close some of the gaps that are a function of legacies of discrimination.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: There's a book out, Farai, called When Affirmative Action Was White, and it talks about all the programs that have basically transferred wealth to basically working class and middle-class white folks.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Primarily the post-World War II period where government subsidies allowed people to get involved in homeownership. Now the homeownership gap, 75 percent of whites own their homes compared to about 49 percent, 50 percent of African-Americans and Latinos. That homeownership gap is a major gap and deals with all those net worth issues.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: You can fund any kind of thing from starting a business to sending a child to school with home, you know, with your home equity. But African-American households have, by and large, missed out on that boom of the '80s because of the initial inequity. Lots of folks will say oh, get over it, it happened a lot time ago. But the fact is that this is intergenerational wealth that's passed on.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: So that I think is key. And then of course significant discrimination remains in job markets, not only in housing markets but - and in education. And so those are things we have to deal with. I think the civil rights establishment has been relatively impotent in trying to close these kinds of gaps, because you're not looking - you're looking at micro inequities not macro inequities.
Let's pick that up. You know, Bob, what do you think?

I am sick and tired of studies comparing black people to white people. You know, if we're are going to race and you have a 300-yard lead - if you have a 300-year lead, the fact that I haven't caught up to you in 30 years is really not that significant to me.

You know what I took from this, Farai? There was this stat that said 26 years ago, blacks had 60 percent of the income of whites. Today, blacks have 60 percent of the income of whites. So what I took from that is in 26 years, our income has grown at the same rate as white people. I don't want to compare myself to white people. If I'm trying to lose weight, I don't compare myself to Kobe Bryant and how he loses weight. I compare myself to how I used to be. You know what I mean?

So - can I just - can I break in for a second? Does this mean that you have resigned the black community to living in a parallel universe economically, and that it's just not going to change and that's the way it is?

Black people continue to progress, that's what I'm talking about. And we continue to progress. We continue to be better than what we were. We come out with all these studies that always portray us as downtrodden and terrible and everything that, you know, we - what are you to, you know, it's sort of like why aren't they even doing this studies anymore?

They should show them the high school students, I agree with that. Because, yeah, they are the people who were, you know, high school students don't know anything. They go around dressed in Nazi uniforms and things like that for Halloween and think it's funny. But for the rest of us it's like black people continue to progress - the thing is not that I am still trailing, but the thing is I still keep running. I keep still trying. That's what I really want black people to take away from all of this.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Bob, with all due respect - and forgive me, Farai, for just jumping in for a second - the fact is that the relative issue is important. We may be progressing and we continue to progress, but the fact is that these gaps are widening...
Yeah. Bob, with all of these things that portrays as downtrodden all the time, Julianne.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: ...because of issues that have been...
We're not a downtrodden people.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: I'm not saying anything about that. I don't think we're downtrodden, either. But I think there are gaps. And those gaps affect the material conditions under which we live and under which our children live, and we can't deny that.
All right. Well, I'm going to...
I'm not denying it. And I'm sorry, Walter.
No. No. No. I didn't say...

No. No. It's all good. Walter, can I redirect you just a little bit to the last topic that really ties right into this, which is that stereotypes actually affect how well African-Americans, Latinos, Asian-Americans, Native Americans can do in a workplace. Because you kind of come in with a presupposition about who you are, what you're education is, how trustworthy you are. Perhaps that's one of the reasons that we are just walking along parallel lines with the white community in terms of earnings.

Well, I think it's all part of it. And if you go back to your earlier segment where you had Bill Spriggs on and you start talking about the lower tier of the labor market, I think that's where it really impacts. Because when you look at hiring that very subjective at that lower tier, I think black men are affected by the perceptions of who they are when they go to seek a job.

But I think both Julianne and Bob are making valid points this morning. I think one thing, you have to put our conditions in context and look at where we've come from. We've only - we're only 40 years out from the Civil Rights Act of 1964. So we have made tremendous progress, but we do see some gaps that are growing in certain segments of the labor market, and we should be concerned about that. And we also need...
Do you think that we're ever going to start moving beyond, like, the parallel track and start making aggressive point-by-point gains?

In time. I mean this country is not even 300 years old. I mean that's the other thing we have to keep in mind. If you look at the history of this country and how far we have come, it's going to take some considerable time before we start talking about equity. And I think that's something that we all need to digest. This thing may seem like it's been a long time. We're in our infancy, so I think that we still have a lot of work to do.

But on the issue of federal enforcement, I think Julianne is absolutely correct. If you look at an agency like the EEOC starting when Clarence Thomas was heading the EEOC, it's been a disaster. It hasn't enforced anything. That's an agency that we need to be looking about, because that agency can start looking at some of the discriminatory practices in the workplace.

If you look at the Civil Rights Commission, that commission was almost bankrupt, broke, under this presidential administration. In fact at one point about 10 months ago, they couldn't even pay it - the agency couldn't pay its rent. So we need to look at those agencies that have civil rights enforcement responsibilities and make sure that they are doing their job. Because at the end of the day what we have always seen in terms of making these adjustments, these equity adjustments, it's always usually done from the perspective of either litigation or government enforcement, very rarely done on the basis of goodwill.

All right. We're going to have to let it go there. Walter Fields, CEO and publisher of the North Star Network; along with Bob Meadows of People Magazine, economist and author Julianne Malveaux. Thank you all so much.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (CEO, Last Word Productions)
text: Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you.
And next on NEWS & NOTES, NPR senior correspondent Juan Williams and his political experts take over Political Corner. Plus, reggae pioneer Lee Perry on aging and his undeniable style.
This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya.
On today's Roundtable, a major hospital company allegedly dumped a patient on L.A.'s Skid Row, and who's really profiting from the new O.J. Simpson book and TV special?

We've got Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition. And, in our New York bureau, Bob Meadows, writer for People Magazine. Plus from the studios at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Callie Crossley, social cultural commentator on the television show “Beat the Press” in Boston.

So guys, I'm just going to move right ahead and start with a topic that's on a lot of people's minds, and… O.J. Simpson's new book titled “If I Did It.” Now Judith Regan, who's this sort of bonzo New York-based publisher. She's the one who signed him to this $3.5 million deal. Fox is airing this special with the two of them talking.
But I want to frame things around a book that Catherine(ph) Russell Brown, an academic, wrote about black support of the O.J. Simpson case. Let's take a listen.

For African-Americans, in some ways it doesn't even matter what the larger society thinks about their response to particular criminal justice cases. For many blacks, they're one or two degrees of separation away from someone who's involved in the justice system. The perception, the reality of the criminal justice system is something different than for white Americans compared to black Americans.
But you're right. There was this sense that blacks were just defending O.J. because he's black. But I would maintain it had everything to do with a different take on the criminal justice system.

Again, that was Catherine Russell Brown who appeared on our air, that's her from our own air. You know, Callie, one of the key questions that I think things come down to here is, first of all, are African-Americans going to be reliving a kind of collective stigmatization. Oh you're the ones that supported O.J. Simpson and look what he's gone off and done now.
And secondly, was African-American support of the O.J. Simpson verdict about the verdict or about the man?

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (TV Commentator, Beat the Press)
text: It was about the verdict just to start there. And she's right, the academic that we just heard from. That black people have a very different view about the justice system. And we, all of us, know some folks who are involved and we know some injustices along the way. So it's difficult to look at it in the same sort of, if you will, black and white terms that most white Americans view the system.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (TV Commentator, Beat the Press)
text: They come to it believing it's fair, it's just, and, you know, people I know who have been involved in it have been served well. So there's that.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (TV Commentator, Beat the Press)
text: Now, the other part of it though, is - I just wonder, if the poll was taken now, where black folks - where most Americans, most black Americans would stand. I mean first of all, I was never one that believed that - I wasn't the jumping up and down kind. I think the guy is guilty. But be that as it may, I had many heated discussions about it at the time with many folks who felt that sincerely, outside of the justice system, he really was innocent, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (TV Commentator, Beat the Press)
text: I don't know if that's the case now. Though, I've just seem some video where, you know, he's traveling around the country and people think he's a hero. I just find that appalling and shocking. And I'm at the point now where they've gotten me agreeing with Bill O'Reilly, who says don't watch this mess that's coming up on Fox television. This is ridiculous for us to continue to support it in this way.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (TV Commentator, Beat the Press)
text: And I think black folks have to stand up and say, okay, yeah, justice system is flawed but this O.J. Simpson thing, that's a different animal.

Michael, at this point, should black people even feel any sense of either collective agreement with the verdict that happened years ago or collective shame. Or should we just say, you know what, he's not our problem. He may be black but he's not our problem.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: The shame belongs to O.J. Simpson. The shame belongs to those people who, despite the facts, despite the overwhelming evidence, continue to identify with racial rhetoric and racial idiocy, and that includes O.J. Simpson.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: O.J. Simpson was never identified with the black community. But aside from that, he had a here's Johnny legal defense, high-powered legal defense team. It wasn't about race at all. It seemed to me, with respect to the O.J. Simpson trial and the O.J. Simpson verdict, although I'm an African-American, color me white.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: The real problem was it was an incompetent prosecution, and an incompetent judge, and a highly-powered legal team. And Johnny did his thing. Nobody was more surprised - if you look at the videotape, let's go to the videotape - nobody was more surprised with that verdict than O.J. Simpson's attorney, Johnny - and O.J. Simpson.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: And for him to now, come years later, with this book, “If I Did It,” after a civil judgment that says, yeah, you did. You know you did it. The man is shameless.
