He has no shame, he should hide his head in shame. But it's not African-Americans who should hide their heads in shame, because African-Americans were not on trial. It was O.J. Simpson was on trial.

Bob, you work for People Magazine, which does everything from, you know, issues-based reporting to celebrity-based reporting. A lot of people are coming down hard on Fox for airing this. If it were a situation where you had to make a decision whether or not, say, People Magazine was going to run an exclusive from O.J., would you do it at this point, or would you consider it too shameful, too taboo, too crass - any of those things.

Well, since I won't be watching this special, I guess I have to say if it was my decision I probably would veer away from something like this. Because O.J. Simpson won't sell. He is the most reviled man in this country. The readership of People Magazine is largely made up of white people. They wouldn't buy our magazine, probably, if they knew that this story was in there.

I don't' think this is going to be a big seller of Judith Regan. I don't think this is going to be a widely watched program for Fox. I really don't understand why they're doing it. I know O.J.'s doing it for the money, I know Judith is doing it for the notoriety. But it's really…
Well, it's sweeps week in television, so presumably they think this is going to be…
They think it will but it's not going to be. It's just going to be something that's going to be talked about, but probably much like Snakes on a Plane, not garner much of an audience.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: I don't understand how O.J. Simpson can be doing it for the money when given the huge size of that civil judgment against him. And I don't know how Judith Regan is going to hide the money from people who are going to go after it, or how O.J. Simpson has already hid the money, the 3.5 - reported $3.5 million deal.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: So he owes the Goldmans a lot of money. It's time for him to pay up. With respect to Judith Regan, you know, going into her own interview, she's got her own issues involving…
And many of them.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Many of them.
She wrote this eight-page letter…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Did you call her a bonzo or a bozo, Farai?
I called her bonzo.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Oh, I thought you said bozo.
I didn't call her bozo. If you want to call her bozo, that's all on you.

Well, I actually want to move ahead to another topic. We have a lot on our plate today. I went to Skid Row. I mean this was a piece that I did with one of our producers, Corey Turner. And we did a two-part piece or series on Skid Row in Los Angeles, and it was shortly after a woman who had dementia was dumped just wearing her hospital gown downtown in, you know, a very rough, dangerous area.

And now Los Angeles prosecutors have filed criminal charges against Kaiser Permanente who they alleged did the dumping, and I believe Kaiser, you know, has said, you know, we apologize if - and we're looking into it. It's really amazing to me how much I learned about how different municipalities, like the smaller cities around Los Angeles will just use L.A.'s downtown Skid Row as a place to dump prisoners - they drop them off with a paper bag full of, you know, their soap and a couple of dollars they've earned.

and what responsibility, I guess, do larger structures like the hospital system, like Kaiser or other police departments have to really not view urban areas as a dumping ground? I guess, Callie, I'll start with you.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (TV Commentator, Beat the Press)
text: Well, they have the ultimate responsibility, which is, you know, to - there is a service of caring for people. Hospitals particularly. I mean there are oaths there that people take, there's responsibility, there's rules, there's laws. So this shouldn't be happening on any level and certainly on a human level.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (TV Commentator, Beat the Press)
text: But the fact that it's going on is, I guess, can't be that shocking. And this is - I'm looking at the fact that when we decided in this country - and I say we because there were lots of policymakers involved in this - that we were not going to fund services to mental health services in the way that we should. Lots of those folks ended on the street. So in effect they were dumped as well.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (TV Commentator, Beat the Press)
text: Maybe they didn't come from the doors of a hospital, sometimes they did. But there they were. And so we're dumping not just in the Skid Rows of L.A. but we're dumping in communities across this country. And by the way, it's not just urban communities. This is happening in small rural communities as well.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (TV Commentator, Beat the Press)
text: So we got a problem about dealing with the, quote-unquote, unwashed and unwanted. And I think it comes home to haunt us. And I hope that this is an example that would wake up folks and - because it could by your relatives.

You know, Bob, at this point in time there are certain areas that are considered okay to dump people and certain areas that are not. Does this mean that we're going to have to have a larger discussion about the not-in-my-backyard syndrome? Because if you dispersed all the people on Skid Row they would have to go somewhere, often back to cities and towns that dumped them there.

You know, I remember back in the mid-90s, when Giuliani came in and I left New York around '95 or so. Then I came back in '98. And when I came back, you know, Giuliani been in power for about five years by that point. I was wondering where have all the homeless people gone. Well, then I took a trip to Seattle and I think they all ended up there. Because you move people around - if you enforce laws that or, like, make it real difficult for people, they're just going to, like you said, they're going to move someplace else.

They're not going to just disappear all of a sudden, not become homeless. There are many, many issues that needs to be address with this, whether it mental health, whether it's AIDS, whether it's poverty just in general that have to be addressed with this. So yeah, the discussion needs to be wider than just, well, we're dumping people here in Los Angeles, because that's not really going to solve the problem by itself.
Michael, you're executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition. To what degree are issues like homelessness and mental health and all that, do these fall under civil rights concerns?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, they fall under human rights concerns, because a civil rights society just doesn't maltreat its citizens. It doesn't maltreat. It doesn't disrespect. It doesn't punish. It doesn't abandon. It doesn't desert. It does not dump its elderly, its sick, its poor onto Skid Row. Not a civilized society. Skid Row is the blight and the shame of a quite prosperous nation, probably the most prosperous nation in the world. And that patient suffering from dementia or all kinds of diseases - of all the diseases, dementia - that they could be dumped, abandoned, consigned to Skid Row is to me paramount to administering a death penalty.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: If true, there is criminal and civil liability. But as senior citizens might say, those responsible for such types of depraved indifference to life should not just be put in jail, they should be put underneath the jail. But society has got to do something about poverty. It has to do something about homelessness other than sweep the homeless away, other than put the homeless out of the public spaces and public places.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: And we've got to do something about homeless. As Bob said, we've got to do something about mental health issues. We have to do something about health issues and health maintenance and insurance. And we've got to get - we've got to build affordable housing. And for those people who can't live on their own, there have to be group homes and group housing so that they will have social services. But we've got - we have to stop declaring a war on the poor and renew our war on poverty.

All right, well, I want to move along to one last topic. Bush - the Bush administration appointed a chief of family planning programs, his name is Eric Keroack and he worked in an organization that believed that distributing contraceptives was quote, demeaning to women, unquote. Now there's a whole statute in federal policy that says that the government has to provide family planning services for low-income people. But is this appointment consistent with that mandate, Callie?

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (TV Commentator, Beat the Press)
text: Of course not. This is just crazy. And I really hope - I mean it's been done. His appointment has been done in this sort of twilight period before the Democrats take over certain key committee positions. So I hope that this is something that they can address right away, because it's already difficult for a lot of women to come to grips with understanding the importance of birth control - and particularly we're talking about teenagers - and just getting access to any kind of healthcare, and this is the most basic for women.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (TV Commentator, Beat the Press)
text: And so for a man, by the way, to tell me, to say to women that it's demeaning to them to seek birth control is just disgusting. That's the only way I can phrase it. It's an - talk about a death sentence, I mean we need to have good birth control, good family planning in this country so that we don't have unwanted children and so that people can take care of themselves. It doesn't make any sense at all.

Michael, you know, I think that this administration, the Bush administration, has often challenged abortion, but this is contraception. This is pre-pregnancy. Does this show kind of a creeping ideological tilt in terms of how these issues are dealt with? And I think in some ways that does relate to the whole topic we've been talking about, the topic of what you do with extreme poverty, because birth control has been link to diminishing extreme poverty.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, don't ask these ideological evangelicals to be consistent. But they are just that, ideological evangelicals. The Bush appointees are shocking with respect to the court, respect to the United States Commission on Civil Rights, for example. He's placed ideologues on that panel. He has a chair of the United States Commission on Civil Rights who has failed remedies to discrimination all the time. They have failed affirmative action. They have failed bussing. They have failed all the court-approved remedies to discrimination, and they are supposed to be in the business of monitoring civil rights enforcement. This is the same situation.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: This is a person who is supposed to be put in charge of contraception and monitoring it, and being the big, quote unquote, guy, but is obviously a guy who's never had to carry a baby or have to make a decision about unwanted pregnancy. But aside from those - his personal inabilities on his part, he's obviously unable to understand the basic notions of justice and privacy and healthcare, and that a woman's right to choose and to control her own value with the attention of medical care is her decision, not his. Who cares about his opinion?
We're going to have to go to Bob. Briefly, go ahead.

I just wanted to say one thing. I went to a woman's concern Web site. And I have to say there's really nothing on there that I found particularly reprehensible or even at all; it was very informative. It talked about condoms. It talked about proper usage. It talked about safer sex. It talked about abortion. And so it did give this type of information that is there. But the thing that I hope is that with Eric Keroack coming in is that, as we all know, teenage pregnancy has dropped dramatically since 1991 across the board. My hope is that we can keep that momentum going. Yeah, preach abstinence. Yeah, preach contraception. Preach safer sex, all those types of things. We all need all of that stuff together to keep that momentum going, and that's what I hope Keroack does.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, he can preach abstinence all he wants. But it isn't going to happen.
He'll preach it, Mike.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: He should abstain himself.
Okay, guys. On that note…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Yeah.

We've been talking to Bob Meadows of People magazine, Callie Crossley, social/cultural commentator on the television show “Beat the Press,” and Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition. Thank you guys so much.
You're welcome.

speaker_label: Ms. CALLIE CROSSLEY (TV Commentator, Beat the Press)
text: Thanks, Farai.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Thank you.

All right. And coming up next on NEWS & NOTES: Well, the influences on his songwriting range from Brazilian pop to Rock & Roll ballads, we're talking about Grammy Award winner John Legend, who talks to us about music, life, and love.

So joining us from NPR headquarters in Washington, D.C., we've got Joe Davidson, an editor for The Washington Post, along with Mary Frances Berry, professor of history at the University of Pennsylvania. Bob Meadows, a writer with People magazine is at our New York bureau.
Welcome everybody, and let's jump right in on this issue of malaria. Are we really making significant strides in the U.S. in terms of what we are able to offer the continent? Bob?

We definitely are. This is - I have to say this, and this may be one of the few times I actually say this - but I think President Bush actually got this one right. This is a very ambitious program. They are talking about 36 million people over the next few years. And that's - as the gentleman who just spoke said, 3,000 kids a day - a day - die from malaria in Africa.

And as he said, this is totally preventable, but I think what we need to see contributing to this great effort, $1.2 billion, there needs to be a bit more political stability in some of these countries as well, because obviously an instable government can destroy this type of program. They also need better plumbing, better sewage, because mosquitoes of course proliferate in standing water. But, no, this is a marvelous effort and I hope that the private sector gets on board as the government is pushing.
Professor Berry, can there be that workable coalition of NGOs, non-governmental organizations, private sector, the U.S. government, African governments - that's a lot of folks to pull together.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Right. And it is working. The Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, as in so many things, is very deeply involved in a partnership on this. So is Marathon Oil Company and Noble Energy. So the private sector is involved. And one of the most heartening things I heard from an expert whom I talked to recently is that of course if children can survive until they are 5 years old, they are more likely to survive, if they can survive this and keep from dying from it by then.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: And one of the things the federal government has done, and USAID agency, is to set up people who are in communities, at least one designated leader in every little community who has medication and who can dispense it to people at all hours when they need it.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: And what that has done is cut down on people trying to get to clinics, trying to see where they get it and all the rest of it, and they said that this has had an enormous effect. So the private sector is involved, the NGOs are involved. And you asked earlier, why would the private sector want to be involved?

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: And I think that part of it is because the private sector - some people have a conscience and just as their foundations are working on other issues, they want to work on this. Also, there are great economic opportunities in Africa if one can figure out how to do something about the many diseases that beset people over there, including malaria, which is the major one.

Joe, there's one slightly controversial part of the whole anti-malaria effort, which is that they are spraying some drugs that they no longer use in the U.S. over wide areas where families who live in farms are - agents that were considered toxic in the United States, but they do kill mosquitoes.
Should we take a second look at issues like that that are part of this complicated effort?

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington post)
text: Well, I think that it's definitely important to look at methods, at the - or perhaps the ethical value, you might say, in certain methods of trying to eradicate diseases. And if something that's not - if it's not good enough to use in the United States, then is it good enough to use overseas?

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington post)
text: I think the reality also is that with malaria still being a major disease in Africa and having been eradicated in the United States, I think it's important that the government, those African governments, also consider that balance and that that balance not necessarily be imposed by people, environmentalists perhaps, in the United States.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington post)
text: I think that there's one other thing that we need to be aware of as it relates to United States policy, and that is that next year, when the Congress considers the budget, there's a cap on spending for some of these malaria programs.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington post)
text: And that might limit just how much can be spent overseas to combat malaria. So there's been - Bush has gotten kind of a break in all of the criticism as it relates to Iraq by getting kudos as it relates to malaria. But the effectiveness of that program could be limited if the Congress is not able to go beyond the current cap on spending.

We'll keep an eye on that and move on to another issue that is very important on the continent of Africa - the Sudan and abuse charges. The new United Nations Human Rights Council is backing a mission to investigate accusations that abuse in Darfur is getting worse.

Now human rights advocates say this is a timid first step in confronting atrocities. Aid officials say more than 200,000 people have been killed, many, many more displaced since the ethnic conflicts turned into a war nearly four years ago.
Prof. Berry, is this a step in the right direction and does it go far enough?

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: It is a tepid response, but it is in fact a response. And to date, we've had practically no useful responses. And I also think that the United Nations Human Rights Council needs to do something on Darfur.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: They do things on other issues and they also have been highly controversial because of some of the stuff that they have done. But I think it's high time, and I was glad that Kofi Annan challenged them to do something. And so now they are going to send these five qualified team members with their special Sudan investigator from the United Nations to actually go there on the ground and come back and have something to say and try to highlight the issues.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: So I think it's a step in the right direction. And even if it's tepid, at least it's something.
Joe?

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington post)
text: Well, it's interesting that the outgoing secretary-general, he gave a speech, not the speech that got so much attention a couple of days ago, his last speech, but his last speech on human rights was last Friday and he talked about the, quote, “shameful passivity of most governments,” close quote, when it comes to the issue of Darfur. And of course President Bush was out in front of this in terms of calling the situation there a genocide, but he's also been under a lot of pressure since then to take that beyond the rhetoric into greater action.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington post)
text: I think it's also worth noting that the former secretary-general also was critical of African governments, and in that speech he said that too often they mischaracterize the U.N. human rights agenda as, quote, “a conspiracy by imperialist powers to take the hard-won on national sovereignty of formerly colonized people.” So we urge them to kind of reject that mindset and to do - and to step up in the fight against genocide, particularly in Sudan, and he mentioned, at least indirectly, China and certain Islamic governments who back Sudan.
Before we get to Bob's response, I just want to make sure everyone is on the same page with us.
This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya.
We are talking on our Roundtable with Joe Davidson from The Washington Post; Mary Frances Berry, professor of history at the University of Pennsylvania; and Bob Meadows, writer with People magazine.

Bob, the African Union forces are very understaffed and don't have enough equipment, and so is it just going to have to come down to the U.N. really stepping up its game? I mean this is a first step; Professor Berry says is a timid first step. What do you think?

Well, the Sudanese government has continuously resisted any U.N. efforts to come in with a military force - heads will roll, I believe may have been a statement, or something to that effect, from the leader over there.

So the U.N. does have to step up. But unless Sudan is going to actually get on with the program, then the effort may actually fall short because I don't think anybody wants another invasion of that sort. But I also don't think there's a lot of incentive for the Sudanese government to really step up to the plate on this because the country is thriving economically at this point.

They have all this oil money that's been pouring in. They're one of the major suppliers to China for oil. So China is never going to vote for sanctions. Saudi Arabia is pouring money into the country. They're prospering right now, and as long as that continues, why should they follow anybody's advice except their own counsel.

Let's move along to a topic right here in the United States. A 25-year-old desegregation case against Alabama has finally been decided. This week, a federal judge approved the agreements that settled the case, ruled that segregation in Alabama's higher education system is no longer an issue.

Now this case has generated $210 million in state funds for the desegregation effort, and most of that is going to historically black colleges like Alabama A&M and Alabama State University. Mary Frances Berry, what are the pros and cons of this 25-year-old effort ending?

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Well, there really are pros and cons. All of the school desegregation litigation in higher education in the South started out as a way to try to get the schools, black and white, to integrate, and that there would be black professors and faculty members and things at the white schools and more black students, and that they would all be integrated and sing together and everything would be happy. And that this would be a way to take care of deficiencies.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: As it went on, it became a litigation that was directed at just trying to improve the black college campuses - which were of course set up under separate but equal and always under-funded - in a way that they would become attractive to other students, that was the argument, and then they would become desegregated by other students becoming attracted. Then it became, in this next phase, blacks who are alums of those institutions and who go to those institutions who simply want their institution to have more resources, to have more of what it needs.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: So we're at a point where the black college, and this is happening in other states, have gotten more money for the things that they need, although they never have - are going to be able to make up for all the things they didn't get for years and years and years and years. But you still don't have desegregation because the predominantly white institutions, except for the football team and maybe the basketball team or whatever, are still largely segregated in terms of white people and the few black faculty, the few black administrators. And the black colleges are the same, although the black colleges are more integrated than the white ones are. They got more white faculty and people who are from foreign countries and the like.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: So it's a good thing to get all this money for the black colleges, but it's not true that the desegregation has really taken place because it really hasn't.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington post)
text: And it's interesting that on some of these historically black colleges - just to take your point a little bit further, Mary - you find a lot of white students too, certainly not just white faculty and staff. But on some of these black colleges they're practically - some of them there may be as many as 40 percent and maybe they've even tipped over to 51 percent in terms of white students.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington post)
text: And so when you look at that, and then you look at the white colleges, and you see still the struggle as certainly as it relates around affirmative action. We've seen these major court cases that relates to affirmative action on predominantly white colleges and the faculty, the staff, you know, you sometimes have to sit back and wonder what - you know, is this the way it was supposed to play out.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: No.

And Bob, you know, one other factor in this is that Alabama's property taxes, one of the lowest in the country, and arguably it affects the ability to get financial aid for college. So black folks, no matter whether they go to a predominantly white school or predominantly black school, are going to have to face the challenge of a growing student loan crisis, which we talked about earlier on the show this week. Is this going to affect that?
Well, it - you mean the case ending? Is it going to affect that?
Yeah. I mean is the case ending and…

Well, I know that of the $210 million, much of it - a lot of it is supposed to go towards scholarships, toward endowments. Perhaps that can offset this property tax and the inability of them to get other types of aid. So you hope that - and obviously scholarships and endowments are much better because you don't have to pay those back at the end, which I'm sure many college students will be clamoring to get something like that. So perhaps it can have that - a positive effect in that way.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: One of the dirty little secrets, Farai, is that in some of these states, including Alabama, what Joe said about the white students on the black college campuses, there are a lot of black students who aren't able to get in school anywhere. They don't have the financial aid money to pay to go anywhere, still. And because of the standards that have been changed in those states, some of them can't even get in the predominantly black college anymore.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: So their standards are changing, not really desegregation at the white school, white students going to the black campuses where the programs have improved and they think that they can get - for example, I go speak at commencement and all the graduates who are getting degrees in physical therapy or…
I'm going to have to…

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: …anything where you can get a job are white.

All right. Mary Frances Berry - we're going to have leave it there -professor of history at the University of Pennsylvania. Joe Davidson of The Washington Post. Bob Meadows of People magazine. Thank you all so much and have a great weekend.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington post)
text: Thank you.
You too.
Next on NEWS & NOTES, we talk politics with NPR's Juan Williams and his guests on Political Corner. And we get really low with the sound of the bass in our latest visit to the lower frequencies.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO of Last Word Productions)
text: Farai, I think that was a really great interview, and it is really important to put a human face behind the people that Mr. Bush so callously refers to as troops. They are not troops; they are human beings.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO of Last Word Productions)
text: When he talks about troops it's easy to lose the personal stories like Kristi's story and so many of the other stories that we've been hearing about people who spent most of their married life apart, about children who are born and haven't seen their fathers and mothers yet - or their fathers, usually. Just the dynamics of the human story is something that I think we are losing sight of.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO of Last Word Productions)
text: This war is - the burden of this war is not being evenly spread in these United States at all. You have 132,000 people there now, we're going to add another 21,500 people, but that - as a nation of nearly 300 million people, that's a tiny number of people who are basically shouldering the burden of this ill-advised war.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO of Last Word Productions)
text: And Mr. Bush really was remiss. I mean that was one of the most delusional speeches I have ever heard in life. It's like telling you that the new Coke is different from the old Coke. You know, new and improved. If we were going to do something, it seems that we, you know, many military strategists don't believe that what we're doing is going to make that much of a difference. We really need to bring these people home.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO of Last Word Productions)
text: But more importantly, people like Kristi have to be embraced by our communities. People have to be, you know, we need to be supporting these people more in both material and in non-material ways. And we really have to hear these human stories. The media must pay attention to the people.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO of Last Word Productions)
text: And I must say that, you know, The Washington Post, The New York Times have done some of it. You're seeing these personal stories. It's the only way we'd know some of the local papers. But we need to see a lot more of that, and these folks are - they are doing our work. We need to be celebrating them.

Walter, what about what Kristi mentioned in terms of her husband being promised four years stateside or in a non-combat position and earlier today the new secretary of defense acknowledging basically that the military was rotating people through Iraq faster than it had before? How much can we expect from these gentlemen, even - and women? Even if they are dedicated Marines and soldiers, they are being put in a position where they are being pushed really hard?

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetwork.com)
text: Well, at this point, you know, I think any enlisted man or woman should just understand that any promises made will be broken by this administration. And I think that they are an overtaxed group of individuals who are serving our country right now.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetwork.com)
text: You know, listening to the president last night, you know, it just really disturbed and he might as well put a gone fishing sign out in front of the White House because he is really - this was the ultimate Hail Mary pass. And we talk about 21,000 troops, but in reality, 4,000 of those troops are going to be in Anbar province. So we are talking 17,500 in Baghdad. By all estimates, even those who wanted an increase in troops, that number is way too low.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetwork.com)
text: And I think what the president is trying to do is to put a Band-Aid on an open sore, and this isn't going to work. And we're going to have our young men and women who are going to rotate through this, and, you know, the fatalities alone are going to be tremendous. But what we're going to have deal with when people come back home after experiencing this war, that is a situation that I don't think we're prepared for, whether it's the physical disability or the mental issues that families and spouses are going to have to deal with as a result of this war. That's a toll that this country I think can't (unintelligible) to think about right now.

And Bob, you know, it was Kristi and I believe also Brian that mentioned that people come back different. People do come back, you know, even if you're not physically wounded, you come back with a different sense of the world and your place in it. We in this country have not always been so good about responding to people who've returned. During the Vietnam era there were a lot of people who felt alienated when they returned to the U.S. Will we do a better job now, you think?

I hope that we do. I know that a couple of years ago that was a very big deal. There were a lot of Vietnam veterans who really, after that war, really went and really took it to Congress - and a lot of them are in Congress now or have served - and really to make it an extra point of yes, we really have to take care of our soldiers. Whether or not that's going to get done. Historically, it hasn't. Back in World War I they called it coming home shell-shocked. Vietnam is different story, but it's all the same thing.

It's your trauma; post-traumatic stress disorders is what they're calling it nowadays. We really have to take care of these soldiers. And you have to wonder, is that really going to happen. Because it doesn't seem like we're allocating money toward this war and all this great fighting, but are we going to take care of the soldiers. That has to be done because, as Walter said, these soldiers are coming home. They're not dead as much as - they're not dying at the rates they used to because of the wonderful medical care that they're getting. But now they're coming home without legs, without arms, without multiple limbs, burnt up, then they have to face the trauma of that now.

I want to turn us to another topic. We - certainly we'll continue to cover the war and the issue for the families at home. But I want to turn to Congress, which is expected to revisit sentencing laws later this month. Under the new leadership of Representative John Conyers of Michigan, the House Judiciary Committee is planning to revisit federal sentencing laws that require lengthy mandated prison terms for certain offenses.

One of the things that you hear a lot about is how crack cocaine is 100 times more of a mandatory sentence than powder cocaine and the racial implications of that. Now the federal judges in particular are eager to see a change because they say these automatic sentences deprive judges of the discretion that they need to do their jobs. Julianne, what can we expect from a real hearing on these issues of mandatory minimum sentences?

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO of Last Word Productions)
text: Well, I think the - injustices will be pointed out, as people have been talking about this for the past decade or so, Farai, since we've had the mandatory sentencing. You know, five grams of crack cocaine will get you 10 years or 5 years, 500 grams of powder cocaine. So, you know, that 100 to one ratio makes no sense at all.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO of Last Word Productions)
text: We have seen the - you know, this is targeted toward the black community. We have seen the disproportionate incarceration of African-American people, especially men, around this. And so I think we will see some changes. But I would like to see the Congress also look at the issue of sentence expunging.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO of Last Word Productions)
text: Reverend Jesse Jackson has been talking about it a bit. Barbara Lee in California, Congresswoman Lee, has been having people petition to have their sentences expunged. There's a state legislator in North Carolina doing the same thing because essentially sideline people from the labor market, when they're convicted of these minor drug offenses, end up spending a very long time in jail.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO of Last Word Productions)
text: So I know that they're looking at the one issue of sentencing. But I wish they would also couple it with some conversation about rehabilitation, taking a look at that, which Congresswoman Lee has been doing.
Walter, why do you think the government has been so reluctant to give up - the government meaning Congress - has been so reluctant to give this power which the judges say should be theirs?

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetwork.com)
text: Well, you need to understand where this all came from. In the 1980s there was an explosion of crack and in there was a knee-jerk reaction to that explosion and we enacted these mandatory minimums. And what happened - because of that, you really had an explosion of the prison industry. That's when we started seeing private prisons being built all around the country because the numbers were just so huge of the people we were putting behind bars. And that was a very profitable industry and continues to be a profitable industry.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetwork.com)
text: I think many lawmakers who took this tough-on-crime attitude for years have stood on that platform, particularly when running for office, because it's a platform that makes people feel secure. But what people have begun to realize is that it's a failed policy. And unfortunately, when we passed these mandatory minimums, we put everybody in the same pot - drug users and drug pushers.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetwork.com)
text: And what I'd like to see happen is not only the relaxation of these mandatory minimums, but I'd like to have more than just a criminal justice response to the drug crisis in America. We really need to have a health policy response to this issue, too, because we are putting behind bars people who are minor users when they shouldn't be there in the first place.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetwork.com)
text: These people need help. They need some healthcare. They need some real professional help. So I think and along with the idea of relaxing this mandatory minimums and giving judges more discretion, I hope Congress will also see that you can't solve this problem simply with a criminal justice reflex. It will never work.

Now Bob, do you think that the new leadership will really make a difference? Obviously, John Conyers is a long time congressional representative. He's African-American. He's someone who understands the African-American community. Will his leadership really make a turn in how things unfold in this discussion?

Not necessarily, and the reason I say that is because back when all these laws were enacted, the Democrats controlled Congress. So they were the ones who did them. And as was pointed out, these laws were a reaction to what was going on.

I mean at the time we'd never heard of drive-bys, carjacking and AK-47s. All those entered during this times, and so that's what all these minimum laws were a response to. And truth be told, black people were the short shrift back before when judges had all this discretion. So I - and they're getting it now.

So even if they go back to it, I don't have any faith that black people are still not going to reach this type - or still going to get a fair shake because historically it just hasn't happened and I don't have that much faith in people.

All right, well, we're going to wrap it up right here. Bob Meadows, writer for People magazine, political consultant Walter Fields, and author economist Julianne Malveaux. She's president and CEO of Last Word Productions Incorporated. Thank you all for joining us.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (President and CEO of Last Word Productions)
text: Thank you.
Thank you.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, NorthStarNetwork.com)
text: Thank you.

Next on NEWS AND NOTES, our Political Corner takes on African-Americans leading powerful congressional committees, and the film "God Grew Tired of Us," shows how Sudan's lost voice found a home in America.
This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Tony Cox.

On today's Roundtable, President Bush talks to NPR about the aftermath of Katrina. Deal or no deal, prison inmates are being offered all sorts of perks to move across the country. And a gas station offers terror-free gasoline.

Joining us today are Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition, Laura Washington, Chicago Sun Times columnist, and Bob Meadows, staff writer for "People" magazine. Hello, everybody.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Yes.

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: Hi.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: Greetings.

Listen. Let's start with the President. NPR's Juan Williams had a chance to talk to President George W. Bush yesterday at the White House. Juan took the chance to ask the president about his omission of Hurricane Katrina when he addressed the nation last week.

Let's talk for a second about the State of the Union speech. You didn't mention Hurricane Katrina, New Orleans, or the Gulf Coast. A lot of people from Louisiana, including David Vitter, the Republican senator, say they regret that. Do you?

President GEORGE W. BUSH: Well, I gave a speech that I thought was necessary to give. On the other hand, I have been talking a lot about Katrina and about the fact that I worked with the Congress to get about $110 billion sent down to both Mississippi and Louisiana to help them on the reconstruction efforts.

Obviously, there's more work to be done. Take the housing issue, for example. We have sent money down to the Louisiana folks - Louisiana Recovery administration - or authority - to fund their plan. And the money is there and the money is available. And now it's up to the folks down there to get this plan implemented so people can start rebuilding their houses.

If there's bureaucratic slowdowns in Washington, we've got a man named Don Powell who's working to address them. But no, our response to the Katrina Recovery has been very robust, and I appreciate the taxpayers of the United States helping the folks down there in Mississippi and Louisiana.
So here's the question, as I see it, to begin with, Mike Meyers. Has the president addressed Katrina enough? He seems to think so.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Look, I salute Juan Williams for the interview. But forgive me, other than NPR's Juan Williams getting the interview with the President, why do we care?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: I can't believe anything this president says about Katrina, no more than I can believe when he said to, you know, Brownie, you're doing a heck of a job. This president will say anything at any time. That's why you have to watch what he does as opposed to what he says. And it's the same situation with Iraq. It's the same situation with his assurances of not going into Iran. But at the same time, he'll talk about - he has to go and find the terrorists wherever they are.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: This is a man who doesn't understand the realities of life. He doesn't manage his agencies well. And he doesn't - how many times has he done (unintelligible) in New Orleans. Does he see that New Orleans is still a ghost town? I don't believe anything President Bush says. The man has discredited himself.
Laura Washington, what do you say? Has he said enough, done enough? Well, let me separate the two. Has he said enough about Katrina?

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: Well, I think neither. And the saying is often as much as it's important as it is to doing. The leadership - and he got also the wrong foot on this one from day one when there was a very slow and seemingly indifferent response when he put everything on Brownie, and Brownie wasn't delivering.

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: And by the time he caught up and actually got himself down there and he got some key people down there, there was so much damage done that, you know, that region will never be the same again. Again, $110 billion is fine, but how is that $110 billion being administrated?

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: He mentioned his top person Powell, who was down there yesterday getting grilled by a number of folks in - leaders in congress, including U.S. Senator Barack Obama. Where is the money going? The money is supposed to be here, but it's not getting spent.

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: I think there's a lot of bureaucratic bungling not just on the federal level, on the local level too. And I think Bush has moved on. He doesn't want to deal with any domestic issues, particularly this one because this is such a horrendous screw up for his administration. He's focusing all his effort on Iraq, and that's why Katrina was not in his speech.

So Bob Meadows, I suppose then taking into account what Laura Washington has just said and Michael Meyers said before her so clearly, there is nothing, is there, that the president can say that can assuage people over what happened earlier on with regard to the federal response to Katrina?

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: There's really not much you can say. As Michael said, it's by his actions, it's what he does. I would not have expected the president to discuss Katrina during this recent State of the Union address. The war on Iraq is so much bigger than that.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: And it's reaching and it's going to be never-ending it seems. And granted Katrina is maybe a situation like that too. But it's Iraq that cost the Republicans the elections, so that's - in 2006. And it could cost them election in 2008 in that Iraq, far more than Katrina, is going to be Bush's legacy. That's what he's really needing to focus on and one of the reasons he talked about Iraq a lot, obviously, during the State of the Union, and the issues around it.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: But he also focused of course on, as you were just talking about, Tony, his health care initiative because he wants to have something at least to say that he did domestically that perhaps has an iota of succeeding, even though I have no hope for any of that.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: But again, I would not have expected him to focus on Katrina during this recent State of the Union.
So just to follow up quickly with you on that one point, Bob. So Katrina, as far as you think the administration thinks, is not only bad news, it's old news.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: Bad news and old news. It was something that happened horribly for - the reaction was horrible. And yeah, it's - the process is going better now. But since you started it negative 100, you're just really working your way up back up to zero on it.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: And don't forget, he did have his blacks in the galleries. In the gallery. He had his blacks.

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: He (unintelligible).

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: He had his moment.

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: Michael, you would call it his minstrel show, I imagine.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: His minstrel show, exactly.

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: But, you know, I just want to take - not issue with Bob. But, you know, he did as Bob - well, you point out - he did get us into some domestic issues in that speech; it wasn't just about Iraq. He does have a optimistic agenda.

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: I just think that for the reasons you state, Katrina is not going to be on that list because it was such an unmitigated disaster, and also because his base is not in Louisiana, that's a primarily Democratic state, primarily Democratic leadership, and he'd rather shift the responsibility to them.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: He doesn't have a base. The man is discredited on the Republican side and the Democrat side.

One last Katrina point before we move on. Laura, I want to direct it towards you, because Barack Obama was front and center during these hearings in Louisiana. What do you expect to come out of those?

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: Well, I think Obama made a very powerful analogy, one that those of us who haven't studied history may not be familiar with, and that is he compared Katrina to the 1871 Chicago fire, which you all know pretty much wiped out the city of Chicago at that time. And he'd made the point that there was a national effort from the ground up to rebuild Chicago, and look at it today.

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: And Chicago was not some luxurious, powerful town. It was a cow town at the time. Well, it was a town full of poor people, full of working-class people. The same kinds of people you see in New Orleans. So he made the point that it can be done if we have a national will, but he just - he and I would agree there has been no national will to rebuild New Orleans.

All right. If you're just joining us, you're listening to NPR's NEWS & NOTES. I'm Tony Cox. With me on today's Roundtable are Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition, Laura Washington, Chicago Sun Times columnist, and Bob Meadows, staff writer for "People" magazine. We've been talking about Hurricane Katrina aftermath, and the fact that the president did not mention it in his State of the Union address, and his explanation for that in an exclusive interview with NPR's Juan Williams on yesterday.

But we move on, topic number two. California and Colorado prison officials are using an innovative marketing campaign to reduce overcrowded cells. They are encouraging inmates to transfer to prisons in other parts of the country through a type of infomercial.

Now hear me on this. In one ad, a felon now housed in Tennessee says - and this is a quote - "you get 79 channels here, including ESPN." End quote. Another one says, and here's another quote, "they talk to us like humans, not like animals." As part of the recruitment drive, folks, wardens are screening to film while reminding prisoners of the violent, overcrowded, racially-charged conditions they face in places like California.
So what was your first reaction when you heard about this, Laura?

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: Well, the humans quote really blew me away. So I guess the California prison system is finally acknowledging, along with a lot of other prison systems that should be acknowledging, that they don't treat their inmates like humans. And if they wanted to be treated like humans, they need to move to another state. I think that's a really profound statement.

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: And all the discussion about changing - moving folks out of the prisons system to relieve the overcrowding, they talked about a lot about overcrowding but they didn't talk about any other conditions that need to be addressed. I would like to see these prison systems address those conditions, which are not just about overcrowding. They're about horrifically poor management, allowing gangs and other criminal elements to run these prisons.

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: One of the interesting things about why they say that some prisons are reluctant to voluntarily move is because there's so much gang intimidation. The gangs don't want their turfs being broken up by these moves. That is a profound problem that the state of California should be addressing.
Well, Michael Meyers, is this a civil rights issue?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Civil rights issue. This isn't - look. This is an issue of people's rights while they're in prison. So here you are, quote, unquote, "this is a civil rights issue." But look. It's not just 79 channels that are going to get people to move out of California prisons. I mean, there are a lot of those inmates who don't want to leave their lovers behind - their lovers in prison, their lovers outside of prison, and they do have lovers in prison. How - and by the way, how long does it take to build the prison building? You know, this enormous amount of time - it takes years to get modern, decent prisons - if you can have a decent prison - maybe it's a job for the Donald, Donald Trump.
Well…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: And maybe we ought to just ask the question, are there too many people in prison? And people who don't need to be in prison, who have not been convicted, for example, of violent crimes - rapists, murderers, people like that - muggers. They belong in prison. But there maybe people in prison who don't - who should be out on parole, or probation, as opposed to parole. And people should be under supervision, but not in prison. So…

Well, you've raised so many - you've so many points, it's hard to sort of respond to one. But let me pick one of them out. You asked about building prisons. And I'll direct to Bob Meadows, because it seems to me, Bob, one of the issues about building prisons is where to build them. And people don't want prisons in their own backyards.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: A lot of people don't, but some communities do because this brings jobs. I mean, this is a super industry in the United States. California was at almost $12 billion that are earmarked toward prison building and reform right now. That is a big business, and there are communities I know that invite prisons because, like I said, it brings economy. It boosts the economy and things like that.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: And one thing we have to remember about this is the reason California and Colorado are doing this is because a federal judge has told them your prisons are too overcrowded, you have to ease them. You have to ease the situation. So they have to come up with something. And I admit, you know, it sounds that whole ESPN thing, and, you know, the guards treat us and so on, walking by with smaller guards. It sounds kind of silly in a way.
Mm-hmm.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: But, you know, you have to see it. Perhaps, when you actually see it, maybe it doesn't come off that way. But it is something that - this is a step that they have to take. I mean, they at least came up with something kind of unique. And, you know, I really - I personally didn't know that you had to ask a prisoner to move them. I thought you can just do it on their own.
Well, we going to…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: It's like the Army commercials. You know, be all you can be. You know if you are dumb enough to enlist.
But we're going to talk about that point in just a moment. But let me just go back to say, because I have been in - I don't want to say in prisons. I have visited prisons all over this…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: (unintelligible)

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: …country. And, you know, ESPN not withstanding, prison is still prison. And it's no, you know, it's no fun place to go. I don't care how many cable channels they may have.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: But the question that this raises, and you just made reference to it, is whether or not states can actually force inmates to accept interstate transfers. Now, here in California, Governor Schwarzenegger is threatening to do just that and soon to relieve this overcrowding, because not enough inmates are volunteering, you know, to go out and move on their own. Can they do that?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, he's in a situation where he may very well be ordered by a court to release some of these prisoners. That's what he's worried about. And the people - so-called, people are worried about…But, you know, there are state constitutional prohibitions with respect to what you can do to prisoners in terms of moving them out of state, in terms of getting them - getting private companies to take over prison responsibilities. There are laws in California that affect these prisoners and involve these prisoners' rights. Prisoners do have rights.
Mm-hmm. Laura?

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: Well, Schwarzenegger is trying to get a waiver - or he, in fact, he has already gotten a waiver to be able to override that law for the time being. But, of course…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Not a waiver. He declared it emergency…

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: (unintelligible) an emergency, sorry.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: …which is also legally questionable.

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: All right. So and prison advocates - prisoner advocates have fought him on that. I don't - personally, I mean, I want to see him follow the law, but I don't understand the law. Yes, prisoners do have rights, but I don't understand the issue of not being able to move people. What does it matter which state they're in as long as they're in a humane environment? And it sounds like the places that they're talking about, saying they maybe more humane than they are. So I don't see anything wrong with that, and I'd like to see that law changed if there's anything it could account for…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, if California imprisons you, then you shouldn't be put into a prison in New York.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: It's just that simple.

Well, that's part about the argument is. All right, let's move on to our last topic. We've only - we spent a little bit more time talking about prisons than we had intended, so we're going to cut this one down a little bit.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: I love prisons.

The question is would you buy terror-free gasoline? Now, Nebraska is the first state to house what is being touted as a terror-free gas station. The terror-free oil initiative is a group planning to offer gasoline that comes from countries that don't financially support terrorists. They say big oil companies like ExxonMobil, Gulf, Shell, finance terrorism because they import oil from the Middle East. Now, we only have a minute or so. So the question is - and a lot of folks are asking, and I'll come to you, Bob - how do you get gasoline that isn't supporting terrorism in one way or another?

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: You really have no way of knowing. I mean, granted, they're going to - this terror-free oil initiative is going to get its gas from a refinery, I guess, in Salt Lake City. But even they admit that they get some of their gas from here in New York, which gets gas from overseas. So we really have no way of knowing. I mean, I personally don't have anything against this. I think that people have a right to protest in any fashion, any form they want. So hey, if they want to this, I think it's great. I remember a couple of years ago, it's like, don't buy SUVs because you're supporting the terrorists or something like that.
I suppose the question I have, really quickly, Mike Meyers, really quickly, Mike Meyers…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Yeah.
…is how much does this stuff cost? Is it going to be cheaper or more expensive?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, if you really have such a thing as something terrorist-free oil, it's going to be more expensive. And it's going to be longer lines than all the other stuff. But it's not - what Bob said, there's no such thing. This is, you know, I do have something against this. I'm opposed to silliness. This is silly. You know, you're going to get oil from Venezuela? People will say that's terrorist. This is like the French fries debate. Calling French fries Liberty fries. People still sell and eat French fries, and they'll still get oil. And if the lines get longer at the gas pump, they'll go to first gas pump they can get.

I suppose that is the Michael Meyers version of quickly, and I appreciate it, because it's going to let us  get out of here. Laura Washington, my apologies to you. We'll pick you up the next time. From our New York bureau, Michael Meyers…

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: Michael, I'll get you for that.

…executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition, along with Bob Meadows, staff writer for People magazine, and Laura Washington, Chicago Sun-Times columnist at our Chicago bureau. Everybody, thank you very much.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: Thank you, Tony.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Thank you.

speaker_label: Ms. LAURA WASHINGTON (Columnist, Chicago Sun Times)
text: Thank you, Tony.
Next on NEWS & NOTES, a middle class on the verge of meltdown, and news from Guinea and Addis Ababa on our Africa Update.
This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya.
On today's Roundtable, Condoleezza Rice visits the Middle East and comes up with very little. Plus, truck displays with words like picaninny cannot be banned in Arizona.
Joining us today are Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition, Laura Washington, Chicago Sun-Times columnist, and Bob Meadows, staff writer for People magazine.

So thanks everybody for being with us, and let's go straight to Condi. She hosted talks on ways to build an independent Palestinian state and also to incorporate the needs of Israel. But it appeared to yield little other than a pledge to meet again. The Israeli prime minister and Palestinian Authority attended - leader. It was hoped that the talks would signal Rice's deepened commitment to resolve the conflict, but instead it looks like more difficulties ahead.

So Michael, you and I have talked previously about whether or not the Palestinian government should deny the right of Israel to exist, that is once again the sticking point here. What's going on? What can break the impasse?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, the Palestinians have got to say those words. You know, it's like that movie on "Delivering Milo." I want to be born. The Palestinians have to say the words: Israel has the right to exist, free of violence. Period. They cannot seem to bring themselves to doing that.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: They can't seem to accept the right of Israel. And its leaders keep saying that, you know, Israel is a mere geographical expression. It's an imaginative expression. It doesn't really exist. It doesn't have the right to exist. And they can't come and speak truth, then they will not have the kind of cooperation they need to make their government in Palestine, or the Palestinian state for that matter, work.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: They're just not going to have that cooperation. They may have prevented a civil war in the interim because of Hamas and Fatah factions, new coalition government. But the money's not going to come in there and they're just not going to get the cooperation of the international community.
Laura, can you top Michael Meyers quoting that movie - what is it?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: "Delivering Milo."
"Delivering Milo." I don't believe I've ever seen that one, but…
I haven't seen it either.
Laura…
I got to go out and get the DVD right away.
Exactly. I will bring you from the pop culture reference.
Thank you.

But, really, this is a situation that sounds like a complete impasse. So many American administrations and presidencies have tried to bring some semblance of cooperation to the Middle East. And a question that comes up again and again is: Is America an honest broker? Can America with it's own foreign policy interests act as a peacemaker? What do you think about that question?
Well, I think that the answer is implied in your question, Farai. Right now our standing and our credibility internationally, but in particular in the Middle East, is so low. And look at this trip.

You know, Condi is - Condi Rice is - by making this trip, basically the only thing she's doing with this - the last several trips she's made to the Middle East is building up her frequent flyer miles because there's just no way at this point she's going to be able to salvage the Bush administration's diplomatic legacy on this issue of Israel.

Now, as you point out, previous administrations haven't had much luck either, but at least they'd made the effort and at least they appeared to be seriously negotiating. And they were again negotiating from a position of strength, from the position of still being seen as the world's great power. I'm not so sure the United States has viewed that way internationally anymore. And we're -because of all the other international promise we have, in particular in Iraq and Afghanistan, it just doesn't allow us either the political capital or the resources, or maybe even the political will, to be able to make any change here.
But I think right now because of the impasse, because of the Palestinian's refusal - and I agree with Michael - their refusal to recognize Israel, it would not matter what we did. It wouldn't work.

Bob, let's look at this from a people perspective, if I can go straight to the name of your magazine. You've got two leaders - Olmert from Israel and Abbas from Palestine - who are in some ways very much in the shadow of their predecessors, two strong men who stood for their entire nation. Is it a good thing or a bad thing that now Israel and Palestine are really run by men who have not as much history as the men who preceded them?

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: Well, it's probably a good thing, I would think. Because you were never going to have a situation and you had a situation where Yasser Arafat came to the table and obviously nothing happened. And people just couldn't get past who he was, who he was connected to, the terrorism that we just tied to his name.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: At least now that you have these two new leaders in there, relatively new leaders in there, it kind of opens up the field. It gives a new horizon and you might think that it's sort of a new day. But as Mike and Laura said, you know, Palestine still is not going to acknowledge Israel and their right to exist. That's just an amazing statement.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: And of course they can't because they have these people back at home who, sure, the leaders can acknowledge that they exist. But that doesn't mean that the people back at home are going to say, well, wait, they killed my brother. They killed my sister. They bombed our village. They're still going to hold these against them. So on a people, personal, non-political level, this is a situation that reminds me very often of the gang situation here in the United States, where people just cannot get past to what happened in the past.

Well, I'm going to move on to another controversial topic - very different. Lawmakers in Tennessee are pushing legislation that mandates death certificates for aborted fetuses, which would in turn create public records of women who have abortions. A Republican representative said his bill would provide a way to track the number of abortions performed in the state. But abortion stats are already available to the state Office of Vital Records.
Now the identity of women who had abortions are not listed on these records but the death certificates could list their Social Security numbers.
Bob, what does this all mean? Is this just a way of trying to put a scarlet A for abortion on women or is this a much needed public health issue?

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: It is not a public health issue. This - I almost applaud this because it's so deviously, evilly brilliant or whatever you have it. This is obviously pro-life, anti-abortion groups. This is a ploy. This is a PR move. They're getting all these attention. They want to - it's an intimidation tactic against abortion. They don't want abortion, so why wouldn't they try do something like this?

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: This, hmm, does it have a chance in hell of passing? I don't think so.
Laura, when you look at abortion statistics, they appear to have been flat. Some argue that they've actually gone down a bit. So is this really something that's necessary?

Well, if you're a pro-life or if you believe that abortion is murder, of course you would still fell it's necessary because you wouldn't want to tolerate any abortions. But I think the real issue was whether or not this law is necessary but whether or not this is a blatant invasion of personal privacy.

And I just can't imagine anybody who's advocating this feeling the same way if we were talking about publishing information that would identify folks who would had other kinds of procedures, personal and private procedures, hysterectomies, what have you. You know.

If they are suggesting that we expose - this is a - it's already been said, it's a form of intimidation. It's just another way around respecting the law. These - some of these same folks have advocated bombing abortion clinics. Some of these same folks have advocated harassing and threatening women and blocking their entrance abortion clinics. These people will try any tactic they can. Now they don't necessarily - they talk about respect for life but they obviously don't have a respect for the folks that they're trying to intimidate.

Well, we have to say that some people do use violent methods and other people - and for anti-abortion do not use violent methods. But Michael, moving on to you. I had a conversation once at a kind of a think-tank gathering with a guy who considered himself very conservative, and he said that there's two things that divide America that we're never going to agree on - racial integration and abortion.
Do you think - I thought it was interesting that those were the two. But do you think that abortion is intractable, it's one of these issues that we will never find peace on in America?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: I'll save my statements about race integration for another program. With respect to abortion, we have an agreement. That's the problem with this effort in Tennessee. It is now settled that women have a right to control their own bodies and that a fetus is not a live birth. You cannot have a death certificate in the absence of a birth certificate. So if there's not a birth, how can there be a death? This is semantics. It is an inversion of the rhetoric, if you will.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: An abortion is a medical record. It is not a birth certificate. So yes, as Laura suggests, there are privacy considerations and there are federal laws that trump any effort on the part of Tennessee to violate a women's right to privacy in terms of her medical record.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: And I have to say, is this Al Gore's state? No wonder he lost, as I recall, in 2000. You have to get back there and do some ground work and some grassroots effort to get people to join the 21st century.
Now he's working on global warming. Anyway, talking to Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition, and you are listening to NPR's NEWS & NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya.
Also with me on today's Roundtable we've got Laura Washington, Chicago Sun-Times columnist, and Bob Meadows, staff writer for People magazine.

Bob, I want to move on to Barack Obama, who will be getting plenty of ink in the upcoming months. Now one of his nemeses or rivals, Democratic Congressman Bobby Rush of Illinois, is questioning how Barack Obama portrayed his role in a community-organizing situation in Chicago.

In "Dreams from My Father," he said that as a 24 year old, he initiated and led efforts to remove asbestos from a Chicago housing project. But Rush says, no. It was another activist, Hazel Johnson. And journalists at the Chicago Reporter who really pushed this to the front burner…

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: Mm-hmm.
Is this just, you know, an inevitable misunderstanding on the campaign trail, or does this speak to burnishing the political image at all costs?

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: Well, it's probably both, but I don't think this is a very serious charge. But, sure. Of course, Barack Obama certainly knew that Hazel Johnson was working on this project, and he certainly knew that because he was so involved. Sure, the layperson wouldn't know, but he had to have known that.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: But, yeah, he - this doesn't take away, though, that it was not an inspirational moment for him. And even the people who were involved say he was our motivator. He was certainly a motivator in this. He had a big role in it. He may not have been the only person doing it, but this is politics. It's not really a surprise.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: Rush - as you mentioned, Farai - has been a rival of Barack's the last couple years. It's just continuing, and we're going to have more of the same for the next year and a half.
Laura, you're in Chicago. What do you make of this?

Well, I haven't seen the actual the story yet, but I suspect that the Chicago Reporter story is a story that I edited. And yes, we did some journalism, we did some journalism around that issue. There were many community activists involved with that issue in terms of environmental racism in a very depressed community. Barack Obama did work out there.

The problem with these kinds of stories is that it's been, what, 15 years since the fact. He wrote an autobiography that in many ways was partially fictionalized because - and he has acknowledged himself, he used fictional techniques. He changed names. He couldn't - he didn't vouch for the complete, total accuracy of every reference to every person in that book, so it leaves a lot of room for interpretation. This is what happens when you write books that they can be scrutinized very careful in many years later.

And there's another example - and L.A. Times broke the story. It's an example of, you know, the good old media. You can always depend on them to build you up, and then as soon as they get you way up there at the top, they knock you down. The media is the institution that made Barack this political rock star. They got them up there, now they're going to take him apart and they're going to analyze every single dot and T that he has done either in his books or uttered in his life.
So Michael Meyers, is this a situation: no memoirs until you win the presidency?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
