text: Those bottom feeders at it again, huh, Laura Look, I think that he wrote a book, and what people do when they write books. They write about themselves. They don't remember every I - to dot every I and cross every T. They don't remember every activist. And even if they do, they're not writing about the activists. They're writing about their own role.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: It's an ego - it's an exercise in ego. Yes, it's breastfeeding. And Barack is guilty of doing the same thing every else does who does an autobiography. They take too much credit. If that's the accusation, he took too much credit.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: But, you know, as Laura has described the book, it's in interesting book. It's a way of constructing a book which tries to make it of interest to your readers. But the most important thing for an autography is that the book is interesting - you, the person who's writing it. And I think this is what Barack Obama did.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: And so, I haven't read his book, and this story doesn't lead me to want to read his book. I will find out about Barack Obama on the campaign trail, as there will be more and more stories coming up examining his background because this is what they do in presidential campaigns.
All right…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: This is what the media does. It's the…
Well, Michael, I have to jump in because we have a speed round question…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Uh-oh.
We only have a minute and a half left.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Okay.
Picaninnies on trucks - splashguard with the word picaninny…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Oh, boy.

…of course, a derogatory term for black kids. Arizona - it had a bill proposed to make these displays of racism or sexism illegal. It decided not to pass that. Are we better off for having free speech, or are we worse off for having derogatory speech? Speed round, Laura.

We've already have - we always had free speech. If you look at some of the bumper stickers you've seen - not just on trucks, but on cars -there's all kinds of outrageous things that people put in their windows, put on their cars, and they have the right to do that. I think when you see crazy stuff like that, it just reflects more on the folks that are driving around with those kinds of things on their cars than it does on anybody else, so let them have it.
Bob?

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: I have to agree. I think that freedom of speech is a great thing. You have to be able to back it up, though. You can say whatever you want, but you got to take the consequences.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Michael Meyers? I say it is very plain that Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech. What's so difficult about understanding that Congress, and you apply it to the state's menial legislatures? You do not abridge people's speech. Let people speak on their bumper stickers, in their community meetings, wherever. Let them speak. Let them speak. And please don't try and legislate what I have on my bumper sticker if I should have a car, which I don't.
Well, if you had a car, would have one of those…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: It would be an outrageous statement, I can tell you that. But it would not be obscene.
Yeah. All right. Well, we will leave it there. I'll have to think of snappy bumper sticker to put on my car.

Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition. Bob Meadows, staff writer for People magazine, both at our New York bureau. Plus, Laura Washington, Chicago Sun-Times columnist at member station WBEZ in Chicago. Thank you all.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Thank you.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: Thank you.
Thank you.

And as always, if you'd like to comment, you can call us at 202-408-3330, or send an e-mail. Just log on to npr.org and click on Contact Us. Plus, next on NEWS & NOTES, retired NBA player John Amaechi speaks out on coming out in book, "Man in the Middle". And one woman shares her thoughts of loving, leaving and letting go of her wedding ring.

Now for the Roundtable. Among today's topics, we'll talk more about the post-Katrina housing problem and discuss the governor's meeting with President Bush, including the chances of one of them moving into the Oval Office.

Joining us on the panel today are E.R. Shipp, professor in journalism at Hofstra University School of Communication, John McWhorter, Manhattan Institute senior fellow in public policy, and Bob Meadows, staff writer for People magazine. Hello, everybody.
Hi.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Good morning.

Nice to have you on today. We heard, of course, about the Bush plans to demolish four public housing projects in New Orleans. And we've just heard from HUD Secretary Alphonso Jackson, who argues the point that affordable housing doesn't always mean safe housing. E.R., let me come to you first. Does he have a point there?

Professor E.R. SHIPP (Journalism, Hofstra University School of Communication): He actually does have a point. It's very easy to say the politically correct thing. We need to provide affordable housing. But what exactly are we talking about? When you mentioned in your opening that the governors might want to move into the White House, I thought you were going to say they might want to move into some of this affordable housing. That might be an idea. So they'll know exactly what they're talking about.

If these apartments are moldy and raggedy - and it probably was, in some conditions, like that before Katrina  - and if the neighborhoods are not safe, the playgrounds are all broken and cracked. Well, what are we talking about sending people into?
That makes sense to me, John McWhorter. Does it make sense to you?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Well, yeah. The housing question is definitely more complicated than we are often told. And it's perfectly understandable for people who lived in a particular area to be nostalgic - and even that word is a little bit trivial - for where they used to be.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: But the fact of the matter is that if certain cultural patterns have become entrenched in particular places, then often the only solution to turning things around is to make sure that people move to other places. And, of course, we have to emphasized - make sure that people do have other places to go.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: But we're already seeing how in New Orleans, many of those projects are being re-occupied by people who are engaged in violent activities. And affordable housing is even a complicated concept, because where that ends up meaning subsidized housing, often subsidized housing ends up being a situation where people don't have the motivation to keep up their housing the way they would if they were paying somewhat more for it. And landlords take advantage of it as a place that they do not have to take care of the way they would take care of other things.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: So it's hard, especially because, obviously, in New Orleans, we also have a situation where people are not being given the basic resources that they would deserve despite all of these policy wonk details about the housing and housing projects.
Well, it seems that we're at a political impasse, Bob Meadows. What do you think it would take to break it?

Boy, what will it take to break it? Well, as you probably know right now, there are several politicians who are trying to - well, one thing I think that one of the main issues here is that insurers are no longer writing policies down there in New Orleans and the Gulf Coast in general. And so there are a lot of politicians right now who are really pushing to get these insurers to step off, and, you know, come on and do things that they promised they would do which is paying people up, insuring new houses that can be built.

I'm not quite so sure that I, you know - Maxine Waters pushing for these houses to be reopened, that really doesn't sound that great to me. I mean, we are all, I'm sure, were in New Orleans prior to Katrina, and you drive around and you could see this was - New Orleans was no panacea before, you know, before Katrina. And that's really not what you want to go back to. There needs to be like - you were speaking with the gentleman earlier - the housing, federal housing coming in and really pushing to get these units open and getting people back there that way.

You know what? It's a - it may go back to the original concept of public housing. It was always meant to be relatively short term in terms of people living there. It was to get them on their feet again. And it was always meant to be more mixed in income than it turned out to be. It turned out to be a dumping ground for the horribly, horribly poor.
You know I should say that we attempted to - we wanted to have Maxine Waters on today to, sort of, speak to her view about pushing this housing. Do I hear you John McWhorter, want to come back in?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Yeah, I just want to insert briefly that one of the hardest things about the New Orleans-Katrina situation is that we have to remember that other than the wonderful tourist district and cultural aspect such as the food and the music and the interesting language situation (unintelligible) been interested in.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: We have to remember that a New Orleans housing project was not a place that any of us would have felt any warmth for if we have seen a story covering it before Katrina.
Absolutely.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Naturally, people want to go back to the familiar, but these were terrible places to live.
That's a good point to make. All right, let's move on to our next topic. President George Bush and America's governors butted heads this week over the Children's Health Insurance Program.

Now, here's a question for you: Should the costs of health care for children -or where should that rank in relation to the cost of the war? And, I mean, especially given today, for example, with the story like the one out of Maryland of the 12-year-old boy who died of an untreated toothache for lack of medical insurance. That certainly doesn't seem to help the White House, John McWhorter.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Yeah, that's a - you can't sugarcoat this one. I mean, I think, really, if you try to put yourself in the Bush administration's head, you don't get villains rubbing their hands together and trying to starve the poor. What they're hoping is that because they are so cash-strapped because of other things we don't even need to mention, that maybe they can force the states to be a little more careful with their bookkeeping. And they're assuming that everything will be all right and that everybody will stay covered.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: As usual, however, it's compassionate conservatism that isn't being attended to carefully enough. And I think we're hearing from the governors that if this money is not increased - that already, there really wasn't enough - and if it isn't increased, then we're going to have some serious problems. And so it's - the Bush administration thinks that this is just a matter of accounting. But really, it's a matter of looking at what actually happens on the ground. And this administration has never been good with that, either internationally or nationally.
Well, E.R., the governor of New Jersey certainly made that point, didn't he?

Yes, indeed. When you think about it, we're talking about a family of four earning somewhere less than 20,000 - $21,000 a year, and having to take care of their children. There's not a lot of money, and I will mention Iraq, though John chose not to.
We're dumping money into Iraq and Afghanistan and various other so-called allies who seem to be doing us more harm than good.

I can see that we should have a real debate about our priorities. I would pick the health of our children over some of the wastefulness we are seeing going on in the name of fighting terror. A lot of money is going into the pockets of people. They lost a whole truckload of money or two - or pallet of money, I guess.
So I think that we need to really think hard, and the governors are making a good point and starting with children they may get more sympathy, more - a greater hearing on the issue.
The (unintelligible)…
In terms of…
Go on.

And to finally say it's on - you know, the flipside of that is, I mean, obviously, if you compare the life of a child to war, you're going to go with a child. But then when you turn it around and say, you do a story on, say, soldiers over there who don't have armor - who don't have proper armor, don't have proper defense - then all of a sudden, you get into the human aspect of it and you can see why, you know, the thing is we're in a war. That's the unfortunate thing. We're in a war.

If you just - if we weren't in a war, it would be really easy to say well, yeah. But since we're in this war and we and you do that type of story, you humanize it, then you can say well, sure. Maybe you do need to send money over there for the troops.

You know you're listening to NPR's NEWS & NOTES. I'm Tony Cox. And in case you're just joining in, with me on today's Roundtable are E.R. Shipp, professor in journalism at Hofstra University School of Communication, John McWhorter, Manhattan Institute senior fellow in public policy, and who you just heard, Bob Meadows, staff writer for People magazine.
To another point about the governors, though folks, and it's this: Are you surprise at all that they are flexing politically in the way they are now that - unheard of a couple of years ago?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: No, Bush, I mean, the Republicans lost, and now in 2006, the elections, everybody's flexing right now. Congress wasn't doing a thing to stand up against Bush - not everybody is. So no, I'm not surprised at all.

Yes, and they know that he is a lame duck. Even Republicans are speaking up in ways they would not have done a year or two ago. So it's not a surprise at all, and it's not a surprise that a lot of governors think they want to become president.

You know, and that's a - it's a perfect segue. Thank you very much, E.R. It brings me right to my next point, because the role of the president, obviously, is a very delicate balance for these chiefs of state, these past state chiefs of state, as well as for the president. A couple of interesting things: four of the last five U.S. presidents have been governors. None came from the Senate.

Now, there's been a great deal of talk, obviously, about Clinton, about Clinton and Obama and McCain and others. Only four senators have been elected president in the last 87 years - not since Harding in 1920. This is kind of interesting. I don't know if that gives those governors who are still in the running, although they are considered dark horses, if that that gives them any hope. What do you think, John?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: I think that we have to always allow for the aspect of chance in this case. And I think that in this case we're dealing in particular with Senators Clinton and Obama. And they are two uniquely charismatic figures. I think it's safe to say that Hillary Clinton got a bounce because of what her husband used to do. And so we happen to have two senators with unusual life stories and unusual circumstances who have come to attention.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: But I think that the general pattern still applies. We're just dealing with a chance matters such as the way many people might pretend that the fact that people are running around in Central Park at 72 degrees about four weeks ago as a matter of chance in terms of climate change is in the world.

Well, E.R., you know, we have Bill Richardson out of New Mexico, Mitt Romney out of Massachusetts, Mike Huckabee out of Arkansas, still in the race, so to speak, although Mitt Romney took a little bit of a hit with his strategy being revealed in the Boston Globe the other day. What does this mean for them? Does it give them any hope at all in your view?

Well, if you just look at the history, yes, it gives them hope. But anyone in politics has hope, that's why they got into the race or have announced that they're thinking about getting into the race. They for some reason think that there is a chance that they may win. And in some cases, they're foolish. A couple of others dropped out of the race, I believe.

So it's an interesting time in our history, as John pointed out, with these unusual characters from the Senate running. But I wouldn't write off the governors just yet. As has been pointed out, they have in many ways more experience managing a large government, larger government than a senator does who is coming from a particular state.
All right, we'll keep an eye on that.

We have one more topic I'd like to get to in the time that we have left. And it's this. A San Francisco weekly newspaper which calls itself the Voice Of Asian America has caught the attention of African-Americans recently. They published a column on Friday that was titled, quote, "Why I Hate Blacks," end quote.

Now in this column, Asian Week regular contributor Kenneth Eng lists reasons to discriminate against black Americans. Here's a couple. One, blacks hate us. every Asian who has ever come across them knows that they take almost every opportunity to hurl racist remarks at us. Here's a second. Contrary to media depictions, I would argue that blacks are weak willed. They are the only race that has been enslaved for 300 years.
So Bob Meadows, was this a slip, something that could have plausible denial or maybe a marketing move to build up circulation?

Well, this wasn't a slip. I mean this gentleman has written other outrageous columns as well, depicting why he hates whites and why whites hate Asians, and so and everybody denouncing him. It seems like he's some, he's a fringe character and Asian commentary, I guess, I'll call it. I don't really know.

And it's also not a slip because I'm certain that the editors read this editorial before they put it into the newspaper. So they knew what it said and they're probably like, oh, that's just him. You know, that's just him doing his thing. Publicity? Sure, I guess.
We're talking about it. I never heard of this publication before.
Yes, exactly.

So and it's all over the place right now. This guy, I think the editors knew what they were doing when they printed his column, published his column. As Bob said, he's done a series of these things looking at whites. He's even said Asians hate each other or something, or maybe there's everybody hates him.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: You know that show "Everybody Hates Chris"?

Well, you know, the thing that I've found a little interesting about this, one of the things, was that the Fang family, which owns this paper, was the first Asian-American family to own a major U.S. Daily. They owned the San Francisco Examiner at one time. And so they are connected to this and there is some embarrassment for them. Now are they so high up the chain, perhaps, that this could go by without their knowledge or would they give tacit approval?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: I think one issue that we have to remember is that the guy who wrote this, he's not 56. This is somebody in his early 20s…
That's true.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: …and you can just imagine he's looking for attention. And what worries me is that we're giving it to him. And you know, if you ask me, we should just get down in the sandbox and mentally lob back at him what he's lobbed at us up. I imagine that whole editorial delivered by the guy with prosthetic teeth that Mickey Rooney played in the "Breakfast at Tiffany's" movie where you cringe when he comes out playing, quote, unquote, "a Chinese person."

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: He's giving cartoon rhetoric and he's getting a lot of attention for it. And I think we certainly should not let it hurt us or give him any more attention than he deserves.

But you know what, one of the things that we should not let pass is that many Asian-Americans have come out to condemn what this man said. And to speak about - well, to say that black people are not the way he depicted us in the column, but to speak about racial harmony. So he is out there on his own it looks like.

The question - my last question, we have about a little over a minute or so and I'm going to direct it to you, E.R., because I know that you teach journalism. What would you tell your students, if you had a class where you talked about articles being printed in publications like this one? How would you handle that lecture?

Well, there's a whole delicate balance about freedom of press and freedom of speech and all that. But ultimately, it's up to the editors and publishers to decide what they're going to publish. So this young man is entitled to his viewpoints and he may find an outlet for them on the Internet - anybody can publish. But for a newspaper, the decision has to be made by someone a bit more responsible to the community at large.

All right, we'll take it right there. E.R. Shipp, professor in journalism, Hofstra University School of Communication, and Bob Meadows, staff writer, People Magazine. They joined us from our New York Bureau. John McWhorter, Manhattan Institute senior fellow in public policy. He joined us by telephone.
Thanks everybody.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Thank you.
Thank you.

As always, if you'd like to comment on any of the topics that you've head on our Roundtable, you can call us at 202-408-3330, 202-408-3330. Or you can send an e-mail. Log on to npr.org and click on Contact Us and please be sure to tell us where you're writing from and how to pronounce your name.
Next on NEWS & NOTES: A nutritionist tells us how to keep our hearts healthy, and we hit the screens to find out who knows what about black history.
You're listening to NEWS & NOTES from NPR News.
This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya.
On today's Roundtable, presidential hopeful John Edwards makes a push for janitors' rights, and the Cherokee nation kicks slave descendants out of the tribe.
Joining us today are Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition, Chicago Sun-Times Columnist Laura Washington, and Bob Meadows, staff writer for People magazine.

Now guys, I know that you have been listening to Ron Walters and Clarence Page just talk about the NAACP, and I know that there's been a lot of desire to jump in on it. All right, Michael, what have you got? There's this struggle between should we change the mission of the organization or stay the course?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, I think that the story behind the story is that there was an internal struggle, and there were a dissing of the board members. And the rank and file, what they called the blood - the lifeline of the NAACP - they thought that Bruce Gordon was arrogant and not really a man of the people.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Didn't they know what they were getting when they interviewed him? Didn't they know - he had to argue his agenda? He must have known - they must have known he wanted to turn NAACP into another bourbon league, as opposed to an Urban League. But the membership is down - way down - in the NAACP. The income was off.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: And so the question for me is not the NAACP's mission, but the NAACP - who's in control. And the board at the NAACP is a kind of board that doesn't suffer fools gladly. If you cross them, you are out. There are not like the ACLU board.
Hmm. I don't know anything about the ACLU board. I don't want to say anything about them. But Bob, I will say that a 64-member board - that's a lot of people to get consensus from.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: A lot of people - I'm sorry, go ahead, Farai.
No, no, please.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: I was going to say, it's a lot of people, and it's a lot of huge egos on that board. And the thing about it is that when you have that many people on a board, you have slights that go back generations. Because somebody's father, somebody's uncle was on that board, put them on the board. They came on as a young gun, trying to change things, but the old heads on the board at that time, they wouldn't let them do anything.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: Now, they are the old heads. The young people coming in, they don't want to change. People don't want to give up power. They don't want to change the course that they're going. So when you bring in somebody like a Ben Gordon, who…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Bruce. Sorry. -Bruce Gordon is - Bruce who?

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: Bruce. Sorry. Bruce Gordon. I'm thinking of Chicago bulls…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Bruce who?

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: …coming in and wanting to change the mission of NAACP. I really don't see how he got on there in the first place, because people - they're stagnant. They're like, no. We want to focus on what we're doing now, and don't you dare come and try and change us. I'm amazed. I was amazed when he got picked.
Laura, how are things playing in Chicago?

Well, I think - I'm glad you mentioned Chicago, because I think one of the big problems which hasn't been mentioned in the long history of dissention - and it's a long history. It didn't start with this current president, where we - we know Kweisi Mfume didn't get along with this board, either. And there's been disarray and dissention in this organization for at least 15 years.

Part of it - one big issue is the disconnect, I think, between the folks in the trenches, the folks that are running a local affiliates - and I know I hear that here in Chicago all the time - and the big shots in Washington and New York.  And when I say big shots, I think that that also gets at the issue of the dissention.

You know, this is the elitist organization. It's a private boys club to a large extent. It's about personality. It's about ego, as has been mentioned by others already. And I think that that's really at the heart of why this organization's not getting much done, because its priority is about keeping power and in creating this sort of elitist platform that it's going to launch a bunch of egos from. That's the real issue here.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, I would have to disagree. In fact, the NAACP is not an old boys network or club.
How many, how many women have…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: If any -
…ran in NAACP in the last 50, 60 years? -

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: If you know anything about the - if you know anyone with the NAACP, the NAACP's membership, and its rank and file, and is on - and virtually, it's leadership, including the former chair and former presidents, have been women. And it's the church ladies in the hats that control things, and…
(unintelligible)

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: you offend - if you offend those church ladies and those hats, you will be out.
Who control things or who pay their dues?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: They control things, that's right.
You got that right. They do the chicken dinners, and they are…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Yeah.
…running those organizations at the local level.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Absolutely.
And believe me they're not very well connected to the leaders on the board. That's what I'm talking about.

Well, you know, I want to move on. There's a lot to say, and I'm sure that in some form or the other we'll be talking about this all week. But I want to move on to presidential candidate John Edwards.

Yesterday, we talked about Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton. They are going head to head. John Edwards at this point, not getting as much press as either of them. But he has gone to bat for better wages on behalf of janitors at the University of California Berkeley over the weekend. He noted that this was the continuation of the civil rights struggle that began in the '60s. And he's gone a lot of talk about two Americas, class divide, all of those issues.

And he also took a moment to respond to Ann Coulter who called him an f-word on Friday. I'm not talking the four-letter kind, but a - more of a gender sexuality slur, and said it's important for all of us to speak out against language of this kind, because it's a place where hatred gets its foothold.
Where is John Edwards right now? Does he have appeal to the black community? I guess Laura, I'll go back to you.

Well, I think he should have left Ann Coulter alone. Ann Coulter's in the business of bringing attention to herself by saying outrageous things. And unfortunately, that marred the presentation he was trying to make out in Berkeley.

I think he has been very consistent in - since he ran last time and in last several years - in making the case for poverty and for the working poor. And I think the appearance over the weekend in Berkeley was another example.

And I think it was kind of ironic that it was in Berkeley, which is not exactly a bastion of black America. And he was trying to make a connection to the Selma march because of the anniversary. But I think he has been consistent in working with labor. He has a lot of close labor relationships. I saw him here in Chicago a year ago, talking with and working with housekeepers.
And I think that that comes across as a sincere effort. You're right. He's getting overshadowed by Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton right now. But I think he's got a hold of a good issue.

Bob, he is, in some ways, the candidate who has been most clear about what he's going to campaign on. He's campaigning on this labor and two Americas issue, whereas Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton have talked about a multitude of issues. Is it smart for Edwards to be focused so much so early?

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: You know, I'm not really certain if it's - I guess - because, you know, we have to remember, we're almost still two years away from this election. A lot can change in this time. Right now, I don't really know if people are going to necessarily remember what he's talking about. I don't know if they're going to remember in November of 2008, what he's talking - or even a year from now what he's talking about right now.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: So sure, he can focus on various issues, and perhaps he's trying to talk about these issues because right now, maybe, most people probably still associate him with John Kerry who was, of course, from, you know, wore his upper crust right out front.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: So Edwards is trying to connect with the people. And really, he's got the - I guess, he's got the cache to do it. Because he's sort of the forgotten kid right now, and I say kid just because he used kind of youthful looking.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: But he's really got a great story, he's - you know, a former senator, lawyer from his bootstraps type of thing. His wife - he stood by her as she had cancer. So he's got a lot going for him that, you know, he just kind of stays of the course, it might began to resonate more and more as he gets well - more well known.
So, Michael, he started his campaign in New Orleans dealing with the issues of Katrina survivors. Again, does this really carry him forward as a candidate?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, let me call him John. John, it ain't working, period. You know, people are going to more remember the f-word, the epithet for sissy, that was uttered by the blonde, skinny mini-skirter whose name I will not call.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Then they aren't going to remember his campaign about two Americas. People don't want to hear that, and it's not working, it's not resonating. Because in a lot of ways, it sounds old hat - janitors, Martin Luther King, Jr. Everybody wants to hitch their wagon onto Martin Luther King, Jr.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: That was a long time ago. And issues, as Clarence Page has suggested earlier, have a least changed in respect to law. And so now it's the question of union rights and negotiation, and what about these politicians that get in the way of negotiating between management and union is, for me, a separate question as opposed to what Martin Luther King, Jr. was doing with respect to promoting and fostering racial justice and social justice.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: So I don't think his campaign is working because it seems like he has that backdrop, that big photograph of King and the movement, and it's not really to his - what he's really saying. You know, the only thing I'm surprised about -following up on that f-word - is that the New York Silly city council has not passed a non-binding resolution to ban the f-word like they did the n-word.

Okay. Well, we'll have to keep an eye on that. I just want to reintroduce everybody. In case you're just tuning in, this is NPR's NEWS & NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya. You were just listening to the inimitable Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition. We've got Laura Washington, Chicago Sun-Times Columnist, Bob Meadows, staff writer for People Magazine. Moving on to Cherokees and black descendants in the tribe.

So, over the weekend, the Cherokee Nation members decided to revoke the tribal citizenship of about 2,800 descendants of slaves who were owned by Cherokees. Over 75 percent of nation members voted in favor of an amendment to the tribal constitution that would limit citizenship to tribe members that are descendants by blood.

Now this is an issue that has not just been limited to the Cherokee Nation but Seminoles have had controversies over whether or not black Seminoles, and there are many, are given the same rights as other Seminoles. What do we make of this? Because in America, Native Americans have kind of a dual citizenship status almost, where you have people who are citizens of America but also citizens of their own tribal nations.

And there were people who were either owned as slaves by different native nations or who were intermixed and intermarried. So does this sound like racism to, at this point in time in the 21st century, decide to kick people out? Laura?

I don't think to me it sounds like money. These Indian nations, of course, have become much more prosperous in the last several years because of casino revenues, because of rights that they have rightly sought in terms of economic power. All of a sudden now they are concerned about who's a member and who's not.

Well, of course, that's because of this new wealth that these tribes are attaining, there are a lot of benefits, economic and governmental provided benefits like health care, which is one of the big issues that's been debated on this Cherokee question.

If you are a member of a tribe, you're likely to be much more prosperous. Maybe a lot these members don't want to share the wealth in the way they did - the way they were willing to do when they were being oppressed.

I can understand on one level the issue of bloodlines and the issue of who is really a Cherokee because of the fact that the American Indians were almost exterminated in this country at one point in time, but this to me is clearly racism.
Michael?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, look, this whole thing about bloodline is race. I don't know if it's racism. It's just a different take on that (unintelligible)on Cherokee people or Cherokee tribe to me. And I now must tell you that this thought of self-determination within the United States is just bogus. It's bogus. You're not going to have a self-determination.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: And you're talking about money? It's not money. It's crumbs. They're fighting over crumbs because, as we have said so many times in this program, ain't going to be no real land distribution; Manhattan isn't going back. So you're talking about the land that is left and the people trying to get their hands on what is left to them, and they're talking about voting and self-determination in the context of the U.S. Congress overseeing Indian tribes and Indian lands and Indian issues and U.S. Indian controlled acts.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: And all these disputes are subject to federal law and the jurisdiction of the federal courts. So there is no such thing as self-determination, Cherokee people.

Well, Michael, the point you make about crumbs is a sad point, in that people of color are always very good at fighting over crumbs. They never see the big picture. You're right, the kind of economic resources that they are trying to pull in are crumbs.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Mm-hmm.

Well, Bob, before I go to you I want to mention, and I hope I'm pronouncing this tribe's name right, the Pequots who own one of the big casinos, Mohegan Sun, and they are very much racially mixed. In fact, one of their tribal leaders who helped start their huge casino looks black to the black eye, if I consider myself the black eye.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Some of us may have some Indian blood in us, huh?
Well…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: We all do.
It's more that so many tribes do have these odd mixtures, and at this point is it fair to separate people out?

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: Well, you know, I mean you're right. Who among us is pure, so to speak? Is it fair? You know, I kind of look at this in the, you know, thinking of the Cherokee dilemmas. I mean, no people in this country have been more marginalized or disenfranchised, or cheated or downtrodden than the Native Americans of this country.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: And it's sort of like, you know, they have that 1866 treaty that assured the (unintelligible) their descendants that they will be, you know, part of the tribe. It took them 141 years to break that treaty. They wish the white man had taken that long to break the treaties they wrote with them.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: I really don't feel so uptight about this because, as Laura pointed out, these people were almost exterminated. You know, they were almost exterminated - they almost don't even exist. They are the original people in this country, at least for the last 700 years or whatever, and they're like the smallest group here because they almost didn't even exist anymore.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: So I really don't have any problem with them trying to hold on to something that may have never really existed, but they're trying to hold on to it now and stay sort of who they are. And, you know, if black people sort of have to, quote-unquote, "suffer" at that, I really don't have that big a qualm, big issue with it.
All right. Well, let me make a small correction. It's the Foxwoods Resorts that the Pequot tribe owns. But I think we've done with this story…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Yeah.

We have two minutes left, so I have a speed round for you. It's about pep, and what kind of pep do you have based on race? In California, a high school called Mt. Diablo High School divided students by ethnicity and featured jazz music for black students, flags from Asian countries for Asian students. They had white students' rallies and Hispanic students' rallies.
Now is this a way to keep kids of different races from being bored or is this a travesty? Bob.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: Well, I think they were also going two, four, six, eight, we don't want to integrate during these pep rallies. I think that was the rallying cry.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: (unintelligible).

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: What really got me about this was the reason they were keeping these kids apart is because they were hoping ethnic groups wouldn't be taunted about their scores on these various tests and I - what is going on? I'm not outraged by this. I'm concerned to a degree that they feel that they have to keep these groups apart much like they have to segregate blacks and Hispanics and whites in prison because they'll kill each other. And I wonder, is that what's going on here? There's got to be some more to this story.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: What is going on here is racial idiocy. That's what's going on here. And it's ethnic separatism and chauvinism and nonsense. You know, it goes back with the separatism in terms of separate counseling in some of these colleges, and separate housing based on race, and separate orientation programs, and separate commencement programs, separate classes for black men at City University of New York, all based on one's race and gender. This is just racial idiocy. People, stop it.
All right.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: It's against the law.
Laura, we're almost out of time.

Well, you know, young people in high school have segregated themselves, and I think that still goes on in a lot of high schools today. You know, kids are more comfortable, you know, socializing and learning with kids that they are more comfortable with. But I don't think school should be in the business of doing it.
All right. Well…

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: When the schools do it, it's official action. Official.

Okay. On that note, got to wrap it up. Laura Washington, columnist for the Chicago Sun-Times, Bob Meadows, staff writer for People magazine, and Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition. Thank you all.
Thank you.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Thank you.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB MEADOWS (Staff Writer, People Magazine)
text: Thank you.

And next on NEWS & NOTES, you down with OPP? Well, the new book "Other People's Property" breaks down why rap is music to white ears. And Haiti and Ghana, two countries with one goal of independence. How they each won their freedom.
